title: The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: What God Wants Has Never Been Merely a Job Done
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a true scene. There was a brother who had served in his church for eighteen years. He was the coordinator of the worship team, a small-group leader, the general organiser of every conference. Wherever someone was missing, there he was. One year, at year’s end, the church held an appreciation evening for him. From the platform the pastor counted off, one by one, all the things he had done, and the congregation applauded again and again. When it was over, he sat alone in the emptied sanctuary and did not get up for a long time. Later he said something to the pastor: “Pastor, in these eighteen years I’ve done so many things. But suddenly I’m not so sure whether God and I still really know each other.”

Brothers and sisters, that sentence is like a needle. What it pierces is not only that brother’s heart, but the hearts of many of us.

It is very easy for us to understand “doing God’s will” as a task list: finish a job, hit a target, run a ministry well. As the items on the list are crossed off one by one, we assume we are drawing closer and closer to God. Yet from beginning to end the Bible shows us a deeper truth —

God’s will is not just about doing things; God’s will is about building relationships.

Look at Genesis. God made the heavens, the earth, the light, the sea, the birds and the beasts, and only last of all did he make man. When God made man, he did not first hand Adam a work schedule; he first breathed his own breath into him, and then walked with him himself in the garden. The first charge God gave Adam was not “This is how much you must get done”; it was that he should live in relationship. And the first thing God called “not good” was this: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). God made man not for work but for relationship; not to complete tasks, but to walk with him and to be connected with others.

Now look at the first thing God did after man fell. He did not begin by pronouncing a sentence. In “the cool of the day” he walked in the garden and called to the man, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9). Brothers and sisters, this is the first question God asks in the whole Bible, and it is a question about relationship. Of course God knew which tree Adam was hiding behind. God was not asking for coordinates. He was asking: How did things between us come to this?

Revival is the same. What is revival? We often think revival means lively meetings, packed sanctuaries, impressive numbers, visible results. But the revival the Bible speaks of has at its core “relationships restored” — our relationship with God, our relationship with ourselves, our relationships with one another, all established anew. In the last verse of the Old Testament, the prophet Malachi foretells the Elijah who is to come: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers” (Malachi 4:6). Do you see? God’s own definition of end-time revival is the repair of relationships.

So this morning we are going to enter together into a truth that lies at the very centre:

The centre of God’s will is building relationships.

In this lesson we will take three steps. First, we will see that doing God’s will is the starting point of building relationships. Second, we will see that doing God’s will brings our lives into eternal value. Third, we will learn the three levels of doing God’s will — living in it, dying in it, and passing it on.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Scenes
sections.html:
To receive today’s message accurately, we first need to know where our three theme passages come from. They come from three entirely different scenes, yet they point to the same centre.

The first is John 15:14.

The author of John’s Gospel is generally held to be John, the disciple whom the Lord loved. It was written around AD 80 to 90, to believers scattered far and wide who were already into their second generation. Chapter 15 belongs to the “Farewell Discourse” (John 13–17); the setting is after the Last Supper, on the way to the Garden of Gethsemane. The Lord Jesus knew that the hour for him to leave the world had come. He did not lay down a constitution for an organisation, nor did he hand out job assignments. He spoke of a vine: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Notice what the Lord says next: “You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you” (John 15:14). And straight after, in verse 15, the Lord says: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you” (John 15:15).

Brothers and sisters, see this key point: the Lord ties “doing” and “friends” together. The difference between a servant and a friend is not how much each one does; it is whether he knows his master’s heart. A servant follows orders; a friend understands intentions. The Lord says that if you do what he commands, you are raised from servants to friends — doing his will is the door into the relationship.

The second is Matthew 12:50.

Matthew’s Gospel is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, by Matthew, the tax collector who once sat at the tax booth. The scene in chapter 12 is Jesus teaching the crowds in a house, when someone tells him, “Behold, your mother and your brothers stand outside, seeking to speak to you.” Jesus answers, “Who is my mother? Who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand toward his disciples he says, “Behold, my mother and my brothers! For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother” (Matthew 12:48–50).

What a staggering statement. The Lord Jesus was not denying natural family ties — on the cross he still remembered to entrust his mother to John. The Lord was declaring a deeper truth: in the kingdom of God, the closest relationships rest not on blood but on “doing the Father’s will together”. Doing his will turns a crowd of strangers into one family.

The third is 1 John 2:17.

First John was written at about the same time as John’s Gospel, to the churches around Asia Minor. False teachers had already arisen, early Gnostic ideas were having their influence, and believers were wavering between “loving the world” and “loving the Father”. In the previous verse John speaks of “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life”, and then he says: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever” (1 John 2:17).

Three scenes, three identities: friends, family, people who remain forever. Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? All three verses are about relationships, not performance.

sections.heading: 1. Doing God’s Will Is the Starting Point of Building Relationships
sections.html:
“You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.” (John 15:14)

“For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50)

From Genesis to the New Testament, God keeps repeating one thing: he wants people to listen to his word.

Look at this clear thread running through it all —

Adam failed because he did not listen to God. God said to him, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and ate from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake.” (Genesis 3:17)

Abraham was blessed because he listened to God. “So Abram went, as Yahweh had told him.” (Genesis 12:4) A man of seventy-five left his country, his relatives and his father’s house, and set out for a place whose name he had not yet been told.

Israel was chosen in order to listen to God. “Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples; for all the earth is mine.” (Exodus 19:5)

Saul was rejected because he did not listen to God. Samuel said to him, “But now your kingdom will not continue. Yahweh has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and Yahweh has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which Yahweh commanded you.” (1 Samuel 13:14) Later Samuel put it even more plainly: “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: it wasn’t that Saul did nothing. He did a great deal — he fought battles, he offered sacrifices, he kept back the best of the sheep and cattle to offer to God. His ministry report looked splendid. What he failed at was not ministry but relationship. He would rather do “things that are good for God” according to his own judgement than do what God actually said. That is the self-centred life.

At the heart of all this history is not “right and wrong” but “relationship”.

To listen is to trust. To obey is to connect.

We need to see this clearly. How far a person is willing to listen to someone usually shows how far he trusts that person. You don’t hand the steering wheel to someone you don’t trust. So when a person is willing to do God’s word, he is not completing an order; he is responding to a relationship. He is saying: Lord, I trust you.

It is like a child listening to his father. A five-year-old at the roadside hears his father say, “Don’t move,” and he stops. He stops not because he has understood the traffic laws, but because he knows that voice, and he knows that voice loves him. Love and trust are the real fuel of obedience.

Turn it the other way round: the root of disobedience has never been a lack of information; it has been a broken relationship. In the Garden of Eden, it wasn’t that Eve didn’t know what God had said — she could recite God’s words. What the serpent did was first to shake her “trust” in God — “Has God really said …?” The serpent was hinting: God is hiding something from you; God doesn’t really have your good at heart. Once trust collapsed, obedience collapsed with it.

Psychology offers a fascinating piece of corroborating evidence here. In the 1950s and 1960s the British psychiatrist John Bowlby put forward attachment theory, and later his colleague Mary Ainsworth tested it with her “Strange Situation” experiment. A child who has formed a secure attachment with a caregiver is actually more willing to leave the mother and explore the world, and also more willing to respond when the mother calls. By contrast, insecurely attached children are not more obedient; they are more resistant and more disorganised. So it turns out that the capacity to obey grows out of a secure relationship. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order of the gospel: it is not that we obey first and then God loves us; it is that God first loved us, and so we are able to obey.

In 1995 the American psychologists Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary published their well-known paper on “the need to belong” in Psychological Bulletin, arguing that forming and maintaining relationships is one of the most fundamental human drives, no less powerful than the need for food. They studied human beings from a secular angle; the Bible had long since explained the reason at its source — man was made in the image of God, and God himself is a God in relationship: Father, Son and Holy Spirit, in perfect love from all eternity.

And here a 321 insight comes into view.

Obey God with the heart and you build the relationship; analyse God with the brain and you lose the relationship.

Brothers and sisters, many people “know a great deal” yet are “far from God”, because relying on the brain is not the same as relying on the heart. When the person who relies on the brain hears God’s word, the first reaction is to assess it: Is it reasonable? Is it worth it? What will others think? By the time the assessment is finished, the prompting of the Holy Spirit has passed. When the person who relies on the heart hears God’s word, the first reaction is to respond: Lord, I am willing.

The 321 vision puts it very clearly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be joyful, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Obedience is not a conclusion of the brain; obedience is a response of the heart. This morning, let me ask you one question: in recent days, has God said something to you that you are still “studying” but have never actually “gone and done”?

sections.heading: 2. Doing God’s Will Brings Our Lives into Eternal Value
sections.html:
“The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

This verse lays bare a staggering fact: everything in the world will pass away; only one thing is eternal — doing God’s will.

Why?

Because doing God’s will is not merely behaving correctly; it is “being connected in God”.

Notice that John’s wording here is unusual. He does not say “the deeds of doing God’s will remain forever”; he says that the “person” who does God’s will remains forever. In the original, the reference here is to the person, not the work. In other words, eternity is not stuck onto your results; eternity is stuck onto you as a person. It is not because what you do is so great, but because you yourself are connected to the Eternal One.

It is like a tree. A branch joined to the root has life and bears fruit; a branch cut off from the root withers and dies. When a branch has just been cut, it looks exactly like the branches still on the tree — just as green, just as leafy, perhaps even still in flower. The difference only shows after a few days. Brothers and sisters, our spiritual condition is like that too. A life cut off from God doesn’t wither at once; for a while it “seems fine”. That is exactly where the danger lies. The Lord could not have put it more clearly: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

A life connected to God endures; a life cut off from God is short-lived.

How did Jesus himself see this? By the well of Sychar he said to his disciples, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.” (John 4:34)

That day the Lord Jesus had walked a long road; he was tired and thirsty. The disciples came back from the town with food and urged him to eat. Yet the Lord said these words. Brothers and sisters, weigh this carefully: the Lord did not say “doing the Father’s will is my job”, nor “it is my responsibility”. He said, “my food”.

That means: doing God’s will is not a burden; it is life’s supply.

It is just like eating — eating isn’t pressure; eating is what sustains life. No one wakes up in the morning sighing, “Oh dear, three meals again today.” We don’t put meals on our to-do list as a chore, because eating is itself a pleasure, itself a source of strength. Brothers and sisters, if obeying God has always felt like a chore in your heart, that usually means one thing: we are still treating it as work, and we haven’t yet tasted that it is food.

Here is a spiritual comparison; keep it in your heart:

If a person doesn’t eat, the body grows weak; if a person doesn’t do God’s will, the spirit dries up.

In 2010 a team led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University in the United States published a large meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine. It brought together 148 studies and more than 300,000 participants, and found that people with strong social connections had roughly a 50 per cent greater likelihood of survival over the follow-up period than those with weak connections. Meanwhile the Harvard Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938 and running now for more than eighty years, has followed the health and happiness of several hundred men across their whole lives. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, sums it up in that now widely known conclusion: good relationships keep us happier and healthier.

Brothers and sisters, even these perishable bodies of ours were made according to the principle of “relationship” — when relationships are good, people live longer; when relationships break, people wither faster. How much more our souls? How much more our relationship with the everlasting God?

At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine says: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Those words were spoken sixteen hundred years ago, and they are still accurate today. The human heart was made to God’s measurements; put anything else in there and it will work loose, it will leak.

The 321 insight here is also very clear:

Doing God’s will is food for the spiritual life; not doing God’s will is famine for the spiritual life.

And the 321 vision speaks of a shift in perspective: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. First John 2:17 is the summary of all four shifts. The world and its lusts are earthly, temporary and worldly; the one who does God’s will is heavenly, eternal and godly. Brothers and sisters, the thing keeping you busy this morning — set it a hundred years from now, set it before the Lord’s judgement seat — how much of it will remain?

Here is a very practical test: spread out your diary for this week, and beside each item ask one question — “Does this connect me to God and to people, or does it pull me away from God and from people?” No need to rush to delete anything; first, mark it honestly. Simply seeing honestly is already the beginning of change.

sections.heading: 3. Three Levels of Doing God’s Will: Living in It, Dying in It, Passing It On
sections.html:
“Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24)

The Lord Jesus spoke these words in Passion Week. Some Greeks had come asking to see him, the disciples went to tell him, and the Lord answered, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” (John 12:23) Then he spoke of this grain of wheat. Brothers and sisters, the Lord put “being glorified” and “dying” in the same breath. It is the most counter-intuitive sentence in the world, and the most powerful.

Doing God’s will is not something you “do once”; it has three levels: living in it, dying in it, and passing it on.

The first level: living in God’s will

Living in God’s will means beginning to obey God, being willing to do what God says.

This is the starting point. Without this step, nothing that follows exists. But at this stage we often meet difficulty, struggle, and the challenge of circumstances.

Why? Because the moment obedience touches the ground, it runs into a cost. When Abraham heard God say, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house,” if he had merely agreed in his heart, nothing would have happened. The moment he set out, his tents, his livestock, his servants, his kinsmen, his standing, his sense of security — all of it had to move with him. Obedience has never been completed in the head; obedience is completed with the feet.

Moses was the same. Before the burning bush at Horeb he said “but” to God five times — Who am I? What shall I tell them your name is? They will not believe me. I have never been eloquent. Lord, please send someone else. Brothers and sisters, when we read it we think Moses was terribly long-winded, but to be honest, which of us isn’t like that? When God’s call comes, the first visitors to arrive in our hearts are often not joy but excuses.

So the most practical exercise in “living in God’s will” is to put “I am willing” before “I understand”. The Lord Jesus in Gethsemane gives us the best example: “Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done.” (Luke 22:42) He understood fully how bitter that cup was, and still he said, “yours, be done”.

The second level: dying in God’s will

Dying in God’s will means holding on to the end, not giving up because of circumstances.

Jesus on the cross is the most complete example. He did not merely “begin to obey”; he was “obedient to the end, even to death on a cross”. Paul describes it like this: “And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross.” (Philippians 2:8)

Notice the words “to the point of death”. If our obedience has a bottom line, that bottom line is our real master. Very often this is how we obey: I’ll obey, so long as it doesn’t affect my income; I’ll obey, so long as it doesn’t hurt my reputation; I’ll obey, so long as my family doesn’t object. Brothers and sisters, those “so long as” clauses are the parts of us that have not yet died.

Hebrews gives us a very deep sentence: “though he was a Son, yet learned obedience by the things which he suffered.” (Hebrews 5:8) Even the Son of God had to “learn” obedience, and learn it in suffering. How could we be the exception?

Psychologists have observed something similar in the secular sphere. In 2007 Angela Duckworth of the University of Pennsylvania and her colleagues published their research on “grit”. They followed new cadets at West Point through an extremely gruelling summer of training, and found that what predicted who would make it through was not their fitness scores, nor their academic entry scores, but “grit” — passion and unrelenting perseverance towards long-term goals. Brothers and sisters, even worldly training works this way: what decides the outcome is often not the ability to start, but the will to stay. How much more the road of the kingdom of heaven?

The German martyr-pastor Dietrich Bonhoeffer wrote that famous line in The Cost of Discipleship: “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Bonhoeffer was not theorising on paper. In April 1945 he was executed at Flossenbürg concentration camp, at only thirty-nine. He signed that sentence with his life.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person obeys up to a certain point and then stops, because going any further would touch the “self”. The selfless person can go all the way to the end, because there is no longer a “self” inside to protect.

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) When that grain of wheat falls into the ground and “dies”, it is not the end; it is the moment it can at last become a whole field of wheat.

The third level: passing on God’s will

Passing on God’s will means not only living it out yourself but also helping others to live it out.

Moses raised up Joshua. Yahweh said to Moses, “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit, and lay your hand on him.” (Numbers 27:18) Joshua was not parachuted in. He was the one who had followed Moses all through the forty years in the wilderness, who kept watch at the tent of meeting for Moses, who went up the mountain with Moses. Passing on is not handing over a post; passing on is handing over a life.

Jesus raised up disciples. “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach.” (Mark 3:14) Look at the order: first “that they might be with him”, then “send them out to preach”. Relationship first, ministry after. This is exactly what the 321 vision says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. For three and a half years the Lord Jesus was not running a training course; he was living life with them — walking together, eating together, getting into boats together, facing the wind and the waves together.

Paul raised up Timothy. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) There are four generations in this one verse: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and others. The nature of the gospel has never been one generation’s firework display; it is a relay, one baton after another.

This is life influencing life, life multiplying life.

And this is the key truth: true revival means life multiplying life. Not one person on fire, but a whole company of people raised up.

Let us come back to that grain of wheat. Sow one grain in the soil; it sprouts and comes into ear, and a single ear can usually yield thirty to fifty grains. And the original grain? You can no longer find it. Its husk has rotted in the soil; its nourishment has become root, become stalk, become new grain. Brothers and sisters, this is both the cost and the glory of passing it on: if you want to keep that one grain, you will only ever have that one grain; if you are willing to be buried, God will grow a whole field out of you.

In the 1960s the psychologist Albert Bandura put forward social learning theory, and with his famous “Bobo doll” experiment he showed that children learn behaviour not mainly from being lectured but from observing and imitating the role models they see. In the early 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma in Italy discovered “mirror neurons” in the monkey brain — when a monkey watches another perform an action, the area activated in its brain is the very same as when it performs that action itself. When God made us, he built this “imitation” circuitry into us. No wonder Paul dared to say, “Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.” (1 Corinthians 11:1)

This is precisely why passing it on cannot be done by courses but only by life: people can’t learn what you say; people can learn what you live.

The 321 insight is sharpest of all here:

Only the selfless can pass it on; the self-centred stop at themselves.

The self-centred person cares only about what he gains; the selfless person is willing to let his life be used to build others up. The self-centred person is afraid of others overtaking him, so he holds something back; the selfless person longs for others to overtake him, so he empties out everything he has. Brothers and sisters, if you want to see whether someone is truly selfless, there is a very accurate test: see whether he can sincerely rejoice in someone else’s success.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Placing This Lesson Back within the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s message back within the framework of the 321 vision, we see it even more clearly.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me”; he obeyed to the end, even to death on the cross; he raised up twelve disciples. Living in it, dying in it, passing it on: the Lord himself walked all three levels to the end. The Bible is my standard — we do not judge by feelings what God’s will is; we first go back to God’s word: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) The Holy Spirit is my guide — God’s will is not worked out by analysis; it is confirmed within us by the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the battle over obedience is, in the end, a battle over the throne. It is not me sitting on the throne issuing orders and keeping God on as a consultant; it is letting Jesus truly reign as King. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when that grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, the field of wheat that grows up is not there to prove itself; it is there to glorify the God who made it grow.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, God’s system is not piled up out of organisational charts; it grows out of one healthy relationship after another. Living in his will is our relationship with God; dying in his will is our relationship with ourselves; passing on his will is our relationship with others. This is exactly the priority of relationships the 321 vision speaks of: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

The fivefold change is here too. When the mindset changes, I no longer see God’s will as a task list but as a road of relationship. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; once daily living changes, relationships change; once relationships change, ministry changes naturally. The order must never be reversed. The mistake we have so often made is trying to use ministry to drive relationships, and busyness to prove life. The result: the bigger the ministry, the emptier the person.

Then there is the 920 practice. 920 means this: every person we are in relationship with is our “2”; before that person we practise living the selfless life, which is the “0”; and what grows from it is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, if this lesson’s practice is to touch the ground, the most natural place is 920: today, whom has God placed in front of you? That person is your “2”. Are you living out the “0” towards him or her?

Then there are the 235 relationships. Becoming a “2” with someone selfless is having a spiritual companion; building a “3” is spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” is a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Today’s third level, “passing it on”, is in fact 235 put into practice — Moses and Joshua are a “3”; Jesus and the Twelve are a “5”; Paul and Timothy are both a “3” and a “5”.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Saul’s failure was exactly a leaving of his originally intended position; the Lord Jesus’ victory was exactly a returning to it. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: From Doing Things to Building Relationships
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three very practical exercises. We will set them within “the eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they are not just three good ideas but can truly grow into our lives.

Exercise 1: Every day, ask yourself one question — right now, am I doing a task, or building a relationship?

In ministry, at home, at work, stop and ask yourself: is my seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing right now drawing the relationship closer, or pushing it further away?

How to practise: every evening, take one minute to look back over three things, and check whether they “made the relationship better”.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: first, remember today’s sentence — the centre of God’s will is building relationships. Put it on your phone’s home screen or on the dinner table.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you “see” in one concrete situation — so the way I answered just now was doing a task, not building a relationship. Information is knowing; revelation is being illuminated.

Conviction: sincerely acknowledge that “people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things” — no longer just agreeing with your lips.

Implementation: start that one-minute review this very evening; don’t wait until next Monday.

Evaluation: after a week, look back — which day was the most distant? What was I busy with at the time?

Correction: identify the one time of day when you most easily “let the task replace the person”, and adjust it.

Repetition: do it for forty days in a row. A change of mindset has never been a one-off decision; it is formed by repetition.

Multiplication: bring this one-minute exercise to your family or your small group, and do it together with someone.

Exercise 2: Practise “obeying with the heart” rather than “analysing with the brain”

When God’s word comes to you, don’t first analyse whether it is “reasonable or not”; first respond: Lord, I am willing.

How to practise: each day choose one verse, and that day deliberately live it out. For example, “be swift to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19): deliberately practise listening in your conversations.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: each morning choose one verse, copy it onto paper and carry it with you.

Revelation: don’t ask, “What does this verse mean?” Ask, “Lord, in which matter today do you want me to live this out?”

Conviction: admit that in the past you have often substituted analysis for obedience, and confess it to the Lord.

Implementation: that same day, find the person you find hardest to listen to, and practise being “swift to hear, slow to speak”.

Evaluation: in the evening, write down honestly: today, did I keep quiet when I should have kept quiet?

Correction: if you failed, try again tomorrow with the same verse; don’t change the subject.

Repetition: one verse can be practised for a whole week. Depth matters more than quantity.

Multiplication: share this week’s verse and your story with one person, and invite them to choose a verse too.

Exercise 3: Deliberately build a relationship rather than complete a task

Today, reach out to one person: a phone call, a word of encouragement, a listening ear. The aim is not to “solve the problem” but to “let the other person feel loved”.

How to practise: every day, show care to at least one person — a family member, a co-worker or a friend.

Deepening it through the eight stages:

Information: write down three names — the “2”s God has placed on your heart.

Revelation: ask the Lord to let you see that person’s real need right now, not the need you assume they have.

Conviction: believe that “letting the other person feel loved” is itself ministry, not extra work on top of ministry.

Implementation: make that phone call today. Don’t send a message — phone; a voice carries warmth.

Evaluation: was I in a hurry to give advice? Did I really listen to the end?

Correction: next time, listen for three minutes before you speak.

Repetition: take turns caring for those three names, and keep it up for a whole season.

Multiplication: when that person is touched by God’s love, invite them to go and care for someone too — this is life multiplying life.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, many people work hard all their lives doing a great many things, yet neglect the most important thing — relationships.

Don’t lose people for the sake of tasks; don’t lose connection for the sake of getting things done.

What God values is not how much you have done, but whether you walk with him in love and stay connected with others.

There is a saying generally attributed to Mother Teresa: “We cannot do great things, only small things with great love.” The reason it moves people is that it shifts the focus from “the size of the task” to “the depth of the love”.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters,

God’s will is not a task list; it is a road of relationship.

When you truly grasp this, your whole life will change —

The focus is no longer “how much I do”, but “how deeply I love”.

The focus is no longer “what I complete”, but “whom I connect with”.

Let us think once more about the brother in our introduction. Eighteen years of service were not in vain; God will surely remember every bit he offered. What he truly needed was not to stop serving, but to put the order back in place: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When he is connected to the Lord again, everything he did in those eighteen years will turn from “performance” into “fruit”; from the earthly and temporary into the heavenly and eternal.

The Lord Jesus said, “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) The definition of eternal life is “knowing” — it is relationship.

So this morning I want to extend three invitations to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let Jesus be King over your obedience. No longer do I decide whether to obey only after I’ve finished assessing; he speaks, and I go.

Second, let Jesus be King over your perseverance. No longer do I keep walking only when circumstances allow; I am that grain of wheat, willingly falling into the ground.

Third, let Jesus be King over your passing it on. No longer caring only about what I gain, but entrusting what I have received to faithful people who will be able to teach others.

May our whole lives be not merely about completing a mission, but about building eternal relationships in God, living out Christ, and becoming overcomers.

May all the glory go to our Lord Jesus Christ.

keyVerses: “You are my friends, if you do whatever I command you.” (John 15:14)
“For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50)
“The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)
declarations: Lord!
I will no longer be just someone who gets things done; I will be someone who builds relationships.
I choose to obey you with my heart, and no longer to analyse you with my brain.
I will live in your will, die in your will, and pass on your will.
Let my life be not merely about getting things done, but about being connected to you, influencing others, and bearing eternal fruit.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Deliberately build a relationship rather than complete a task
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we are still before you.

Lord, please forgive us — we have so often substituted busyness for closeness, results for obedience, and ministry for relationship. We have done a great many things, yet grown like strangers before you. Lord, we want to turn back.
Give us a heart that obeys with the heart, and take away our habit of analysing you with our brains. When you speak a word, let us answer with a word: Lord, I am willing.
Help us to live in your will and not draw back in difficulty; help us to die in your will and not turn aside before the cost; help us to pass on your will, handing our lives on to the next person.
Lord, make us that grain of wheat that willingly falls into the ground. May every person we care for today come a little closer to you because of us.
Your will be done; your name be glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my brother, and sister, and mother.” (Matthew 12:50) Looking back over this year, in what area have you been “doing a lot, yet far from God”? What has made you treat God’s will as a task list rather than a road of relationship?

“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” (John 12:24) Of the three levels — living in it, dying in it, passing it on — which one have you reached so far? Is there a specific person to whom God wants you to begin passing on your life?
l147.title: The Centre of God’s Will Is Building Relationships
l147.subtitle: Live in His Will, Die in His Will, Pass On His Will
l147.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: Are You Walking in God’s Will?
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

There was a sister who had served in her church for twelve years. She led the choir, ran the administration, did the visiting; whenever anyone asked, she never said no. One early morning she was sitting in her car, hands on the steering wheel, and suddenly she burst into tears. She said, “I’ve done everything, but I don’t know what I’m doing. My husband and I have nothing to say to each other, my son avoids me, and with God it feels as if there’s a pane of glass between us. Am I walking in God’s will at all?”

Brothers and sisters, this is not a question asked by a lazy person. It is a question asked by someone extremely busy and extremely earnest. What she was asking is really a question hidden in many of our hearts:

What exactly is God’s will? How do I know whether I am walking in it?

We often imagine God’s will to be like a sealed envelope hidden in some drawer in heaven. We have to pray long enough, fast devoutly enough, receive some special confirmation, and only then will God hand us the envelope. And so many people spend their whole lives “searching for” God’s will, yet rarely “live” in it.

But in the last lesson we saw that the heart of God’s will is building relationships. Today we will go a layer deeper — God’s will is not hidden, nor is it complicated. He revealed it long ago, plainly and clearly, in the Bible.

The problem has never been “not knowing”; the problem is “whether we live it out”.

In this lesson we will distil God’s will into a single word, and then put that word into practice as a single thing:

God’s will can be summed up in one thing, and that is love; and the practical expression of love is building relationships.

Brothers and sisters, please listen carefully to this sentence, because today’s whole lesson revolves around it: you do not first find God’s will and then go and love. The moment you begin to love, you are already walking in God’s will.

In the 321 vision this is called a change of mindset. The second of the Three Foundations is “the Bible is my standard”. Since the Bible is the standard, God’s will is not something to guess at by feelings; it is settled by his word. God has already written down his heart — in the Law, in the Prophets, and finally in the life of his Son. What we have to do is not uncover a secret but obey a command that has already been made public.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. This morning, may the Holy Spirit first change our mindset about “God’s will”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, Three Scenes, One Centre
sections.html: To understand today’s message correctly, let us first set out clearly the background of our three main passages. The first step in letting Scripture interpret Scripture is to put each passage back in its original place.

sections.heading: 1. Matthew 22: The Last Debate in the Temple
sections.html:
Matthew is the first of the four Gospels. It is generally held to have been written by the apostle Matthew, a former tax collector, sometime between AD 50 and 70, mainly for Jewish readers. That is why Matthew loves to quote the Old Testament: he wants to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament.

The scene of Matthew 22 is the temple in Jerusalem, in the week before Jesus’ passion. That day one group after another took its turn: the Pharisees came to ask whether it was lawful to pay taxes to Caesar; the Sadducees came to ask whose wife a woman with seven husbands would be in the resurrection; finally a lawyer stood up to test him: “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?” (Matthew 22:36)

We need to know that the Jewish rabbis of the time counted the Law of Moses as 613 commandments, 248 of them “thou shalts” and 365 “thou shalt nots”. The rabbis often debated which was the weightiest and which the lightest. Among them this question was an endlessly disputed puzzle, and also a trap — whichever commandment Jesus picked, he would offend one group or another.

Jesus did not pick one out of the 613. He compressed the whole Law and the Prophets into two: love God, love people. The first line he quoted comes from Deuteronomy 6:5 — the Shema, which Jews recited every morning and evening; the second comes from Leviticus 19:18. Jesus put these two verses together and said that on them the whole law and the prophets “depend”.

The word behind “depend” in the original (Greek kremannymi) literally means “to hang”: the whole Law and the Prophets hang like a door on two hinges. If the hinges are crooked, the whole door won’t open. Brothers and sisters, the Bible is not a list of 613 rules; the Bible is a door that opens onto God, and that door hangs on two words — love God, love people.

sections.heading: 2. John 13: The New Commandment in the Upper Room
sections.html:
John’s Gospel was written by the apostle John, generally thought to be in the AD 80s or 90s, for readers throughout the world. Its purpose is stated plainly in John 20:31: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.”

John 13 is the beginning of the “Upper Room Discourse”. It was the night of the Passover, and Jesus knew that the hour for him to leave the world had come. The first thing he did was take off his outer garment, wrap a towel around himself and wash his disciples’ feet — including the feet of Judas, who was about to betray him. When the feet had been washed, Judas went out, and Scripture says, “It was night.” (John 13:30) It was on that darkest of nights that Jesus gave his new commandment.

Someone may ask: loving one another was already there in the Old Testament (Leviticus 19:18), so why call it a “new” commandment? The word “new” in the original (Greek kainos) does not mean new in time but new in nature, new in quality. What is new about it? It is new in that phrase “just as I have loved you” — the standard of love is no longer “as yourself” but “as the Lord”. The kind of love with which he washed his disciples’ feet, the kind of love with which he laid down his life for them — that is how we are to love one another.

sections.heading: 3. 1 Corinthians 13: A Prescription for a Church in Chaos
sections.html:
First Corinthians was written by the apostle Paul around AD 55, while he was preaching in Ephesus, to the church in Corinth. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, a port city — thriving in trade, crowded with idols, morally corrupt. That church had a very peculiar feature: it was extremely rich in spiritual gifts, yet extremely divided. They formed factions and quarrelled — one said, “I belong to Paul,” another, “I belong to Apollos”; they took one another to court; at their shared meals some got drunk while others went hungry; they argued over which was greater, tongues or prophecy.

Paul spoke about gifts and the members of the body in chapter 12 and about order in worship in chapter 14, and in between he inserted chapter 13 — introducing it with the words, “I show a most excellent way to you.” (1 Corinthians 12:31) Brothers and sisters, 1 Corinthians 13 is not a prose poem for weddings; it is the surgeon’s scalpel handed to a church that had fallen into uproar. Paul was speaking to a group of people who were richly gifted but had no love.

Three books, three scenes: a debate in the temple, a dark night in the upper room, a church in chaos in a port city. The three scenes differ, but the centre is one and the same — love, and the relationships love builds.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the 321 shift in perspective: from man’s perspective, we assess whether a person is spiritual by how much they do; from God’s perspective, he assesses a person by how truly they love. From the earthly perspective, ministry is a report card; from the heavenly perspective, relationships are the eternal assets.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: God’s Will Has Been Made Plain — Love God, Love People
sections.html:
“…know his will, and approve the things that are excellent, being instructed out of the law.” (Romans 2:18)

“ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” (Matthew 22:37–40)

sections.heading: 1. God’s Will Is Not a Secret but a Revelation
sections.html:
In the context of Romans 2, Paul is speaking to Jews who boasted. He says that you “bear the name of a Jew, rest on the law, glory in God, know his will … being instructed out of the law” (Romans 2:17–18). Notice Paul’s logic: they knew God’s will not because they were more spiritual, but because they had God’s word. The channel for knowing God’s will is God’s word.

The word “know” in the original (Greek ginosko) is a knowing that comes from acquaintance. And Paul’s rebuke that follows is very severe: you know, but you do not do it (Romans 2:21–23). So Romans 2:18 is, on the one hand, grace — God has already made it plain; on the other hand, responsibility — once it has been made plain, it must be done.

Brothers and sisters, many people say to God in prayer, “Lord, please tell me your will.” In heaven God probably answers something like this: “My child, I’ve already said it, and I’ve written it down. Have you read it? Having read it, have you done it?”

In fact the Bible three times uses the direct formula “this is the will of God”:

“For this is the will of God: your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality.” (1 Thessalonians 4:3)

“Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In everything give thanks, for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus toward you.” (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)

“For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men.” (1 Peter 2:15)

Being holy, always rejoicing, praying without ceasing, giving thanks in everything, doing good — not one of these is about “which school should I go to, whom should I marry, should I change jobs”. God’s will is not mainly about a script he has written for me; it is about the kind of person he wants me to become. When you become that kind of person, many choices become clear of their own accord.

And the sum of it all, Jesus put in just two sentences: love God, love people.

sections.heading: 2. Two Commandments, One Order
sections.html:
Jesus’ answer has an order, and it must not be reversed. The greatest is to love God; the second is to love people. This order is the priority of relationships the 321 vision speaks of: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Why must loving God come first? Because love has to have a source. First John 4:19 says, “We love him, because he first loved us.” We are not power stations of love; we are transformers of love. If the power station isn’t generating, the newest transformer is just a metal box.

Yet Jesus said the second is “likewise”, meaning the two are of the same nature and bound together in weight. So 1 John 4:20 puts it very bluntly: “If a man says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” Loving God is the root; loving people is the fruit. You can’t want the root without the fruit, nor pick the fruit and say you have no need of the root.

sections.heading: 3. Jesus Adds One More: Love One Another
sections.html:
Beyond the two great commandments, on the night he left the world the Lord gave his disciples one more, still more concrete command:

“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” (John 13:34)

“By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35)

The Lord did not say, “Everyone will know that you are my disciples because you can preach, heal the sick and build great churches.” He said: because you love one another. Love is the Christian’s identity badge.

So these three commands — love God, love people, love one another — have only one word at their heart: love.

sections.heading: 4. A Reminder: Can Love Be Commanded?
sections.html:
Some say love is a feeling, and how can a feeling be commanded? But love in the Bible (Greek agape) is first of all not an emotion but a choice of the will and an offering of action. John 3:16 says God “loved” the world, and the next verb is “gave”; 1 John 3:18 says, “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” Love can be commanded, because love can be chosen.

Brothers and sisters, here is an illustration from daily life. The most dangerous sentence in a marriage is “I just don’t feel anything for him any more.” The marriage expert John Gottman ran a marriage laboratory at the University of Washington in the United States, where for many years couples’ interactions were videotaped and analysed. His research with Levenson (Gottman & Levenson, 1992) found that the stability of a marriage could be predicted from the ratio of positive to negative interactions between husband and wife; stable marriages kept to roughly five to one. Notice: that five to one is not a feeling but behaviour — one more word of appreciation, one less sneer; one more turning towards the other, one less turning away. Feelings follow behaviour; behaviour does not follow feelings.

God’s commands are the same. He doesn’t tell us to “wait until we feel it and then love”; he says, “Go and love first, and the feelings will catch up.”

sections.heading: 5. The Key Truth: God’s Will Is Living in Love
sections.html:
So we can write down the conclusion of today’s first key point:

God’s will means living in love.

Not how much you do, but how genuinely you love.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine has a prayer usually rendered: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The human heart is built for relationship; away from love, a person is always caught in a kind of agitation — and trying to fill it with more service only makes us more exhausted.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Loving with the Heart, or Working with the Brain?
sections.html:
The 321 vision has a saying that cuts to the heart: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you will be joyful, rely on the brain and you will be troubled. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Love with the heart and you are in God’s will; work with the brain and you easily drift away from God.

Brothers and sisters, we must honestly face a phenomenon: many people are busy serving yet have no love, and as a result the more they do the more tired they become, and the further their relationships drift. The psychologist Christina Maslach has studied occupational burnout since the 1980s. She identifies three core features of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (treating people as cases to be processed), and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. The second deserves our special vigilance — when someone who serves begins to treat brothers and sisters as “work items” rather than as “people”, burnout has already begun.

This is exactly what the 321 vision says: people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. Life first, then relationships, then ministry. If the order is reversed, ministry will devour relationships, and once relationships collapse, life withers.

The Lord Jesus’ rebuke to the church in Ephesus deserves a place in the heart of every busy servant: “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance … But I have this against you, that you left your first love.” (Revelation 2:2, 4) The works, the toil, the perseverance were all there, but the love was gone. Brothers and sisters, this morning let us rather do a little less than love a little less.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Without Love, Every Spiritual Act Loses Its Value
sections.html: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal. If I have the gift of prophecy, and know all mysteries and all knowledge; and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but don’t have love, I am nothing. If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3)

sections.heading: 1. Three “Ifs”, Three Times Back to Zero
sections.html:
What Paul lists in these three verses is not the low bar of the spiritual life but the highest of the high:

Speaking with the languages of men and of angels — the summit of spiritual gifts.

Having the gift of prophecy, knowing all mysteries and all knowledge, having all faith so as to remove mountains — the summit of revelation, knowledge and faith.

Giving away all one’s goods to feed the poor, and giving one’s body to be burned — the summit of giving and sacrifice.

Then after each one Paul adds the same phrase: “but don’t have love”. And the result?

Gifts without love, and I have become sounding brass, a clanging cymbal — sound, but no life. In the pagan temples around Corinth, worship came with the beating of gongs and clashing of cymbals, a deafening din. Paul is in effect saying: if your gifted performance on the platform has no love, then to God’s ears it is no different from the noise in a heathen temple.

Knowledge without love, and I am nothing (literally, “I am zero”).

Giving without love, and it profits me nothing. Notice the wording here: it may still be of some benefit to others — the poor did get a meal after all — but “it profits me nothing”; before God, I gain nothing at all.

Brothers and sisters, these three verses are like three bolts of lightning. They give us a staggering spiritual equation: any number multiplied by zero gives zero. Gifts are a number, knowledge is a number, giving is a number; love is the multiplier. If the multiplier is zero, however big the numbers in front of it, it makes no difference.

Earlier in the same letter Paul had already said: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” (1 Corinthians 8:1)

sections.heading: 2. What God Values
sections.html:
So what does this mean?

Gifts without love have no value; knowledge without love has no meaning; giving without love still profits nothing.

What God values is not what you have done, but whether there is love within you.

Why? Because the essence of love is relationship. Gifts can operate without any relationship — you can preach into a microphone without knowing a single person in the room; you can send off a sum of money without knowing the name of the person who receives it. But love can’t. Love must have someone to love; love must enter the other person’s world. The essence of love is relationship.

sections.heading: 3. Two Pictures: A Lamp without Power, a Body without Life
sections.html:
Service without love is like a lamp with no electricity. The shade is beautiful, the base is top quality, the design is the latest, yet the room is still dark. For a lamp’s value lies not in the lamp itself but in whether it is connected to the power supply.

Service without love is also like a body without life. All the features are there, the limbs are whole, the clothes are neatly worn, but there is no breath. The form is right; the life is gone.

This is exactly the vision the prophet Ezekiel saw: a valley full of bones; “the bones came together, bone to its bone”, with sinews, flesh and skin, “but there was no breath in them” (Ezekiel 37:7–8). Only when breath entered them did they live: “and they lived, and stood up on their feet” (Ezekiel 37:10). Brothers and sisters, an organisation can be made to stand up by management, but a church can only come alive by life and love.

sections.heading: 4. Obedience Is the Fruit of Remaining in Love
sections.html:
“If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love; even as I have kept my Father’s commandments, and remain in his love.” (John 15:10)

This verse sits within the parable of the vine. The Lord first says, “Remain in me” (John 15:4), and then says that keeping his commandments means remaining in his love. The order is clear: connection first, fruit after; relationship first, behaviour after.

Obeying God is not the pressure of law; it is the fruit of remaining in love.

Here is a spiritual comparison everyone understands: if a child loves his parents, his obedience is not a burden but something natural. You will never see a five-year-old calculating in his heart, “Shall I keep my promise to Mum today? I need to weigh up the pros and cons.” He simply loves his mum, so his mum’s wishes are his direction.

By contrast, a child who has only fear of his parents and no love gives an obedience that is a performance: obedient while the grown-ups are there, disobedient once they are gone.

Brothers and sisters, which kind is your obedience? True obedience flows out of love.

Paul puts it vividly: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision amounts to anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.” (Galatians 5:6) If faith is not working through love, that faith has not yet reached where it ought to go.

sections.heading: 5. Psychology’s Confirmation: The Pain of Rejection Is Like Physical Pain
sections.html:
God made us for relationship, and even our brains bear witness to it. In a study published in the journal Science in 2003, Naomi Eisenberger of the University of California, Los Angeles and her colleagues had participants play a virtual ball-tossing game, during which the participant was suddenly left out by the other players. Brain scans showed that the brain region active during social exclusion (the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) overlapped heavily with the region active during physical pain.

In other words, the pain of a broken relationship travels the same neural pathway in the brain as the pain of a bodily injury. That is how God made us: being rejected really hurts. Since God made us this way, we can understand all the better why the centre of his will is relationship — and all the better why one cold word can leave such a long-lasting wound in a brother’s or sister’s heart.

sections.heading: 6. Applying the 321 Vision: Only Selflessness Can Truly Love
The 321 vision says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.
sections.html:
Only selflessness can truly love; with the self-centred life, love turns into a transaction.

Self-centred love asks, “What do I get?” Selfless love asks, “What can I give?”

Self-centred love says: I love you because you give me face, security and returns; the moment you stop supplying these, my love withdraws. That isn’t love; that is an investment, complete with a profit-and-loss statement.

Selfless love says: I love you because Christ first loved me; my love doesn’t draw from you, it draws from the Lord. Only this kind of love is stable, because its source is not in people who can run dry.

When Paul describes this love he says: “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil.” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5) Notice the phrase in the middle — “doesn’t seek its own way”. Those words are selflessness itself.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. As Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, there is a saying generally attributed to Mother Teresa: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love. What we are to learn today is not how to make our deeds bigger, but how to make our love real.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: Building Relationships Is the Standard for Whether We Are in God’s Will
sections.html: “…even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we would be holy and without defect before him in love, having predestined us for adoption as children through Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his desire.” (Ephesians 1:4–5)

sections.heading: 1. The Purpose of Salvation: Not Only Forgiveness, but Restored Relationship
sections.html:
Ephesians 1:4–5 is the deepest passage in the whole Bible on God’s eternal purpose. Paul uses two key terms here: “chose” and “adoption as children”.

“Adoption” in the original (Greek huiothesia) is a term from Roman law, meaning formal adoption. In the Roman Empire, a person who was legally adopted had his old debts wiped out and his old identity brought completely to an end; from then on he held the full family standing and inheritance rights of his new father.

See clearly what God is aiming at: he saves us not merely to release us from prison and leave it there, but to bring us into his home. Forgiveness is the paperwork; adoption as children is the purpose.

God’s purpose in redeeming us is not only forgiveness but restoring and building relationship.

And notice: all this was settled “before the foundation of the world”. In other words, God’s desire to build a relationship with us is older than the universe, older than sin, older than our failures.

sections.heading: 2. Seeing from Genesis: We Were Made for Relationship
sections.html:
“Yahweh God said, ‘It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make him a helper comparable to him.’ ” (Genesis 2:18)

In Genesis 1, seven times “God saw that it was good”; yet in chapter 2 the first “not good” appears. Notice: at that point there was no sin yet. Everything in Eden was perfect. The only thing God called “not good” was being “alone”.

God created man for relationship: relationship with God and relationship with others.

“Alone” in Hebrew (from the root related to badad) carries the sense of isolation and separation. Man was made in the image of God, and God himself, in the Trinity, is relationship — the eternal love and fellowship of Father, Son and Holy Spirit. So man, made in God’s image, is by nature a relational being.

Science confirms this from another angle. In 2010 Julianne Holt-Lunstad of Brigham Young University in the United States and her colleagues published a meta-analysis in the journal PLoS Medicine that pooled data from 148 studies and more than 300,000 participants. They found that people with stronger social connections had a survival rate roughly 50 per cent higher than those with weak social connections. The researchers pointed out that the health risk of lacking social connection is comparable to recognised risk factors such as smoking and excessive drinking.

Brothers and sisters, today happens to be Lesson 148, and that study happened to pool 148 studies. This is of course only a coincidence, but the coincidence reminds us of a serious fact: when God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone,” it wasn’t just a poetic line; it is a truth bearing on the survival of body and soul.

sections.heading: 3. The Essence of Sin: Breaking Relationship
sections.html:
“The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’ ” (Genesis 3:12)

Man’s first reaction after sinning was not repentance but shifting the blame. And listen carefully to Adam’s words: in one sentence he offends two parties — “the woman whom you gave to be with me”: first he blames God, then his wife. Only a chapter earlier he had exulted, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23); now he says “the woman whom you gave”, and doesn’t even use her name.

The moment sin came in, relationships collapsed on every side:

The relationship with God broke — when they heard God’s voice, they “hid themselves … among the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8).

The relationship with others broke — Adam accused Eve.

The relationship with themselves broke — they found they were naked and began to feel shame.

The relationship with creation broke — the ground was cursed for his sake and yielded thorns and thistles (Genesis 3:17–18).

This is the essence of sin: breaking relationship.

Brothers and sisters, we usually measure sin with a checklist of behaviours: lying, greed, anger. But the Bible measures sin by relationship: does this push me away from God or draw me closer? Does it push me away from people or connect me with them?

sections.heading: 4. The Substance of Salvation: Restoring Relationship
sections.html:
But God’s salvation is the restoring of relationship. God called out in the garden, “Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9) — the first question God asks in the whole Bible, in which the one who had been forsaken spoke first, seeking the one who had forsaken him.

“I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people.” (Leviticus 26:12)

This phrase, “I will be your God, and you will be my people”, is the Bible’s covenant formula. It stretches from Leviticus and Jeremiah all the way to Revelation 21:3: “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” The Bible begins with walking together in Eden and ends with living together in the new heaven and new earth, and the thread between has only one strand — God wants to be with people.

“But if we walk in the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from all sin.” (1 John 1:7)

Notice John’s wording: the result of walking in the light is not “we become holier” but “we have fellowship with one another”. Fellowship (Greek koinonia) means holding in common, sharing, communion. When our relationship with God is restored, our relationships with people will surely be restored with it. This is the structure of the cross: the vertical beam joins God and man; the horizontal beam joins person to person.

“He who keeps his commandments remains in him, and he in him. By this we know that he remains in us, by the Spirit which he gave us.” (1 John 3:24)

Remaining in God — this is the highest expression of relationship. Not visiting, not clocking in, but living within.

sections.heading: 5. The Key Conclusion: Relationship Is the Standard
sections.html:
And so we arrive at a very practical spiritual standard:

Whatever builds relationship is God’s will; whatever breaks relationship is not God’s will.

Brothers and sisters, you can put this standard to use straight away. Today, facing a decision, a message, a sentence you are about to say, you don’t need to wait for a special vision. Just ask one question: will doing this build the relationship or break it?

Of course, we must be clear in our discernment: building relationships is not the same as pleasing people, nor is it the same as tolerating sin. Paul once opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11); that was for the truth of the gospel, and the aim was still to preserve unity. Truth and love are not opposites; the Bible tells us to be “speaking truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). The principle is: the truth must not be compromised, and the manner must not wound.

sections.heading: 6. Even Forgiveness Is a Matter of Relationship
sections.html:
“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you don’t forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” (Matthew 6:14–15)

These two verses come straight after the Lord’s Prayer. The Lord’s Prayer contains seven petitions in all, and the Lord Jesus singled out just this one — forgiveness — to explain further. You can see how much weight he gives it.

To forgive is to restore relationship; not to forgive is to sever relationship.

What makes unforgiveness so dreadful is that it cuts two lines at once: the horizontal line breaks, and we stop having anything to do with the other person; the vertical line tightens with it, and things with God no longer flow freely either. This is exactly what the 321 vision means by “pride provokes pride, and both sides lose” — I won’t be the first to bow my head, and you won’t either, so we both stand our ground and the relationship dies along with us. Conversely, “humility inspires humility, and both sides win”: as long as one person first lays down their rights and returns to their originally intended position, a door appears in that wall.

Medical research also sees the cost of unforgiveness. An experiment by Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet and colleagues at Hope College in the United States, published in the journal Psychological Science in 2001, found that when participants were led to recall and hold on to unforgiving thoughts, their blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose markedly; and when they were led to recall the same event with empathy and forgiveness, these physiological stress responses dropped significantly.

Brothers and sisters, we often say, “If I don’t forgive him, he’ll be the one who suffers.” The truth is, he is sleeping very well; the one who suffers is you. The Bible’s commands are never meant to deprive us but to protect us: “And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you.” (Ephesians 4:32)

sections.heading: 7. Applying the 321 Vision: The Focus Is Not Right and Wrong but Relationship
The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.
sections.html:
So in conflict, the focus is not right and wrong but relationship; the focus is not winning or losing but connection.

This is not to say right and wrong don’t matter. It is to say that when you focus on “I must prove I’m right”, you put yourself at the centre — that is the self-centred life. When you focus on Jesus, you will ask: Lord, what do you want to build in this situation? That is selflessness.

The Lord Jesus said: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23–24) Look at the Lord’s order: first repair the relationship, then come back and worship. God would rather leave your gift unreceived for a while than not have you go and reconnect that relationship first. Life first, then relationships, then ministry — this is how the Lord himself taught it.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Love Is the Lifeblood of the System
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, when we place today’s message within the framework of the 321 vision, we will see it more completely.

sections.heading: 1. The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal
sections.html:
The first of the Three Foundations is “Jesus is my role model”. The standard of love is not our experience but his life. He said, “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” He washed his disciples’ feet, and he washed the feet of the man who betrayed him; on the cross he prayed for those who crucified him. This is the standard and the height of our love.

The second of the Three Foundations is “the Bible is my standard”. God’s will doesn’t need guessing; it is written in the Bible. Love God, love people, love one another — in black and white. We don’t wait for some special prompting before we love; we love according to the command already written.

The third of the Three Foundations is “the Holy Spirit is my guide”. Because by ourselves we simply cannot produce love. Romans 5:5 says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.” Love isn’t squeezed out; it is poured in. Galatians 5:22 says that the first fruit the Spirit bears is love.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. Letting Jesus reign as King in our relationships means that in every relationship his heart counts for more than my emotions. Letting him receive the glory in conflict means I would rather lose face than let the Lord’s name be put to shame.

The Goal: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, a system is made up of relationships, and relationships are held together by love. So love is the lifeblood of God’s system. If the blood doesn’t circulate, even the sturdiest body will die.

sections.heading: 2. The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness
sections.html:
The self-centred life wants to prove itself, protect itself and expand itself, and so relationships become a battlefield. Selflessness returns to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God — and so relationships become an altar.

Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. The most common pride in relationships is “I have to be the one who’s right”. Without realising it, we have sat down in the judge’s seat — and that seat is God’s alone.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. One of Satan’s specialities is tearing relationships apart — his name (Greek diabolos) originally means “accuser, one who sets people against each other”. In Eden he tore man away from God; in Cain he tore person from person. So every time we choose to forgive, choose to repair, we are rebuilding on the very spot he tore down.

sections.heading: 3. The Fivefold Change
sections.html:
Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

Today’s lesson begins with the very first link. Once the mindset changes, God’s will is no longer a hidden map but a public command to love. When the mindset changes, life turns from “seeking to perform” to “seeking to be real”; when life changes, daily living turns from “rushing through the schedule” to “keeping time for people”; when daily living changes, relationships turn from cold to connected; and only when relationships change will ministry have genuine vitality.

The order cannot be reversed. Many people walk it backwards: they charge ahead with ministry, hoping ministry will bring relationships and relationships will bring life. The result: the bigger the ministry, the thinner the relationships and the drier the life.

sections.heading: 4. A Shift in Perspective
sections.html:
From man’s perspective: results, numbers, applause. From God’s perspective: love in the heart, genuine relationships.

From the earthly perspective: once the job is done, that’s success. From the heavenly perspective: only when people are built up is it success.

From the temporary perspective: I won the argument this time — how satisfying. From the eternal perspective: I am going to live with this person for eternity — so how should I treat them today?

From the worldly perspective: relationships are resources. From God’s perspective: relationships are the very content of God’s will.

sections.heading: 5. The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships
sections.html:
The 920 practice: every person who is in relationship with us is our “2”.
