Before that person we practise living the selfless (0) life, so that the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — are truly borne in that relationship.

Brothers and sisters, notice that the first of the nine graces is love, and the other eight are really love unfolding: love that lasts is patience, love that reaches out is kindness, love in our words is gentleness, love in our promises is faithfulness. This morning you can pray for your “2” by name: Lord, let your love flow through me to him, to her.

The 235 relationships: become a “2” with someone selfless, supporting each other; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children — passing life on; and go on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades, establishing God’s system together. This whole structure is relationship from beginning to end — which is why today’s message is so crucial: if we don’t know how to love, we can’t establish the system.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Building Relationships in Love, Living in God’s Will
sections.html: Brothers and sisters, to hear the word and not do it is to deceive ourselves (James 1:22). This lesson has three exercises; let us take them one at a time.

sections.heading: 1. Check Each Day: Did I Live in Love Today?
sections.html:
Don’t ask: how much did I get done today? Ask instead: did I truly love people today?

How to practise: every evening, grow quiet and ask yourself three questions —

Did I respond to God with love?

Did I treat people with love?

Did I bring my relationships closer?

These three questions take only three minutes a day. But three minutes of self-examination beats three hours of regret. I suggest you keep a small notebook and write just one line each day: today, in which person did I live out love, or miss the chance to love?

sections.heading: 2. Practise “Letting Relationships Matter More Than Tasks”
sections.html:
In conflict or under pressure, deliberately choose: not to hurt people, not to break relationships.

One less word of blame, one more word of understanding; one less argument, one more time of listening.

How to practise: when conflict arises, first pause for three seconds and ask yourself one question — will these words build the relationship or break it?

Three seconds seem very short, yet they are enough to change a relationship. Physiologically, those three seconds are the gap in which control passes from emotional reflex back to reason and the Holy Spirit. James 1:19 puts it superbly: “let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” Notice the rhythm of this verse — one swift, two slow. Our problem is often exactly the opposite: slow to hear, swift to speak, swift to anger.

sections.heading: 3. Take the Initiative to Repair a Relationship
sections.html:
If there is unforgiveness, distance or coldness in your heart, take the first step: be the first to apologise, the first to show care, the first to forgive.

Because restoring relationship is living in God’s will.

How to practise: this week, deliberately repair one relationship — a family member, a co-worker or a friend.

Please notice one word: initiative. The Lord Jesus said, “First be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:24); he did not say to wait until the other person comes first. And let me also add a reminder: repair will not always win an immediate response from the other side. Paul says, “If it is possible, as much as it is up to you, be at peace with all men.” (Romans 12:18) “If it is possible” means that sometimes it isn’t possible; but “as much as it is up to you” is the responsibility on our side. Do everything on our side, and leave the rest to God.

Turning practice into life: the eight stages of changing our mindset

The 321 vision teaches that real change has to go through eight stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let us put today’s three exercises into these eight stages.

Stage one, Information. Today you have received the information: God’s will is love, and the practical expression of love is building relationships. Copy out a few key passages and put them where you can see them — Matthew 22:37–40, John 13:34, 1 Corinthians 13:1–3.

Stage two, Revelation. Information enters the head; revelation enters the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light: Lord, which relationship in my life do you want to point out today? Be still for three minutes and let that name rise to the surface. That name is the assignment God is giving you today.

Stage three, Conviction. Settle it in your heart: whatever builds relationship is God’s will; whatever breaks relationship is not God’s will. Conviction means that even if my emotions disagree, I still choose to stand on the side of God’s word.

Stage four, Implementation. Fix one concrete thing: tonight, go through the three questions of self-examination; this week, make one phone call or send one sincere message. Don’t set ten things; set one, but do it today.

Stage five, Evaluation. After a week, look back honestly: did I pause for those three seconds? Did the words I spoke build relationships or break them? When did I fall back into “I have to prove I’m right”?

Stage six, Correction. When you find you’ve failed, don’t condemn yourself; correct your method. Perhaps you find you hurt people most easily when you’re tired — then correct the timing: don’t hold important conversations late at night. Perhaps you find that misunderstandings arise whenever you use text messages — then correct the medium: meet in person or phone instead.

Stage seven, Repetition. Once doesn’t count; it must be repeated. Psychology calls this habit formation; the Bible calls it “exercise”. First Timothy 4:7 says, “But refuse profane and old wives’ fables. Exercise yourself toward godliness.” The very meaning of exercise is repetition upon repetition. Love is not a single heroic feat; it is ten thousand choices.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When you have tasted the sweetness yourself, pass it on. Do these three exercises together with your “2”, and once a week ask each other: which relationship did you repair this week? This is moving from relationships to a system, from life to multiplication.

A Gentle Reminder: Direction Matters More Than Performance

Brothers and sisters, here is a serious reminder: you can do many right things and still be living in the wrong direction.

If you have lost love, if you have broken relationships, then what God values is not your performance but whether your love is genuine.

Here is a picture well worth pondering: a man rowing with all his might, going at great speed, drenched in sweat — but the bow is pointing the wrong way. The faster he rows, the further he gets from his destination. Brothers and sisters, the greatest danger in the spiritual life is not rowing too slowly; it is rowing very fast in the wrong direction.

The prophet Micah made this plain long ago: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8) What God requires is to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with him — every one of them is a relationship.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Not Doing More, but Loving More Truly
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, God’s will is actually very simple, and yet very deep:

Not doing more, but loving more truly; not being busier, but being more connected.

When you begin to measure everything by “love”, you will be walking in God’s will.

This morning the Lord is issuing a call to us. This call is not for us to take on one more ministry, but for us to let Jesus reign as King in our relationships.

Let him reign as King in your home — let that cutting word stop on the tip of your tongue.

Let him reign as King in your church — let that brother you have always walked around be greeted by you, first, today.

Let him reign as King in your heart — hand over that name you have locked away deep in a drawer.

For when relationships are restored, the glory goes to Jesus. The Lord said, “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:35) The world recognises us not by our achievements but by our love for one another. So every time we repair a relationship in love, we bear witness to Jesus, and we give the glory to him.

May our whole lives be not merely about obeying commands, but about walking with God in love and staying connected with others, building godly relationships, living out a heavenly life, and becoming overcomers.

keyVerses: Jesus said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” (Matthew 22:37–40)
“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” (John 13:34)
“…know his will, and approve the things that are excellent, being instructed out of the law.” (Romans 2:18)
practices: Check each day: did I live in love today?
Practise “letting relationships matter more than tasks”
Take the initiative to repair a relationship
prayer: Lord! I want to live in your will — not just doing the right things, but living out genuine love.
I will love you, I will love people, I will love one another.
Let everything I do bring relationships to be built up, not broken down.
Make my life connected to you and connected to others, living out Christ and becoming an overcomer.
Dear Heavenly Father, thank you that your will is not hidden; you wrote it long ago in your word: love God, love people, love one another.
Lord, forgive us. We are so often busy doing things and forget to love people; we so often insist on who is right and wrong, and lose the relationship.
Pour your love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, so that we can love those we cannot bring ourselves to love, and forgive those we cannot bring ourselves to forgive.
Lord, help us take a step today: pause for three seconds and speak a word that builds up; make a phone call and repair a relationship.
Let Jesus reign as King in our families, our church and our lives, and let all the glory go to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “If I speak with the languages of men and of angels, but don’t have love, I have become sounding brass, or a clanging cymbal.” (1 Corinthians 13:1) Please share: in your present ministry or work, is there anything that has become “all sound and no love”? How do you plan to put love back into it?

“For if you forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.” (Matthew 6:14) Please take a moment of quiet and think of one relationship you need to take the initiative to repair. What concrete small step are you willing to take this week? Say it out loud, and let the small group pray for you.
l148.title: Building Relationships in Love
l148.subtitle: The Heart of God’s Will Is Building Relationships
l148.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: It’s Not That We Lack Relationships — the Order Is Wrong
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

Let me begin with a scene we see again and again in the church. There was a sister whom everyone in her church praised as a wonderful co-worker. She led a small group, ran the choir, looked after the kitchen and drove the sick to hospital. Her weekly calendar was packed solid; even Sunday lunch she ate standing up. One day, after a time of service, she broke down and wept. The pastor asked her what was wrong, and she said something heartbreaking: “I’ve done so much for God, but it’s been a very long time since I last talked with him.”

Brothers and sisters, every one of us should stop and ponder those words. Was it relationships she lacked? No. She had relationships with people, with tasks, with the church, with her ministry. So what did she lack? She lacked “order”. She had put “what I do for God” ahead of “my relationship with God”, and so things that were good in themselves became burdens, one after another, until at last they crushed her.

In our last lesson we saw together that God’s will is to build relationships. When God made us, he did not intend to make a machine that runs, but a child who can be with him face to face and heart to heart. Today we go a step further, to grasp something absolutely crucial: not every relationship is God’s will; the key lies in “order”.

For many people the problem is not a lack of relationships, but relationships in the wrong order. And once the order is wrong, things become very subtle: good things can turn wrong, and even spiritual actions can offend God. This is not alarmism; it is a warning Scripture gives us again and again.

Let a few pictures from everyday life help us feel it. Take the same seven digits: in the right order, the call goes through; in the wrong order, you ring a stranger. Take the same seven notes: arranged differently, they can make a requiem or a lullaby. More remarkable still, chemists have long told us that graphite and diamond are made of exactly the same element — carbon. The only difference is the order in which the carbon atoms are arranged. One is black and soft, good for writing with; the other is crystal-clear and hard, the most precious gem in the world. The same material, in a different order, and the value is worlds apart.

Our lives are just the same. The same twenty-four hours, the same family, work, ministry, money and health: in the right order, they become a diamond that glorifies God; in the wrong order, they become a heap of black coal that wears us down.

So in today’s lesson we will see together three vitally important truths: relationships have an order; order determines right and wrong; and order determines whether we are living within God’s will.

We will look together at three key points: first, the first priority in relationships is our relationship with God; second, when the order is wrong, even the right thing becomes wrong; third, God values relationship more than service.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The High Priest’s Prayer, the Farewell Charge
sections.html:
Today’s theme verse comes from John 17:3. To receive the full weight of these words, we first need to know when and in what circumstances they were spoken.

The author of John’s Gospel, by the consistent testimony of church history, is John the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. This Gospel is generally thought to have been written at the end of the first century AD, roughly between AD 85 and 95, while the elderly John was shepherding the churches around Ephesus. By then most of the first generation of apostles had been martyred, and the church faced persecution from the Roman Empire as well as the troubling heresy of early Gnosticism — people who exalted “knowledge” yet denied Jesus, the Word made flesh. John’s purpose in writing is crystal clear: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Chapter 17 is one of the most sacred chapters in the whole Bible. Chapters 13 to 17 are known as the “Upper Room Discourse”: the farewell words the Lord Jesus spoke to his disciples after the Last Supper and before going to the Garden of Gethsemane. He had already washed the disciples’ feet, foretold Judas’s betrayal, promised the coming of the Holy Spirit the Comforter, and given the parable “I am the true vine.” By chapter 17 he no longer speaks to the disciples; he lifts up his eyes and speaks to God the Father.

This chapter is called “the High Priestly Prayer”. Once a year the high priest of the Old Testament entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement and intercede for the people; now this eternal High Priest, before going to the cross, intercedes for his disciples and for all, in every age, who would believe in him through their word. In other words, brothers and sisters, on that night two thousand years ago, you and I were in the Lord Jesus’ prayer.

At just such a moment, the Lord Jesus gave a definition. He said: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) Please notice: this is the only place in the whole Bible where the Lord Jesus himself defines “eternal life”. And that definition is not about the length of time; it is about the depth of relationship.

And precisely because it was spoken just before his death, these words weigh all the more. What someone leaves as a parting charge is always what lies heaviest on their heart. The Lord Jesus did not say, “Do a bit more for me — this is eternal life.” He said, “Know me — this is eternal life.”

With this background in mind, we can step into today’s first key point.

sections.heading: 1. The First Priority in Relationships: Our Relationship with God
sections.html:
“This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3)

“For God so loved the world, that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” (John 3:16)

sections.heading: 1. Eternal Life Is Not a Length of Time but a Depth of Relationship
sections.html:
Many people think “eternal life” simply means going to heaven when we die, or never dying. That understanding isn’t entirely wrong, but it falls far short. For by the Lord Jesus’ own definition, eternal life equals “knowing God” — that is, entering into a relationship with God.

The word “know” here is the Greek γινώσκω (ginōskō). It does not mean how much information is stored in your head; it means coming to know a person gradually, through experience and through relationship. It corresponds to the Hebrew יָדַע (yada’). Genesis 4:1 says, “The man knew Eve his wife” — and the Hebrew word there is exactly yada’, the most intimate kind of knowing. So when the Bible speaks of knowing God, it never means studying God; it means walking closely with him.

Now look at the phrase “eternal life”: in Greek, ζωὴ αἰώνιος (zōē aiōnios). Αἰώνιος certainly carries the sense of “for ever” in time, but in John’s usage the emphasis falls more on “the quality of life that belongs to the Eternal One”. That is why John 3:36 says, “One who believes in the Son has eternal life” — in the present tense. It is not something we have only after death; we have it now. Eternal life is not a ticket for the future; it is a kind of life that begins today.

Brothers and sisters, this distinction matters enormously. If eternal life is only a length of time, then believing in the Lord becomes buying insurance, and the point is “the future”. But if eternal life is a depth of relationship, then believing in the Lord is entering a relationship of love, and the point is “now”. Someone who treats faith as insurance can ignore it most of the time; someone who has entered a relationship of love wants to draw near every single day.

sections.heading: 2. What Matters Most in Life Is Not Success but Our Relationship with God
sections.html:
Jeremiah puts this with a razor’s edge: “Yahweh says, ‘Don’t let the wise man glory in his wisdom. Don’t let the mighty man glory in his might. Don’t let the rich man glory in his riches. But let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me, that I am Yahweh who exercises loving kindness, justice, and righteousness in the earth, for I delight in these things,’ says Yahweh.” (Jeremiah 9:23–24)

Wisdom, might and riches are the three summits people strive for: learning, status and money. Yet God says none of these is anything for you to boast about. The only thing worth boasting in is “knowing me”.

That is why the Lord Jesus said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first and great commandment.” (Matthew 22:37–38) Notice the word “first”. The commandments are not a jumbled list; they have an order. The greatest commandment is to love God, and only second comes “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39). The Lord also said: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) That one word, “first”, sets the order of a whole life.

sections.heading: 3. The Source of Love: We Love Because God First Loved Us
sections.html:
“We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)

This verse is short, yet it is the master switch for every relationship. All love has its source in God. We have no stored supply of love within us, only a flow of love; God is the source, and we are the pipe. If the pipe is cut off from the source, however hard you squeeze, no water will come out — only cracks.

I often use this picture. When you fly, the cabin crew’s safety demonstration always says that when the oxygen masks drop, you should “put on your own mask first, before helping others”. It sounds rather heartless, but it is a life-saving order. Someone who has already passed out from lack of oxygen can save no one. In the same way, someone whose own connection with God is cut off will serve others only to the point of burnout.

sections.heading: 4. Without This Foundation, Everything Goes Crooked
sections.html:
Our relationship with God is the foundation of every other relationship. Without this foundation, three things happen. Our relationship with others becomes twisted — because we start demanding from people the affirmation only God can give. Our relationship with ourselves falls into confusion — because we have lost the coordinates we were created with and can only measure ourselves through other people’s eyes. Our relationship with things falls out of balance — because work and service are no longer a response to God’s love but a means of proving ourselves.

Augustine put it beautifully at the opening of his Confessions: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Pascal, too, in his Pensées, observed that there is an infinite abyss in the human heart which can be filled only by one who is infinite and unchanging — that is, by God himself. If we do not let God sit in first place, that seat will not stay empty; something else will certainly take it — perhaps work, perhaps our children, perhaps money, perhaps a person, perhaps even “service” itself.

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has, since 1938, followed more than seven hundred men across more than eighty years; it is one of the longest studies of adult life ever undertaken. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, summing up the study, said: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Elsewhere, a 2010 meta-analysis by Julianne Holt-Lunstad and colleagues, published in PLoS Medicine, brought together 148 studies and more than three hundred thousand participants, and found that people with stronger social connections had about a fifty per cent greater likelihood of survival. Science confirms it again and again: human beings are made for relationship. And the Bible tells us earlier and more deeply than science: we are made first of all for “a relationship with God”.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Focus on Jesus, and the Order Is Right
sections.html:
The first of 321’s foundations is “Jesus is my role model”. In his thirty-three years on earth, what did the Lord Jesus value most? Mark 1:35 says: “Early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up and went out, and departed into a deserted place, and prayed there.” The evening before, the whole town had gathered at the door; the sick were healed, and demons were driven out. By human logic, the next day he should have pressed home his advantage. But before dawn the Lord Jesus went first to be alone with the Father. The power of his ministry came out of his relationship with the Father.

So 321 says: focus on Jesus, and the order is right; focus on yourself, and the order falls apart. If the focus is on ourselves, our priorities will be set by three things — other people’s expectations, the urgent matter in front of us, and the fear in our hearts. If the focus is on Jesus, our priorities are set by one thing alone — what pleases him.

Brothers and sisters, this morning ask yourself one question: is God truly first in my life? Or is God merely near the front, but not first? Between “near the front” and “first” lies the whole gospel.

sections.heading: 2. When the Order Is Wrong, Even the Right Thing Becomes Wrong
sections.html: “Samuel said, ‘Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying Yahweh’s voice? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.’” (1 Samuel 15:22)

sections.heading: 1. Saul’s Two Falls: Good Things Done in the Wrong Order
sections.html:
Saul was the first king of Israel. He stood head and shoulders above everyone; he humbly hid among the baggage rather than come out to be anointed; he began as a man richly blessed. Yet the Bible records two falls of his, and neither came from doing anything obviously evil. Both came from doing the right thing in the wrong order.

The first was at Gilgal. 1 Samuel 13 records that the Philistines gathered as many as the sand on the seashore; the people trembled and scattered. Saul waited seven days, the time Samuel had set, and still Samuel had not come. So “Saul said, ‘Bring the burnt offering to me here, and the peace offerings.’ He offered the burnt offering.” (1 Samuel 13:9) The very moment he finished offering it, Samuel arrived. Samuel said: “You have done foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of Yahweh your God, which he commanded you” (1 Samuel 13:13).

Brothers and sisters, please notice: offering sacrifice was a spiritual act, something Scripture commanded, a good thing. So where was the wrong? The wrong was that he did not wait for God. He put “sacrifice” ahead of “obedience”, and put “the task” ahead of “God”.

The second came after the battle against the Amalekites. God commanded that everything be destroyed, but Saul spared King Agag and the best of the sheep and cattle. When Samuel came to confront him, Saul’s answer sounded very spiritual: “But the people took of the plunder, sheep and cattle, the chief of the devoted things, to sacrifice to Yahweh your God in Gilgal.” (1 Samuel 15:21) He wanted to offer sacrifice to God! Yet Samuel’s reply is our theme verse today: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22)

More telling still is Saul’s later confession: “I have transgressed the commandment of Yahweh, and your words, because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice” (1 Samuel 15:24). Now the truth comes to the surface — he had put “people” ahead of “God”. He feared people more than he feared God. The result: “Because you have rejected Yahweh’s word, he has also rejected you from being king.” (1 Samuel 15:23) His throne was taken from him, and he was rejected by God.

sections.heading: 2. To Obey Is Better Than Sacrifice: The Weight of the Original
sections.html:
The Hebrew for “obey” is שָׁמַע (shama’), meaning “to hear and to act on what you hear”. In the Hebrew mindset, to hear without doing is the same as not hearing at all. The Shema, which Israel recites every day, opens with: “Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.” (Deuteronomy 6:4) The starting point of faith is not “you must do” but “you must hear”.

Sacrifice is a person giving something to God; obedience is a person giving themselves to God. People would often rather sacrifice than obey, because sacrifice is something I can control, while obedience requires me to hand over my sovereignty. Hosea 6:6 says: “For I desire mercy (or, goodness), and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.” See how God once again places “the knowledge of God” above “burnt offerings”. From Samuel to Hosea, from the Old Testament to the New, God’s heart has never changed.

So the spiritual principle is very clear: once the order of relationships goes wrong, everything goes wrong. Even something done for God, even an action that looks completely right — if it damages our relationship with God, it is not God’s will.

sections.heading: 3. Martha’s Kitchen and the Church in Ephesus
sections.html:
The New Testament has a gentler version too. Martha welcomed Jesus, was distracted with much serving, grew flustered, and complained that her sister wasn’t helping. What did the Lord say? “Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’” (Luke 10:41–42)

The Lord did not say that serving is wrong. What he said was, “one thing is needed.” Martha’s problem was not doing too much; it was having the order back to front — she was in the kitchen busy for the Lord, while Mary was at the Lord’s feet, with the Lord. Busyness itself is not sin; the danger comes when busyness replaces closeness.

In Revelation 2:4 the Lord says to the church in Ephesus: “But I have this against you, that you left your first love.” The Ephesian church toiled, endured and discerned false teaching — good on every count — yet the Lord rebuked them, because they had lost “love” and were left with only “doing”.

Most sobering of all is Matthew 7:22–23: “Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’” They had ministry, they had gifts, they had results; the only thing they lacked was “knowing”. Brothers and sisters, what a sobering reminder this is.

sections.heading: 4. What Psychology Confirms: We Are Born in a Hurry to “Do Something”
sections.html:
In a study published in 2007 in the Journal of Economic Psychology, the Israeli scholar Michael Bar-Eli and his colleagues analysed how top football goalkeepers respond to penalty kicks. The statistics showed that a sizeable proportion of shots go to the centre of the goal, yet goalkeepers almost always dive left or right and very rarely stay where they are. Rationally, staying in the middle gives a better save rate, yet still they dive. The researchers called this “action bias” — under pressure, people would rather do something than stand still, because standing still makes them feel they have failed in their duty.

Saul was a man taken captive by action bias. The people were scattering, the Philistines were pressing in, and Samuel still hadn’t come; he could no longer stand firm — he had to do something. Brothers and sisters, the mistake we most easily make under pressure is not laziness; it is “reaching out to act ahead of God”. Waiting often takes more faith than acting.

Martin Luther is commonly said to have remarked: “I have so much to do today that I must spend an extra hour in prayer.” Whatever the true source of the saying, the order it describes is entirely biblical — the more there is to do, the more we must first return to God, not the more we must skip past him.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: The Self-Centred Life Revolves Around Tasks; Selflessness Revolves Around God
sections.html:
321 teaches us that the root of humanity’s fall is the self-centred life, and that pride is the root of the problem. What is pride? Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place. When Saul offered sacrifice at Gilgal, that is exactly what he did: he left his position as “king” and reached out to do the work of a “priest”; he seized control and tried to decide the timing in God’s place.

The self-centred person revolves around tasks; the selfless person revolves around God. The self-centred person will sacrifice relationships to get the job done; the selfless person will lay down the job to keep the relationship. This difference plays out every day — in the church, in the family and in the workplace. To get one thing done, we may speak harshly to a co-worker, lose our temper with our children, or stay up so late that there’s no time left for devotions — the job gets done, people get hurt, relationships break, and God’s heart is grieved.

321 also reminds us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. The harder Saul tried to save face, the more he lost God’s presence. In the end he begged Samuel, “please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel” (1 Samuel 15:30) — what he still cared about was how people saw him.

Brothers and sisters, humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position. Let man be man and let God be God. That is the right order.

sections.heading: 3. God Values Relationship More Than Service
sections.html:
“The four living creatures, each one of them having six wings, are full of eyes around and within. They have no rest day and night, saying, ‘Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come!’” (Revelation 4:8)

“He who overcomes, I will give him these things. I will be his God, and he will be my son.” (Revelation 21:7)

sections.heading: 1. In Eternity, What Remains Is Relationship
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, come with me and lift your eyes to the farthest horizon of all — eternity.

Revelation 4 lets us see the throne in heaven. There are no meetings there, no reports, no performance targets, no league tables. The four living creatures worship day and night without rest, and the twenty-four elders lay their crowns before the throne. The whole picture of heaven is about one thing only: relationship with God.

Now look at Revelation 21. When the new heaven and the new earth come down, what does God proclaim? “Behold, God’s dwelling is with people, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.” (Revelation 21:3) Then comes that most tender promise: “I will be his God, and he will be my son.” (Revelation 21:7)

The Bible begins in the Garden of Eden in Genesis, where God walks in the garden and is with humankind; it ends in the New Jerusalem in Revelation, where God’s dwelling is among people and he lives with them. The beginning and the end of the whole Bible are the same thing — relationship. All the history, law, prophets, poetry and letters in between are God repairing this relationship that sin had broken.

So in eternity, what remains is not ministry, not achievement, but relationship — the relationship between people and God. Paul says: “Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.” (1 Corinthians 13:8) Prophecy will stop, languages will cease, knowledge will be done away with; only love, only relationship, lasts for ever.

sections.heading: 2. What God Cares About Most Is Not What You Do for Him, but Whether You Walk with Him
sections.html:
Genesis 5 records a long litany: “and he died… and he died… and he died.” Only one man is different: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, for God took him.” (Genesis 5:24) The Bible does not record what Enoch built, what he wrote or what great exploits he achieved. It records only this: he walked with God. And that alone was enough for him never to taste death.

Micah distils God’s requirement into one sentence: “He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8) Acting justly and loving mercy are directed towards people, and then it all comes to rest on one phrase — walk with your God.

Paul’s lifelong pursuit was the same: “Yes most certainly, and I count all things to be a loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus, my Lord, for whom I suffered the loss of all things, and count them nothing but refuse, that I may gain Christ” (Philippians 3:8). The Greek word for “refuse” here is σκύβαλον (skybalon), meaning kitchen scraps, dregs, rubbish thrown out. Paul’s pedigree, education, zeal and righteousness under the law — the things he had once been so proud of — he threw them all in the bin. Why? Not to gain a ministry, not to gain results, but “that I may gain Christ”.

Brothers and sisters, this is the watershed. Are you pursuing “gaining something”, or “gaining him”?

sections.heading: 3. God Doesn’t Want Workers; God Wants Sons
sections.html:
Our lesson text uses a fine illustration: if a child only helps his father with the work but has no relationship with him, the father will not be satisfied.

The elder son in Luke 15 is a living example. He said to his father: “Behold, these many years I have served you, and I never disobeyed a commandment of yours, but you never gave me a goat, that I might celebrate with my friends.” (Luke 15:29) He was in the house, but his heart was outside; the word he used was “served”, not “with you”. The father’s answer is the most heartbreaking and yet the warmest line in the whole Bible: “Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.” (Luke 15:31)

So what the father wanted was not his labour but his presence. The father had long since given him everything, yet there he stood outside the door, demanding a young goat.

The Lord Jesus himself spelled this relationship out: “No longer do I call you servants, for the servant doesn’t know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, for everything that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you.” (John 15:15) And Paul says: “So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.” (Galatians 4:7)

A servant earns wages by performance; a son receives an inheritance by identity. A servant who does poorly fears being thrown out; a son who does poorly is still a son. Many of us have believed in the Lord for years; we act like sons, but think like servants — tense when we serve, despairing when we fail, at ease only when praised. That is because the order is wrong: we use ministry to buy relationship, instead of letting ministry flow out of relationship.

sections.heading: 4. What Developmental Psychology Confirms: Babies Need More Than Feeding
sections.html:
In the 1970s the American developmental psychologist Edward Tronick designed the famous “Still Face Experiment”. In it, a mother first interacts normally with her baby: the baby smiles, points and makes sounds, and the mother responds to each one. Then the mother suddenly goes expressionless, neither responding nor speaking. Within a few dozen seconds the baby begins trying every way possible to call the mother back, then squirms and twists, and finally breaks down in tears. The mother is still right there; she hasn’t left, and she hasn’t stopped meeting the baby’s needs — she has only stopped the “relationship”.

Brothers and sisters, this experiment shows us that, deep down in how we are made, we need not only to be fed but to be responded to, to be seen and to be loved. The self-determination theory put forward by the psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan holds that people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and “relatedness”. When God made us, he placed the longing for relationship within us.

So God does not want “workers”; God wants “sons”. A father who wanted only productivity could hire employees; he wouldn’t need to have children. God created and redeemed us in order to have children of his own.

sections.heading: 5. A 321 Insight: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
sections.html:
321 says it very clearly: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Moreover, the order of service is life first, then relationships, then ministry.

These three stages cannot be reversed. Relationship without life is mere socialising; ministry without relationship is mere engineering. Many rifts in churches arise not because too few people love God, but because we so often do things backwards — charging into ministry first, patching up relationships afterwards, and only at the end discovering that life has long since run dry.

321 also gives us the order of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson fastens the first link in that chain. When our relationship with God is right, only then can we see ourselves rightly — no longer defining our worth by achievement; only then can we love others healthily — no longer demanding from people what only God can give; only then can we work freely — tasks are no longer our master, simply a way of responding to God’s love.

The first question of the Westminster Shorter Catechism asks: What is the chief end of man? Answer: Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever. Please notice: not “to do lots of things for God for ever”, but “to enjoy him”. Glorifying God and enjoying God have never been two separate things.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: When the Order Is Right, Life Comes Alive
sections.html:
Let’s place what we have seen today into the overall blueprint of 321.

The Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. When it comes to the order of relationships, each of the three has its role. Jesus is my role model: before dawn he went first to pray; in everything he first looked to what the Father was doing; he put his relationship with the Father ahead of his ministry. The Bible is my standard: when our feelings say, “Get the job done first and then we’ll see,” the Bible says, “to obey is better than sacrifice.” The Holy Spirit is my guide: he will gently remind us in our hearts, “You haven’t been still for three days now.”

The Two Core Values — let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. In the end, the question of order is a question of the throne. Who sits on the throne of my life? If tasks are king, I am ruled by my schedule; if people are king, I am ruled by the look on other people’s faces; if I myself am king, I am ruled by my own emotions. Only when Jesus reigns as King does everything find its proper place.

The Goal — establish God’s system. A system must have order; without order it isn’t a system, it’s chaos. God’s system is ordered: first the foundation, then the walls, and only then the roof. God’s system grows out of our relationship with God.

From the self-centred life to selflessness. The self-centred person puts themselves first, and so God gets squeezed into the gaps in the calendar. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When I no longer need achievement to prove myself, I am truly free — free to give the first part of my time to God, unhurried and unflustered.

The fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Please notice: these five changes are themselves an order. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. What we are doing today is exactly the first step: a change of mindset. When we truly believe that “my relationship with God matters more than what I do for God”, our life, daily living, relationships and ministry will all change, layer by layer, in turn.

The shift in perspective — from the human perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From an earthly perspective, praying for half an hour first “wastes” half an hour; from a heavenly perspective, that half-hour places the whole day in God’s hands. From a temporary perspective, what gets done is what’s most real; from an eternal perspective, only those who walk with God remain for ever.

The 920 practice — everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. When my relationship with God is right, then I can live out the “0” life in front of my “2” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice that fruit is something “borne”, not something “made”. A branch not joined to the vine can strain as hard as it likes and never produce a single grape. The order is this: first connection, then fruit.

235 relationships — become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with selfless people; establish “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. But remember, the foundation of 235 is still our relationship with God. Two people who have both lost their connection with God will not become spiritual companions by being put together; they will only end up warming each other and wearing each other out. First comes the vertical connection; then comes horizontal unity.

Finally, 321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. A life in disordered priorities is always a troubled life, because the brain is forever counting how many things are still left undone. A life in the right order is a glad life, because the heart has already come to rest in God.

sections.heading: 5. Putting It into Practice: Reorder Your Relationships, Return to God at the Centre
sections.html:
Our lesson text gives us three very concrete practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Each day, build your relationship with God first, then step into the day’s tasks

Don’t reach first for your phone, your tasks or your busyness; come first before God — pray, draw near to God, fix your focus on Jesus. How to practise: set aside a regular time each day to “connect with God first”, five to fifteen minutes.

Why does “first” matter so much? Because the first move of the day takes hold of the day’s steering wheel. In research published in 1927, the psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik showed that unfinished tasks stay especially vivid in our memory and refuse to go away — what later came to be called the “Zeigarnik effect”. This explains why, the moment we open our eyes, yesterday’s unfinished business automatically jumps up and queues for attention. If the first thing we do on waking is scroll our phone or answer messages, then before the day has even begun, our hearts are already filled with other people’s agendas.

So please put these five to fifteen minutes “first”, not “whenever I have a spare moment”. Same place, same time, phone left in another room. At the start, don’t aim for long; aim only for real.

Practice 2: Before each thing you do, ask first — will this affect my relationship with God?

For example: will this decision draw me closer to God, or take me further from him? How to practise: stop at least three times a day and ask this question.

This question has power because it moves the standard of right and wrong away from results and back to relationship. Many decisions in this world look good in terms of gain and loss but are dangerous in terms of relationship: this overtime gets me promoted, but leaves me without a Sabbath for three months; this opportunity lets me shine, but starts me living on people’s applause.

I suggest you fix these three times: once in the morning before you go out, once before lunch, and once at night before bed. After asking, just write one line. A month later, look back, and you’ll see how your order has been adjusted, little by little.

Practice 3: When tasks and people clash, choose to guard your relationship with God

When pressure comes, things are urgent and emotions are running high: don’t lose obedience because of the hurry; don’t lose closeness because of the busyness. How to practise: when pressure hits, first pray one sentence: “Lord, I choose to align myself with you first.”

That sentence is very short, yet it is exactly the sentence Saul most needed that day at Gilgal. The moment pressure rises, our body triggers the fight-or-flight response; the heart races and our thinking narrows. A one-line prayer is like grabbing hold of the handrail before stepping into the rapids. It doesn’t solve the problem; it steadies you first — and only a steadied you can truly solve the problem.

Deepening these three practices with the eight stages of changing our mindset

Stage 1, Information: write down today’s truth — relationships have an order, and order determines right and wrong. Copy out John 17:3 and 1 Samuel 15:22 on a piece of paper and put it somewhere you’ll see it.

Stage 2, Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, so that this is not just a doctrine but God’s word to me personally today. You might quietly ask: Lord, where has my order gone wrong?

Stage 3, Conviction: acknowledge and accept it from the heart — I truly believe that my relationship with you matters more than what I do for you. Conviction is the surrender of the will, not a stirring of the emotions.

Stage 4, Implementation: do it straight away — today. Don’t wait until “starting next week”. Tomorrow morning, the first thing is not your phone; it’s prayer.

Stage 5, Evaluation: each evening take two minutes to look back — was my order right today? At what moment did I put a task ahead of God?

Stage 6, Correction: when you find you’ve drifted, adjust at once, without condemning yourself. Saul’s tragedy was not that he made mistakes, but that he covered up, made excuses and feared people. David made mistakes too, but he fell down at once and confessed.

Stage 7, Repetition: once doesn’t count as a practice; thirty days does. Order is a kind of muscle memory, built by repetition.

Stage 8, Multiplication: take what you’ve experienced to your “2”. Tell a brother or sister: “Lately I’ve been practising connecting with God first every day — would you like to do it with me?” Then check in with each other once a week. Once a spiritual practice begins to multiply, it’s no longer easy to stop.

A Gentle Reminder

Brothers and sisters, please keep these words in your heart: you can be very busy serving and yet be far from God. You can do many right things and yet live in the wrong order.

God doesn’t want you to replace him with tasks; God wants you to come back to him first.

sections.heading: 6. Closing and Call: Whom You Connect with First Decides Everything
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, the key to life is not how much you do, but “whom you connect with first”.

When the order is right, everything is right; when the order is wrong, everything is in disarray. This is not a motivational slogan. It is the lesson Saul bought with his throne, the lesson Martha learned in her kitchen, the reminder the church in Ephesus heard when the Lord rebuked them, and the surpassing treasure Paul truly gained only after counting a lifetime of achievements as refuse.

This morning the Lord is calling us. He is not asking us to lay down our service; he is asking us to put our service back in its proper place. He is not complaining that we do too much; his heart simply aches that we do it so alone. He says: “My child, come back first. Come back to me first, and then go and face all the people and all the tasks.”

To let Jesus be King means to let him sit in first place — not second place, not “near the front”, but first place. When he truly reigns as King, our calendars will be rearranged, our priorities will be readjusted, our relationships with others will be healed, and what we do will have meaning again.

To let Jesus receive all the glory means we no longer need to steal a little glory for ourselves from our ministry. When our worth has already been satisfied in relationship, we can give all the fruit wholly to him.

May we, all our lives, put our relationship with God first, set out from his love, build every right relationship, live out the life that belongs to God, and become overcomers.

For the one waiting for us in eternity is not a report card, but a Father. What he will say is not “How much did you do?” but “I will be his God, and he will be my son.”

keyVerses: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3)
practices: Each day, build my relationship with God first, then step into the day’s tasks
When tasks and people clash, choose to guard my relationship with God
prayer: Lord! I want to reorder my life and make you first in my life.
I will no longer put tasks ahead of you; I will no longer let busyness replace relationship.
I will connect with you first, and then face all people and all tasks.
Lord, forgive me for the many times I reached out to act ahead of you, for the times I pushed you aside because I feared people or was in a hurry to get things done.
Place a fresh longing for you within me, so that each morning you are the first one I think of, and under pressure you are the first one I call on.
All my life, let me not just do many things for you, but walk with you and live out Christ.
Let Jesus reign as King in my life; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
discussion: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) The Lord Jesus defines eternal life as “knowing God”. Looking back over the past month, has your relationship with God been more like “knowing him” or more like “knowing about him”? Please share one specific occasion when you put “what I do for God” ahead of “my relationship with God”.

“To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” (1 Samuel 15:22) At Gilgal, Saul could not bear to wait any longer, so he offered the sacrifice on his own. In your life right now, what is it that you “can’t bear to wait for” any longer? This week, what concrete way will you use to practise aligning yourself with God first, and only then acting?

l149.subtitle: Connect with God First, Then Face Everyone and Everything Else

sections.heading: Introduction: The Hardest Person to Live With Lives Inside You
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

A sister once said to me: “Pastor, I get on quite well with the people at church, and I’m on reasonably good terms with my colleagues. With my family there’s the occasional friction, but it’s manageable. But there’s one person I fight with every day, from morning till night, and it hasn’t stopped for thirty years.” I asked her, “Who is that person?” She lowered her head, and after a long, long pause she said quietly: “It’s me.”

Brothers and sisters, have you ever known that? Late at night, when all is still, the lights are off and the door is locked, and you’re lying in bed alone. At that moment, the voice that is quickest to condemn you, quickest to rake over your past, quickest to remind you that “you’re not good enough”, does not come from your enemy; it comes from your own heart. By day you can forgive others; by night you refuse to forgive yourself.

We often think the pain in our lives comes from difficult circumstances, from clashes with people, from things not working out. We pour enormous effort into changing our circumstances, changing other people, changing things. Yet for all the changing, the pain is still there. Why? Because the root of the problem is not outside; it is inside. If someone has no good relationship with themselves, even if they moved to a deserted island, they would still have to live with someone very hard to live with — themselves.

In our last lesson we saw together that the first priority in relationships is “our relationship with God”. God is the source; cut off from the source, every relationship runs dry. Today we take one step further, to see the second key in the order of relationships: our relationship with ourselves.

Here are two sentences, brothers and sisters; please hold them in your hearts:

Without a relationship with God, there can be no relationship with ourselves.

Without a relationship with ourselves, there can be no relationship with others.

This is not a slogan from psychology; it is the order of Scripture. When God created humankind, first came the relationship between God and man — God breathed the breath of life into man’s nostrils; then came man’s relationship with himself — “The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25); and only last came the relationships between people, and between people and all creation. When people sinned and their relationship with God was broken, the very first thing that happened next was that their relationship with themselves broke — they realised they were naked, sewed fig leaves together to make coverings for themselves, and then hid. Brothers and sisters, covering up and hiding are the oldest symptoms of a person’s broken relationship with themselves.

The Reformer John Calvin, at the opening of Book One, Chapter One of his Institutes of the Christian Religion, wrote a sentence that has been quoted for nearly five hundred years: nearly all our wisdom consists of two parts — the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. He goes on to say that the two are bound together, and that no one ever truly knows himself unless he has first looked upon the face of God. That is the heart of today’s lesson.

So today we are not here to learn a set of psychological techniques for “loving yourself”. We are here to see afresh, in God’s light, one truth: our relationship with ourselves grows out of our relationship with God; and a life in which the inside and the outside agree is lived out by the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Passages, Three Settings
sections.html:
Today’s message rests on three passages. Let’s first get to know their background briefly, so that we don’t read them out of context.

The first is Matthew 22:37–40. These words were spoken during Passion Week. The Lord Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey on Sunday and cleansed the Temple on Monday; in the days that followed, the chief priests, scribes, Pharisees and Sadducees took turns testing him with one question after another. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar? In the resurrection, whose wife will that woman be? Finally a lawyer came forward and asked him: “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law?”

The Jewish rabbis of the time divided the Law of Moses into six hundred and thirteen commandments and argued endlessly over which weighed most. This was an academic trap and a spiritual trap — because whichever commandment Jesus chose, he would offend one faction or another.

Yet Jesus’ answer gathered up the whole mountain range of the law in one stroke. He quoted Deuteronomy 6:5, the Shema that every devout Jew recited morning and evening; and he quoted Leviticus 19:18: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” He put one first and the other second, and then said: “The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” The Greek word behind “depend” means “to hang” — the whole Old Testament is like a door hung on these two hinges. Brothers and sisters, for a door to open smoothly, both hinges must be aligned; lose one, and the door hangs crooked.

The second is James 1:22. James was the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh and the leader of the church in Jerusalem. His letter may well be one of the earliest books of the New Testament, written to Jewish Christians scattered abroad and suffering persecution. James is practical, direct and doesn’t beat about the bush: in its one hundred and eight verses there are nearly sixty commands. What concerned him most was this: faith without works is dead. So he says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.”

The third is Romans 7:15 and 8:2. Romans is Paul’s letter to the church in Rome, which he had not yet visited, written around AD 56–57, probably from Corinth. Chapter 7 is the most naked confession in the whole Bible: “For I don’t know what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15) Paul is not describing here how bad an unbeliever is; he is describing how utterly powerless a person becomes when relying only on the law and on their own willpower. He writes all the way to Romans 7:24, where he cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” Then his pen turns, and chapter 8 opens with the light of dawn: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus… For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:1–2)

Brothers and sisters, notice the order of these three passages: Matthew tells us “the relationship we should have”, James points out “the symptoms of the break”, and Romans gives us “the way out to victory”. That is also the order of today’s three key points.

sections.heading: 1. The Precondition for Loving Your Neighbour as Yourself: A Healthy Relationship with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the first key point.

“A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” (Matthew 22:39)

When we read this verse, we usually see only the first part: “love your neighbour”. We put the whole weight of the verse on “love your neighbour”, and then reproach ourselves: why can’t I manage to love? But in this sentence the Lord Jesus has placed a key, and that key is in the last word — “yourself”.

“Love your neighbour as yourself” — in the original, “love your neighbour as you love yourself”. The little Greek word for “as” is both a scale and a measuring cup. What the Lord Jesus means is this: the way you treat yourself is the mould for the way you treat others.

Life confirms it everywhere. Someone who is extremely harsh on themselves finds it hard to be lenient with others; someone who judges themselves in their heart every day will judge others the moment they open their mouth; someone who will never forgive themselves finds it hard to truly forgive others. Conversely, someone who lives in God’s grace every day has a gentle gaze and gracious words. For no one can give what they do not have.

Many people cannot love others, not because others are bad, but because there is no love inside themselves. If you draw water from a dry well, however many times you lower the bucket, it comes up empty.

So here is the question: on what basis can I accept myself?

If the basis is “I perform well”, then on the day I fail I cannot accept myself. If the basis is “other people praise me”, then on the day they turn away, I collapse. If the basis is “I’m better than so-and-so”, then I must live my whole life in comparison and never find rest.

The Bible gives us an entirely different basis:

“For we don’t have a high priest who can’t be touched with the feeling of our infirmities, but one who has been in all points tempted like we are, yet without sin. Let’s therefore draw near with boldness to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and may find grace for help in time of need.” (Hebrews 4:15–16)

Brothers and sisters, look at the logic of these two verses. We can come “with boldness”, not because we are good enough, but because the throne is “the throne of grace”; not because we have no weaknesses, but because that High Priest can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities”. When we come, we are not holding a report card; we come with empty hands. And what we receive is not wages, but mercy and grace.

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, let’s look at four more passages:

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8) God loves us not after we have become better, but while we were yet sinners.

“to the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he freely gave us favor in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). Our standing as accepted is “in the Beloved”, not in ourselves.

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). The authority to condemn is in God’s hands; since God does not condemn, what right do I have to condemn myself every day?

“We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) All love — including that healthy way of regarding yourself, neither inflated nor belittling — flows from this source: God first loved us.

Brothers and sisters, we must make a particular distinction here. The self-acceptance the Bible speaks of is not at all the “feeling good about yourself” that is so fashionable today. In a major literature review published in 2003 in the journal Psychological Science in the Public Interest, the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues found that high self-esteem in itself does not make people do better at school, get on better with others or behave less badly, and that educational programmes designed to boost self-esteem have limited effect. In other words, trying to build your worth by constantly telling yourself “I’m amazing” is a house built on sand.

What truly makes us secure is not “my assessment of myself” but “God’s declaration over me”. The difference between the two is the difference between sand and rock.

I often use this illustration. Take a hundred-dollar note, screw it up into a ball, trample it underfoot and smear it with mud — what is it worth? Still a hundred dollars. Because its value lies not in its appearance but in the central bank that issued it. Brothers and sisters, your worth does not lie in the state you’re in today, but in the one who issued you — God created you in his own image and bought you back with the blood of his beloved only Son. The psalmist says: “I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.” (Psalm 139:14)

In the light of 321, this becomes even clearer.

The self-centred person is either insecure or proud.

Notice that insecurity and pride look like opposite poles, but they actually share the same root — both put the focus on the self. The proud person says, “I’m better than you.” The insecure person says, “I’m worse than you.” The subject of both sentences is “I”, and the yardstick of both is “other people”. So the proud person, once they fall, becomes insecure; the insecure person, once they succeed, becomes proud. They ride up and down on the same seesaw and never know peace all their lives.

The selfless person, however, has a third way. Selflessness is not having no self, not destroying the self, still less despising the self God made. Selflessness is “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me — “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20) Selflessness is not entering emptiness but entering into the fullness of Jesus; not being erased but being filled.

So the selfless person can honestly say: I have weaknesses, but I am not defined by my weaknesses; I have gifts, but I don’t boast in my gifts. That is exactly what Paul says: “But by the grace of God I am what I am… yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:10) What a free thing to say! No need to put yourself down, no need to puff yourself up; simply return to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, please store this key truth in your heart: our relationship with ourselves comes from our relationship with God.

You don’t first learn to love yourself and then become worthy to come before God; you are first loved by God, and then you learn how to see yourself. Reverse that order, and your whole life goes out of shape. This is exactly the order of relationships 321 speaks of: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. This order can’t be skipped, and it can’t be swapped.

sections.heading: 2. A Good Relationship with Yourself: A Life Where Inside and Outside Agree
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the second key point. Since our relationship with ourselves matters so much, is there a mark by which we can test whether that relationship is healthy? There is.

“But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” (James 1:22)

“Deluding your own selves” — the Greek verb carries the sense of “miscalculating”, like someone who has done their sums wrong yet is convinced they’re right. James says that a person who hears the word but doesn’t do it is keeping false accounts on themselves. The income column in their heart is full of teachings heard, tears shed and amens said, but none of it has ever truly been entered into the books.

James then gives a very vivid picture: “For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man looking at his natural face in a mirror; for he sees himself, and goes away, and immediately forgets what kind of man he was.” (James 1:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, what does it mean not to have a good relationship with yourself? It means hearing one thing, thinking another, saying another and doing another. What you believe in your heart isn’t lived out; what you say with your mouth, you can’t do yourself. What happens to such a person? Conflict within, a painful life, no peace, no joy.

A little earlier in the same chapter, James has already given his diagnosis of such a person: “He is a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.” (James 1:8) “Double-minded” in the original is literally “two-souled”. When a person has two voices, two directions and two sets of standards inside, how can they have peace?

On the other hand, when what a person believes in their heart, thinks in their mind, says with their mouth and does in their actions all agree, they become joyful, free and light.

The Lord Jesus said: “But let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes’ and your ‘No’ be ‘No.’ Whatever is more than these is of the evil one.” (Matthew 5:37) The psalmist prays: “Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (Psalm 51:6) What God values has never been the surface: “for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7)

There’s a spiritual illustration here that fits very well.

Think of a car: the steering wheel turns left, but the tyres point right — what happens? It pulls, it judders, it loses control. Anyone who drives knows that when the wheel alignment is out, you have to keep fighting the steering wheel and the car still drifts; the tyres wear unevenly, fuel consumption goes up, and by the end of the journey you’re especially tired. But when everything points the same way, the car runs smoothly; you only need to rest your hands lightly on the wheel, and it goes straight and true by itself.

The same is true of us: when inside and outside don’t agree, life goes out of control; when inside and outside agree, life is lived in peace.

Here’s one more illustration. Before an orchestra plays, the oboe sounds a standard A, and the whole orchestra tunes to it. The International Organization for Standardization has set this note at four hundred and forty vibrations per second — that is, 440 hertz. Notice: it isn’t the violins tuning to the cellos; the whole orchestra tunes together to the same standard note. If everyone tuned to their own pitch, it wouldn’t be music; it would be noise. Our lives are the same: it isn’t me tuning to you, but each of us first tuning to God, and then harmony between us comes naturally.

Psychology offers supporting evidence here too. In his 1961 book On Becoming a Person, the humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers put forward the idea of “congruence”. He held that when a person’s inner experience, their conscious sense of self and their outward expression match one another, that person is on the road to health and maturity; but when inside and outside are split, they become anxious, defensive and exhausted. Another social psychologist, Leon Festinger, proposed his famous “theory of cognitive dissonance” in 1957: when a person’s beliefs and behaviour don’t agree, a marked discomfort arises within them, and they instinctively look for a way to remove it — either by changing their behaviour or by bending their beliefs.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where the danger lies. When what we believe and what we do don’t agree, if we refuse to change our behaviour, we will slowly lower the standard, revise the truth and find excuses for ourselves. This is the most frightening process in “deluding your own selves” — not a single lie, but a shift, inch by inch.

Let me give you another scene from life. A brother shared in his small group that God had moved him to forgive his father, and everyone was moved to tears. After the meeting, in the car park, his father rang. He glanced at the phone and rejected the call. What did he feel inside at that moment? It wasn’t peace; it was being torn apart. Brothers and sisters, our pain often comes not from being insufficiently spiritual, but from our inside and our outside being out of alignment.

In medicine there is a class of illnesses called autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. The principle is simple but very sad: the immune system, meant to protect the body, mistakes the body’s own tissue for an enemy and attacks it. The body isn’t brought down by an outside enemy; it is wounded by itself. Brothers and sisters, a life in which inside and outside don’t agree is a spiritual autoimmune disease — your greatest drain comes not from attacks outside, but from self-attack within.

So we must hold on to this key truth: the mark of a good relationship with yourself is that the inside and the outside agree.

In the light of 321: rely on the heart, and you’ll be whole; rely on the brain, and you’ll be divided.

The person who relies on the brain is calculating how others see them, while also calculating how to look spiritual, while also calculating what’s most to their own advantage. Three lines pull against each other — how could they not be tired? The person who relies on the heart looks only to Jesus, listens to the voice of the Holy Spirit, speaks the truth and walks in the truth; inside there is only one line. That is why 321 says: rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Solomon wrote this principle down long ago: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 3. From Inner Struggle to Victory: Building Your Relationship with Yourself by the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at the third key point.

The first two points may already have pierced our hearts. We admit it: I often don’t accept myself, and I’m often not the same inside as outside. So where is the way out?

The Bible does not leave us in self-reproach. First it lets one of the greatest apostles put into words what is in our hearts:

“For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: it is Paul who says this. Not a new believer, but Paul — who made three missionary journeys and was thrown into prison for the Lord. He says: I want to do good, but I can’t; I know what’s right, but I can’t live it out.

He describes the dilemma in even finer detail: “For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18)

Notice this line: “desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.”

Brothers and sisters, this sentence hits the nail on the head. We never lack resolutions. We make resolutions every New Year’s Day, at every special conference, after every Sunday sermon. What we lack is not resolve; what we lack is power.

This is where we struggle too: we know we shouldn’t get angry, yet we can’t control it; we know we should love others, yet we can’t do it; we know we should obey God, yet we keep failing.

Why?

Paul gives the answer, but not at the start of chapter 7 — only after chapter 7 has reached a dead end. He goes all the way to the bottom and cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24) Brothers and sisters, notice that he asks “who”, not “what”. He doesn’t ask, “What method is there?” He asks, “Who is there?” No method could save him; only one person could. So the next sentence is: “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)

And then the door of chapter 8 swings open:

“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

The word “law” here carries the sense of “a law of nature, a principle”. There are two laws here: the law of sin and of death, and the law of the Spirit of life. Brothers and sisters, a law can’t be abolished by effort; it can only be overcome by a higher law.

We all know about gravity. Let go of a pen and it falls; however hard you grit your teeth, you can’t change that. Yet an aircraft weighing hundreds of tonnes can climb thirty thousand feet into the sky. Has gravity disappeared? No. A higher law — aerodynamics — has overcome it. Once the plane’s engines cut out, gravity takes effect immediately.

Brothers and sisters, the Christian life is exactly like this. The law of sin has not been abolished, but there is a higher law — the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus — that has set us free. So the secret of our victory is not gritting our teeth against gravity; it is keeping the engines running and letting the wind of the Holy Spirit hold us up.

There is another illustration hidden in the original languages of the Bible. The word for “Spirit” is ruach in Hebrew and pneuma in Greek, and both words mean “wind” and “breath” at the same time. The Lord Jesus said: “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.” (John 3:8) For a sailing ship to cross an ocean, no sailor is strong enough to row across the Pacific; the sailor’s skill lies not in making wind, but in setting the sails and holding the rudder true. Brothers and sisters, yet we so often furl our sails and then row with all our might. That is “relying on the brain and ourselves”.

So the answer is clear: not by effort, but by the Holy Spirit.

In Galatians Paul puts this secret very practically: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) And again: “If we live by the Spirit, let’s also walk by the Spirit.” (Galatians 5:25) The Lord Jesus himself said: “I am the vine.
