You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice the Lord’s words: not “you can do a little less”, but “you can do nothing”. A branch doesn’t need to worry about bearing fruit; a branch needs only one thing — to stay joined to the vine.

When we return to our relationship with God and rely on the Holy Spirit, something wonderful happens: our faith and our actions begin to agree. Not that we grit our teeth and haul our behaviour up to match our faith, but that life grows from within and naturally bears fruit. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice: fruit is “borne”, not “manufactured”.

Here I want to give a special reminder to brothers and sisters who are in a weak place: when you can’t do it, don’t reproach yourself, don’t give up — turn.

Self-reproach puts the focus on yourself; turning puts the focus on Jesus. Self-reproach pulls you deeper and deeper; turning gives you strength at once.

Psychological research also confirms this direction. Since 2003, Kristin Neff, a psychologist at the University of Texas at Austin, has developed research on “self-compassion”, and the results consistently show that people who beat themselves up harshly after failing are actually more likely to avoid, procrastinate and fail again; while those who can acknowledge their weakness and keep going are more willing to take responsibility and get back on their feet more quickly. Of course, our foundation goes deeper than psychology — we rely not on being kind to ourselves, but on the High Priest who can be “touched with the feeling of our infirmities”.

The Church Father Augustine, in the first chapter of his Confessions, wrote the summary of his whole life: Lord, you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Brothers and sisters, that sentence says everything about the human condition. The restlessness inside us is not because we haven’t tried hard enough, but because we have not yet come to rest in him.

So hold on firmly to this key truth: rely on yourself, and you struggle; rely on the Holy Spirit, and you overcome.

In the light of 321: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you can live it out; rely on the brain and yourself, and you can’t.

When a person is connected with God and lives by the Holy Spirit, they will be the same inside and out, have peace in their heart and live with joy.

That is what it means to have a good relationship with yourself.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Order of Relationships Cannot Be Reversed
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, when we set today’s message within the whole picture of 321, it becomes clearer still.

First, the Three Foundations.

Jesus is my role model. The Lord Jesus is the only person in history whose inside and outside agreed completely. What he thought in his heart, said with his mouth and did with his hands were one and the same. He said he was gentle and humble in heart, and he really did wash his disciples’ feet; he said he would lay down his life, and he really did go to the cross. He did not merely speak the truth; he is the truth.

The Bible is my standard. My view of myself cannot take other people’s comments as its standard, nor my own feelings; it can take only God’s word as its standard. Feelings deceive, but God’s word stands firm in heaven for ever.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. As we said in the third point: agreement between inside and outside is not something we achieve by self-cultivation; it is the fruit the Holy Spirit bears within us.

Second, the Two Core Values.

Let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, that chaotic kingdom inside you needs a King. When you sit on the throne yourself, you are at once the defendant, the prosecutor and the judge, and you will judge yourself to exhaustion. When Jesus takes the throne and the authority to judge is handed back to him, you are set free.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. A truly selfless person need not take the credit when they succeed, and need not fall apart when they fail, because the glory was never theirs in the first place. This is the deepest secret of being at peace with yourself — no longer needing achievement to prove yourself.

The Goal: establish God’s system. What God wants is not a group of people who are harmonious on the surface and torn apart inside, but a people who are the same inside and out and love one another, to be his system on earth.

Third, the self-centred life and selflessness.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Today we have seen that in our relationship with ourselves, the self-centred life bears two kinds of fruit: the pride of self-exaltation, and the pride of self-rejection. Yes, self-rejection is also a form of pride, because it is still saying: “God’s view doesn’t count; mine is the one that counts.”

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. This principle applies not only between people, but also between a person and themselves. The more harshly you treat yourself, the stronger the resistance inside you; the more you return to God in grace, the faster you are healed within.

Fourth, the fivefold change.

Mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice the order: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. Today’s lesson begins precisely with the mindset — exchanging the mindset “I must be good enough to deserve love” for the mindset “I am already loved, so I can become good”. Once the mindset changes, life loosens up.

Fifth, the shift in perspective.

From the human to God’s — not asking “How do others see me?” but “How does God see me?” From the earthly to the heavenly — my worth lies not in an earthly report card but in heaven’s book of life. From the temporary to the eternal — today’s failure is not the end of the story. From the worldly to the godly — the world says “love yourself” and puts the self at the centre; the Bible says true freedom is putting Jesus at the centre.

Sixth, the 920 practice.

Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. Brothers and sisters, there’s a lesson here that is often overlooked: the “2” you have known the longest is in fact yourself. If you can’t be patient and gentle with yourself, how will you be patient and gentle with others? Start today practising the fruit of the Spirit on yourself — be patient with yourself, because God is patient with you.

Seventh, 235 relationships.

Become a “2”, a spiritual companion, with selfless people; establish “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, someone whose inside and outside don’t agree cannot have a true spiritual companion, because they don’t dare let anyone see their real self. Only when you are at peace with yourself can you open up to others; and only when you open up can you have real companions. So our relationship with ourselves is not a private matter; it directly decides whether we can establish God’s system.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living: Building a Right Relationship with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, hearing the word without doing it is deluding ourselves. So we must turn today’s message into three actions we can practise.

Practice 1: Each day, declare and receive God’s love, and learn to accept yourself

Don’t define yourself by your past, your failures or your performance; see yourself through God’s love.

Every morning, declare your identity with one sentence of truth: “I am loved by God.” “I am accepted.”

Brothers and sisters, declaring is not self-hypnosis; it is putting back into your heart what God has already said. God says: “you have been precious and honored in my sight, and I have loved you” (Isaiah 43:4). This isn’t boasting; it’s agreeing with God’s word.

How to practise: each morning, declare your identity with one sentence of truth. You can use today’s verses: I am accepted in the Beloved (Ephesians 1:6); in Christ Jesus I am not condemned (Romans 8:1).

Practice 2: Practise “doing what you say”, building a life where inside and outside agree

Don’t just hear the word and be moved; choose to live it out. The truth you hear today, go and do today.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t make ten resolutions at once; ten resolutions made together are as good as none. Choose just one today — the smallest, simplest one you can actually do today.

How to practise: each day, choose the simplest act of obedience and carry it out. For example: the phone call you need to make today — make it now; the name that came to mind today — pray for that person now; the thing you promised your child today — do it this evening.

Practice 3: When you are weak, don’t rely on yourself — turn to the Holy Spirit

When you find you can’t do it, don’t reproach yourself and don’t give up; turn to God.

Just say one sentence in your heart: “Lord, I rely on you. I can’t do it; please help me.”

Brothers and sisters, this one short prayer is worth more than an hour of self-condemnation. Self-reproach is going round and round inside yourself; prayer is plugging straight into the power supply.

How to practise: whenever you struggle, pray one sentence at once and turn to the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 6. Taking the Practices Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
321 teaches us that there are eight stages in changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Let’s use these eight stages to carry the three practices above all the way through.

Stage 1, Information. Today you have received this: our relationship with ourselves comes from our relationship with God; agreement between inside and outside is the mark of health; only by the Holy Spirit can we overcome. Please copy today’s three passages onto a card — Matthew 22:39, James 1:22 and Romans 8:2 — and put it where you’ll see it every day.

Stage 2, Revelation. Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you: Lord, in what area have I kept refusing to accept myself? In what area do I hear one thing and do another? Pray: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.” (Psalm 139:23–24)

Stage 3, Conviction. Once you’ve seen it, agree with God’s view and stop arguing. If God says you are forgiven, don’t rake over the past again. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9) To keep condemning yourself after confessing is to disbelieve God’s faithfulness.

Stage 4, Implementation. Do that smallest thing today. Don’t wait until you feel right; don’t wait until circumstances improve. Faith has never been seeing first and then walking; it is walking first and then seeing.

Stage 5, Evaluation. Each evening, take three minutes: did what I said and what I did line up today? Was there anything I said but didn’t do? David said something very honest: “When I kept silence, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.” (Psalm 32:3) Without evaluation, things pile up inside; with evaluation, there is release.

Stage 6, Correction. When you find a mismatch, adjust at once. It might mean going to apologise, going to make good on something you promised, or deleting an exaggerated remark. Correction is not humiliation; correction is freedom.

Stage 7, Repetition. Obedience once is an event; repeated obedience is a life. Wheel alignment isn’t something you set once and never have go out again; after a long time on the road the car still has to go back to the garage for a check. Our hearts, too, need to come back to the Lord every day to be recalibrated.

Stage 8, Multiplication. When you yourself have experienced freedom, go and take someone with you. Tell them today’s three sentences: our relationship with God decides our relationship with ourselves; only when inside and outside agree is there true peace; only by the Holy Spirit can we overcome. Then walk alongside them for a while. This is 235 — once you have your “2”, you begin to have your “3”, and in the end it grows into a “5”.

Brothers and sisters, these eight stages are not a course; they are a road.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call: Align with God First, Then Be at One with Yourself
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, I want to remind you of one thing: your greatest enemy is not other people, but that “self that is out of agreement within”.

Stop deceiving yourself. Stop living divided.

What God wants to give you is a life that is real, free and joyful. The Lord Jesus said: “You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.” (John 8:32) Notice: not “you will know doctrine”, but “you will know the truth”; and not that the truth gives you knowledge, but that the truth makes you free.

True joy is not outward smooth sailing, but inward agreement.

Aligned with God, at one with yourself. Such a person, whatever their circumstances, can stand firm and live with joy.

A compass is a fine picture of this. The needle of a compass doesn’t look at the needles beside it; it points to one place only. And every navigator knows that there is an angle of difference between true north and magnetic north, which must be corrected for, or on a long voyage you will drift away from your destination. Brothers and sisters, our hearts have an angle of difference too — our old mindsets, old wounds, old condemnation. We need to come back every day to God’s word to correct it.

This is the order of our whole lives: first connect with God, then align with ourselves, then love others, and only last get on with tasks. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. Don’t reverse it; don’t skip over it.

This morning I want to invite you to do three things.

First, hand over to the Lord that self you have never been willing to forgive. Since God does not condemn you, stop condemning yourself.

Second, that thing you “said but never did” — go and do it today. Even if it is only a phone call, an apology or a hug.

Third, put down the oar you’ve rowed with until you’re exhausted, and set your sails. Stop relying on the brain and yourself; start relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit.

Let Jesus be King — King of your thoughts, King of your tongue, King of your actions, King of every hidden corner within you. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when you live out a life that is real, whole and free, what people see is not how strong you are, but how real Jesus is.

May we, all our lives, first connect with God, then align with ourselves, live out a real life, build healthy relationships, and step by step become overcomers.

keyVerses: Jesus said to him, “ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ The whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments.” (Matthew 22:37–40)
But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves. (James 1:22)
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death. (Romans 8:2)
practices: Each day, declare and receive God’s love, and learn to accept myself
Practise “doing what I say”, building a life where inside and outside agree
When weak, don’t rely on myself — turn to the Holy Spirit
prayer: Lord! I want to build a right relationship with myself.
No more rejecting myself; no more deceiving myself.

I confess that I often define myself by my performance, and often condemn myself in my heart. Lord, please forgive me, for you have already accepted me in Christ, yet I still refuse to accept the one you have accepted.
I will accept myself in your love, and live out the truth in the Holy Spirit.
Let my heart, my thoughts, my words and my actions all be at one in you.

Whatever I believe in my heart, give me strength to live it out; whatever I say with my mouth, keep me to doing every bit of it. When I am weak and cannot do it, remind me not to reproach myself, not to give up, but simply to turn to you.
Make me live a life of peace, joy and freedom, live out Christ, and become an overcomer.
May my home, my small group and my workplace all see your glory through one real life.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
discussion: Matthew 22:39: “A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Please be still for a minute and think: how do you usually treat yourself? Harshly, neglectfully, or in grace? Is that the very same way you treat a particular person close to you? Please share one specific example.

James 1:22: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves.” Is there something you “know but haven’t done” lately that has left you without peace inside? This week, what is the smallest, most concrete act of obedience you plan to take? Say it out loud, so the group can pray for you and ask how it went at the next meeting.
l150.title: Our Relationship with Ourselves
l150.subtitle: The Priority of Relationships (Part 2)
l150.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: Not a Problem of Technique, but a Problem of Life
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a scene that could happen in a great many churches.

Two sisters had stood in the same choir for seven years. One stood on the left, the other on the right, with only three people between them. For seven years, every Lord’s Day, they praised God together, sang “We Are One Family” together, said “Amen” together. But when the service ended, one went out by the east door and the other by the west door, and in seven years they never exchanged a single complete sentence.

What started it? Nobody remembers any more. Probably a disagreement at rehearsal; probably a remark that got twisted as it was passed along. The matter was small — so small you’d be embarrassed to mention it. But the wall was high — so high that seven years were not enough to climb over it.

Brothers and sisters, I have to ask a very honest question: is worship like that pleasing to God?

Together we now come to the third level of the priority of relationships. We have learnt that relationships have an order that must never be turned upside down — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last of all with things. In the first lesson we looked at our “relationship with God”, the source of everything. In the second we looked at our “relationship with ourselves”, the outlet of everything. Today we look at the third level — our relationship with others.

It is an intensely practical subject, and one that cuts very close to the heart.

In today’s bookshops, books on interpersonal relationships are piled high; online, course after course teaches people how to communicate, how to talk, how to manage their emotions. These things are not without value. But, brothers and sisters, the Bible shows us a deeper root —

our relationships with others are not a problem of technique; they are a problem of life.

Let me give you a picture. Take an electric fan that isn’t plugged in. Push the blades with your hand and they’ll turn. One push, one turn; push harder and you get a couple of extra spins. But the moment your hand stops, the fan stops. You could stand there all afternoon pushing until you’re drenched in sweat, and you would not get one second of breeze that came easily.

Loving people by technique is exactly like that. You can learn to smile, learn to listen, learn to wrap harsh words in pleasant packaging. But it’s all being pushed by hand: each push gives you one turn, and you yourself are the one who ends up exhausted.

Once the plug goes into the socket, though, everything changes. You don’t have to push; it turns by itself. You don’t have to strain; it turns all day. Because the turning doesn’t come from your hand — it comes from the power source.

Brothers and sisters, without love that comes from God, however hard we try, we cannot truly love people.

This is not telling us not to try. It is telling us to put our effort in the right place — to strive to be connected to the source, not to strive at pushing the blades.

Psychology, from a different angle, confirms how much relationships weigh. Harvard University has a study that began in 1938 and is still running today, the Harvard Study of Adult Development. It followed more than seven hundred men across their whole lives, and later extended to their spouses and their descendants. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled decades of findings into one sentence: what truly keeps people healthy and happy across a lifetime is not wealth, and not fame, but good relationships.

Again, a team at Brigham Young University in the United States led by Julianne Holt-Lunstad published a meta-analysis in PLoS Medicine in 2010. Bringing together 148 studies and data from more than three hundred thousand people, it found that those with stronger social connections had roughly a fifty per cent greater likelihood of survival than those whose connections were weak.

Science can measure the importance of relationships, but it cannot measure their source. The Bible tells us where that source is —

“Love is of God.” (1 John 4:7)

So in this lesson today we want to see two things:

First, our relationships with others are the overflow of our relationship with God.

Second, our relationships with others are a vital fulfilment of God’s will.

Today’s message in one sentence: let God’s love flow within you — through you, out to others, on to the next generation, until it flows into God’s kingdom.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Aged Apostle, and a Sermon on a Mountain
sections.html:
To receive today’s message accurately, we first need to know where our key passages come from.

The first is 1 John chapter 4.

The author of this letter is generally held to be the apostle John — the disciple who leaned against Jesus’ breast at the Last Supper (John 13:23), the disciple whom the Lord loved. It is generally dated somewhere between AD 85 and 95, and was very likely written from Ephesus in Asia Minor. By this time John was a white-haired old man. Almost all the rest of the Twelve had already been martyred; he alone remained. He was writing to the churches he shepherded, and he calls them again and again “little children” — this is a spiritual father speaking to his sons and daughters.

What situation was the church facing? Early Gnostic ideas were seeping in. This way of thinking held that matter is evil and only spirit is good, so Christ could not really have come in the flesh; and it held that salvation depends on a special kind of “knowledge” available only to a select few. Such thinking produced two terrible results: first, a denial of the Incarnation; second, the turning of faith into lofty, abstract theory that has nothing to do with daily living or with one’s brothers.

Some people began to say, “I know God.” “I am in the light.” “I love God.” Yet in their everyday lives they were cold towards the brothers around them, scornful, even hateful.

So old John wrote this letter to give several “touchstones” that would help believers tell the genuine from the false. He uses one sentence pattern again and again: “If a man says … he is a liar.”

“He who says he is in the light and hates his brother is in the darkness even until now.” (1 John 2:9)

“If a man says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20)

Brothers and sisters, please notice: old John does not want us to go and inspect other people; he wants us to inspect ourselves honestly. He doesn’t ask how great your knowledge is; he asks how genuine your love is.

The second passage is Matthew chapter 5.

The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew — the tax collector the Lord called as he sat at the tax booth (Matthew 9:9). This Gospel is generally thought to have been written around AD 60, mainly for Jewish readers. Throughout the book it keeps quoting the Old Testament to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — that he is the King.

And chapters 5 to 7 are the Sermon on the Mount we know so well — the constitution the King proclaims to the people of his kingdom.

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus six times in a row uses the pattern “You have heard that it was said … But I tell you,” pressing the demands of the law from behaviour into the heart, from the outside to the inside. And the last of these, the highest of them all, is about loving our enemies:

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you,” (Matthew 5:43–44)

It’s worth noticing that “hate your enemy” is something the Old Testament never commanded. What the Old Testament says is “you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18). “Hate your enemy” was an inference added by the rabbinic tradition of the day. Jesus tears down that human addition, and then lifts the standard all the way up to heaven —

“that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.” (Matthew 5:45)

Brothers and sisters, remember this background: 1 John tells us that “loving people is the proof that we love God”; the Sermon on the Mount tells us that “loving our enemies is the mark of the Father’s children”. One speaks of the source, the other of the height. Put the two passages together and you have the skeleton of today’s lesson.

sections.heading: 1. Our Relationships with Others Are the Proof of Our Relationship with God
sections.html:
1. Love has a source

Let’s first read the key passage in full:

“Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God. He who doesn’t love doesn’t know God, for God is love.” (1 John 4:7–8)

Brothers and sisters, notice the logic here. John doesn’t say, “We should love one another because things will be more peaceful that way.” Nor does he say, “because that’s how the church will grow.” What he says is — “for love is of God.”

The word for “love” used in the original here is ἀγάπη (agapē). Greek has more than one word for love: στοργή (storgē) is family affection, φιλία (philia) is the love of friends, ἔρως (erōs) is passionate desire. All three of these assume that “the other person deserves it” or that “I feel something”. But when the New Testament describes God’s love it uses ἀγάπη — a love that springs from the will, that gives itself away, and that does not depend on how lovable the other person is.

This distinction is crucial. The first three loves are in us by nature; you don’t need to be born again to have them. Only the fourth is received from God.

That is why verse 8 says something that shakes the heart: “God is love.” The Bible doesn’t say “God has love”; it says “God is love.” Love is not one item among God’s many attributes; love is the very being of God.

And verse 19 puts it even more plainly: “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)

Brothers and sisters, the word “first” fixes the order of the whole matter. It isn’t that we squeeze out some love first and then God loves us; it is that God loved us first, and so we have love to pour out.

Paul says the same thing: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.” (Romans 5:5) The picture in that word “poured” is of something tipped out, brimming over. God doesn’t hand you a single drop and tell you to make it last; he pours it out until you are so full that it overflows.

2. Whoever loves God will surely love people

Then John speaks with the utmost bluntness:

“If a man says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20)

There is no wriggle room in this sentence. John’s reasoning runs like this: if you can’t bring yourself to love the brother you can see, how could you possibly love the God you cannot see?

It’s like someone saying, “I’m an excellent swimmer — I just never get into the water.” What would we think?

Brothers and sisters, loving God is invisible; loving people is visible. God sets “loving people” in front of us as the testing ground of “loving God”.

So verse 21 goes on: “This commandment we have from him, that he who loves God should also love his brother.” (1 John 4:21)

The Lord Jesus himself bound the two commandments together:

“ ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the first and great commandment. A second likewise is this, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ ” (Matthew 22:37–39)

Notice the words “A second likewise”. “Likewise” means of the same nature and of equal weight. These are not two things; they are two sides of one thing — like the two faces of a coin. You can’t keep heads and throw away tails.

3. Love is the clearest mark of a disciple

On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus gave his disciples a new commandment:

“A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” (John 13:34–35)

Brothers and sisters, what is “new” about this commandment? The Old Testament had already said, “love your neighbor as yourself.” What’s new is the standard — “Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” From then on, the measure of love is no longer “as yourself” but “as the Lord”. And how did the Lord love us? He died for us.

Then the Lord said something that has become the church’s most important sign for two thousand years: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples.”

The Lord did not say: everyone will know you are my disciples by your gifts.

The Lord did not say: everyone will know you are my disciples by your eloquence.

The Lord did not say: everyone will know you are my disciples by your learning, your achievements, the size of your congregations.

What the Lord said is: everyone will know you are my disciples by your love for one another.

The church father Tertullian, in his Apology at the end of the second century AD, recorded what the pagans of his day said about Christians: “See how they love one another.” It was an age of martyrdom. Christians had no social standing, no political power, no splendid buildings. What they had was love for one another. And that alone was enough to make the whole Roman Empire stop and stare.

4. An example from daily life, and supporting evidence from psychology

Let me describe another familiar scene.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever noticed what we do first when the tap at home suddenly runs dry? Most people start by tapping the tap, tightening it a bit, loosening it again. But someone with experience walks somewhere else — he goes to check the water tank, the main valve. Because a problem at the outlet very often isn’t at the outlet.

Our relationships with others are that outlet. When they run dry, turn rough, go bitter, don’t just keep working away at the outlet. Go back to the source.

Psychology has a phenomenon confirmed by a large body of research, called “emotional contagion”. Elaine Hatfield of the University of Hawaii, John Cacioppo of Ohio State University and their colleagues showed in a 1994 book that people unconsciously mimic the facial expressions, tone of voice and posture of those around them, and as a result genuinely catch the other person’s emotions.

Brothers and sisters, emotions are contagious, and so is life. When someone who walks with God every day comes into a room, the very air of the room changes. When someone with resentment stored up in their heart sits down, the whole table grows uneasy. Whatever is inside you is what will flow out.

5. A 321 Insight

In the 321 vision we set out the priority of relationships very clearly: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Once that order is turned upside down, the whole of life is thrown into confusion.

Get it right with God, and you’ll get it right with people.

Get it wrong with God, and things will certainly go wrong with people.

So when you find that whatever you do you simply can’t love a certain person, don’t rush to fix that person, and don’t rush to fix your temper. First go back before God and ask: “Lord, is something blocked between you and me?”

This is where the Three Foundations come into play. Jesus is my role model — as he loves me, so I love others. The Bible is my standard — it isn’t my feelings that have the final say; it’s God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — loving people isn’t done by gritting our teeth; it’s the Holy Spirit pouring God’s love into our hearts.

Brothers and sisters, this is why 321 says again and again: life first, then relationships, then ministry. If life isn’t flowing, relationships certainly won’t flow; if relationships aren’t flowing, ministry will certainly become a burden.

sections.heading: 2. The Highest Level of Loving People: Loving Our Enemies
sections.html:
1. The hardest command of all

“But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.” (Matthew 5:44–45)

Brothers and sisters, this is the hardest command the Lord Jesus has given us.

Loving lovable people isn’t hard. Loving people who love you isn’t hard. What’s hard is loving the unlovable — loving the person who has hurt you, loving the one whose name alone makes your stomach knot the moment it crosses your mind.

The Lord himself explained why the standard is set so high:

“For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same? If you only greet your friends, what more do you do than others? Don’t even the tax collectors do the same?” (Matthew 5:46–47)

What this means is that tax collectors can love their own people, and so can the Gentiles; that needs no new birth, no Holy Spirit. What truly shows you to be a child of the Father is that you can love those who do not love you.

So the conclusion of this passage is: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

2. Why is it so hard? Because of the self-centred life

Why is loving our enemies so hard?

Brothers and sisters, the answer lies in the core message of 321: because there is still a “self” inside us.

When we are still keeping score, still getting even, still passing judgement, that is not a lack of good breeding. It means the “self” is still sitting on the throne.

We keep score because “I” feel I’ve been short-changed.

We get even because “my” dignity has been touched.

We pass judgement because “I” need to prove I’m more right than he is.

You see, underneath all three lies the very same word — “self”.

321 says it very plainly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

When I refuse to forgive, I am in fact climbing into the judge’s seat. That seat isn’t mine; it is God’s. Romans says: “Don’t seek revenge yourselves, beloved, but give place to God’s wrath. For it is written, ‘Vengeance belongs to me; I will repay, says the Lord.’ ” (Romans 12:19)

Brothers and sisters, forgiveness doesn’t say, “This doesn’t matter.” Forgiveness says, “This isn’t mine to deal with; it’s God’s.” Forgiveness doesn’t just wipe the debt off the books; forgiveness hands the account book over to the righteous Judge.

And 321 puts it in a way that cuts deep: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

In a broken relationship, as long as both sides insist, “I’ll apologise when he apologises first,” that relationship will stay stuck there for ever. Whoever humbles himself first is the first to go free.

3. Forgiveness is good medicine for the body too

On this point psychology and medicine offer some fascinating supporting evidence.

In 2001 the psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College in the United States and her colleagues published an experiment in the journal Psychological Science. They asked participants to recall a real experience of being hurt, under two different frames of mind: “holding a grudge and replaying the hurt”, and “empathy and forgiveness”. The results showed that while participants dwelt on grudge-holding imagery, their blood pressure, heart rate and facial muscle tension all rose markedly; and when they turned towards empathy and forgiveness, these physical indicators promptly came down.

In other words, refusing to forgive doesn’t make the other person ill. It only makes you ill.

There’s a widely circulated saying, generally thought to come from a devotional writer’s image: holding a grudge is like drinking poison yourself and expecting the other person to die. Accounts of where the image comes from differ, but it states the truth precisely.

Brothers and sisters, you think you’re the one holding on to that person. In fact it’s that person who is holding on to you.

4. A true testimony: Corrie ten Boom’s hand

During the Second World War, Corrie ten Boom of the Netherlands and her whole family were arrested for hiding Jews in their home. Her father died in prison, and Betsie, the sister she loved most dearly, died in the German concentration camp at Ravensbrück.

After the war Corrie travelled all over Europe preaching God’s forgiveness. In 1947, as the crowd dispersed after she had spoken at a church in Munich, Germany, a man came up to her, held out his hand and said, “That was a fine message, sister. It’s true — he has washed all my sins away.”

Corrie recognised him at once — he was a guard from Ravensbrück, the man who had stood at the door while she and her sister suffered every humiliation.

She later described the moment like this: she had only just finished speaking about forgiveness, yet her hand stayed frozen at her side and simply would not reach out. Anger churned within her; she remembered her sister’s wasted face. She knew she had to forgive, but she could not do it.

So she prayed silently: “Lord Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness.”

Then, she said, she thrust out her hand — mechanically, woodenly. And in the very instant their two hands clasped, a wonderful warmth flowed from her shoulder down her arm and into her hand. With tears she cried, “I forgive you, brother, with all my heart!”

Brothers and sisters, notice the order: she didn’t have the feeling first and then reach out her hand. She reached out her hand first, and then the feeling came.

Corrie ten Boom drew her own conclusion: forgiveness is an act of the will, and the will can function regardless of the temperature of the heart.

This is exactly what 321 says — loving our enemies is not human ability; it is God’s life. If only you’re willing to stretch out your hand, God takes responsibility for pouring the love down.

5. A 321 Insight

On the cross our Lord prayed for the people who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” (Luke 23:34)

Under the stones, Stephen prayed for the people who were killing him: “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” (Acts 7:60)

Brothers and sisters, both these prayers are selfless prayers.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

And so —

Only selflessness can love its enemies.

The self-centred life will only ever love its own.

And the Bible gives us a very concrete practice: “Bless those who persecute you; bless, and don’t curse.” (Romans 12:14) “Don’t be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.” (Romans 12:21)

Dr Martin Luther King, Jr. wrote a much-quoted line in Strength to Love (1963): darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.

Brothers and sisters, that is an echo of the Sermon on the Mount.

sections.heading: 3. Our Relationships with Others Exist to Pass On and Complete God’s Plan
sections.html:
1. The purpose of relationships is more than getting along nicely

“Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20)

Brothers and sisters, when we build relationships with people, we often stop at two levels: getting along nicely, and supporting one another.

Both are very good, but neither is the finishing line.

In the Lord’s Great Commission there is one main verb — “make disciples of all nations”. In the original, μαθητεύσατε (mathēteusate) is the main verb, in the imperative, while “go”, “baptizing” and “teaching” are all participles, revolving around that main verb. In other words, the whole passage has only one centre of gravity: making disciples.

And disciples cannot be produced by broadcast; disciples are brought up by life.

Paul puts it like this: “For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you don’t have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, I became your father through the Good News.” (1 Corinthians 4:15)

Brothers and sisters, tutors by the ten thousand, but not many fathers. Tutors pass on information; fathers pass on life.

2. God’s work has never been completed by one person

In the Bible, God’s work is never finished by one person alone. It goes on generation after generation, life touching life.

Moses to Joshua. Moses led the people out of Egypt but never entered Canaan. As his death approached he called Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel: “Be strong and courageous, for you shall go with this people into the land which Yahweh has sworn to their fathers to give them; and you shall cause them to inherit it.” (Deuteronomy 31:7) The one who led them out of Egypt was Moses; the one who led them into Canaan was Joshua.

David to Solomon. David prepared the plans for the temple, the gold and silver, the materials, but he did not build it with his own hands. On his deathbed he charged Solomon: “I am going the way of all the earth. You be strong therefore, and show yourself a man; and keep the instruction of Yahweh your God, to walk in his ways … according to that which is written in the law of Moses” (1 Kings 2:2–3). The one who prepared was David; the one who built was Solomon.

Elijah to Elisha. Before he was taken up to heaven, Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask what I shall do for you, before I am taken from you.” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be on me.” (2 Kings 2:9) The prophetic office was not broken off, because someone picked up the cloak.

Mordecai to Esther. At the moment when the survival of their people hung in the balance, Mordecai spoke to the queen words that have rung down the ages: “Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14)

Brothers and sisters, listen to that sentence. The position God has given you isn’t there to make you comfortable; it is there for “such a time as this”. Your workplace, your family, your profession, your network — none of them is an accident; all of them are a trust.

Paul to Timothy. Before his martyrdom, Paul passed on the baton, and spelled out four generations of handing on: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) Paul is the first generation, Timothy the second, the faithful men the third, and the others they teach the fourth.

3. A scientific picture of life touching life

The natural world gives us a beautiful picture.

Professor Suzanne Simard, a forest ecologist at the University of British Columbia in Canada, has studied forests since the 1990s using isotope tracing. She found that the trees of a forest do not stand each on its own, but are connected to one another through underground networks of mycorrhizal fungi, and can pass carbon, nitrogen, water and chemical signals back and forth. Large old trees can send nutrients to the seedlings struggling for light in the shade beneath them, helping them survive.

A forest that looks perfectly still is, underground, a bustling network of life.

Brothers and sisters, the church should be just such a forest.

Not a row of roadside trees each going its own way, but a forest whose roots are all joined. The older send nourishment down, the younger grow up in their shade, and one day the young become great trees themselves and send nourishment on to the next generation of seedlings.

Again, in the 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma in Italy discovered “mirror neurons” in the brains of monkeys — when a monkey watches another perform an action, the neurons in its own brain responsible for that action fire as well. Later research in humans has shown that our brains come equipped with a built-in mechanism of “see it, copy it”.

This makes one thing very clear: people don’t learn by listening to how you talk; they learn by watching how you live.

So 321 says: life influences life; life multiplies life.

4. A 321 Insight

The “235 relationships” of 321 describe exactly this structure of passing on —

First comes the “2”: becoming spiritual companions with a selfless person, supporting one another and holding one another accountable.

Then comes the “3”: establishing spiritual parents and spiritual children — someone above you leading you, and someone below you whom you lead.

Then you become part of the “5”: entering a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team working in partnership, to accomplish God’s will together.

Brothers and sisters, true relationships are relationships that lead to passing on. They don’t stop at “I’m fine, you’re fine”, but go on to “together we accomplish God’s will”.

When we build the right relationships, God’s kingdom is established and revival will come.

sections.heading: 4. Relationships Across Generations and Communities: Bringing Revival to the Kingdom
sections.html:
1. God’s heart is for the whole kingdom to be connected

God’s heart is not only for individuals, nor only for small groups, but for the whole kingdom to be connected.

In his high-priestly prayer before Gethsemane, the Lord Jesus interceded earnestly for this:

“that they may all be one; even as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be one in us; that the world may believe that you sent me.” (John 17:21)

Notice the second half — “that the world may believe that you sent me.” Unity exists so that the world may believe.

Paul too urges us: “being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” (Ephesians 4:3) The word “eager” tells us that unity doesn’t happen automatically; it has to be guarded at a cost.

So when churches compete with one another, God’s kingdom suffers loss; when churches connect with one another, God’s kingdom expands.

The psalm says: “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1) And the psalm ends: “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (Psalm 133:3)

Brothers and sisters, the blessing God commands comes down “there” — on the place where brothers live together in unity.

2. Between generations: opposition or partnership

When generations oppose one another, the handing-on breaks; when generations work in partnership, revival comes.

In the last verse of the Old Testament, God’s final promise to Israel is: “He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.” (Malachi 4:6)

On the day of Pentecost in the New Testament, Peter quoted the book of Joel and proclaimed: “It will happen afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh; and your sons and your daughters will prophesy. Your old men will dream dreams. Your young men will see visions.” (Joel 2:28)

Brothers and sisters, see the partnership here: old men dreaming dreams, young men seeing visions.

The passion of the young plus the wisdom of the old equals the power of God’s kingdom.

The young have fire but often no stove; the old have a stove but often no fire. Fire without a stove blazes up fast and dies out fast; a stove without fire, however solid, is just cold iron. Put the fire into the stove and it can keep a whole household warm all winter long.

3. The witness of church history: outpouring after unity

Church history gives us a very clear witness.

From 1722 onwards, a band of persecuted Moravian brethren fled to Saxony in Germany, where Count Nikolaus von Zinzendorf took them in. On his estate they built a village called Herrnhut, meaning “the Lord’s watch”.

But these people came from different backgrounds and different traditions, and they argued endlessly; they were on the verge of splitting apart. The count laid aside his aristocratic dignity, visited them house by house, exhorted them, and led them into a covenant to be of one heart and mind. On 12 May 1727 they drew up a covenant for living together in unity.

Three months later, on 13 August 1727, at a gathering where they took Communion together, they experienced a mighty outpouring of the Holy Spirit. From that day Herrnhut began a round-the-clock prayer watch, kept in shifts — twenty-four hours a day without a break, one shift after another, for more than a hundred years. From that little village, missionaries were sent out to the West Indies, Greenland, Africa and the Americas.

Brothers and sisters, remember this order: first unity, then outpouring.

It isn’t that revival comes first and then unity; it’s that unity comes first, and then revival.

4. A 321 Insight

321 says: the Goal — establish God’s system.

What is God’s system? It is a company of selfless people, in right relationships, connected to one another, working in partnership with one another, passing life on to one another, and letting Jesus reign as King among them.

And so —

Unity brings revival; division brings loss.

Paul describes how this system works: “from whom all the body, being fitted and knit together through that which every joint supplies, according to the working in measure of each individual part, makes the body increase to the building up of itself in love.” (Ephesians 4:16)

“The working in measure of each individual part” — not grabbing someone else’s place.

“That which every joint supplies” — not living as solitary individuals.

“The building up of itself in love” — not wearing ourselves out in comparison.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at today’s message once more within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he loved his disciples to the end, he prayed for his enemies, he passed his life on to twelve men. The Bible is my standard — whether or not I love someone is not decided by my feelings but by God’s word. The Holy Spirit is my guide — the power to love people isn’t squeezed out of us; it is poured down by the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — in every relationship, let him sit on the throne, and then I don’t have to sit in the judge’s seat. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when I forgive, it isn’t to show how big-hearted I am; it is so that people may see the beauty of the Lord.

The Goal. Establish God’s system — not building my own network, but building God’s kingdom.

The fivefold change. When the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry changes. In today’s lesson the first step is a change of mindset — relationships with people are not a technique but a life; not an ornament but a mission.

The shift of perspective. From the human perspective to God’s perspective: that person isn’t just “someone who makes me uncomfortable”; he is someone the Lord bought back at a great price. From the earthly to the heavenly: this relationship doesn’t only affect this life; it will affect eternity. From the temporary to the eternal: one word of blessing today may become the turning point of someone’s whole life. From the worldly to the godly: I am not managing a network of contacts; I am building God’s household.

The 920 practice. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. In front of every “2”, we practise living out the selfless “0”, so as to bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice that the very first fruit of the Spirit is love. Not one of these nine graces can be produced by yourself, alone in your room. Patience needs someone to be patient with; kindness needs someone to be kind to; gentleness needs someone to be gentle towards. God puts people beside you precisely so that fruit may grow in you.

The 235 relationships. Find your “2” — a spiritual companion with whom you can be completely open. Establish your “3” — spiritual parents above you, spiritual children below you. Enter your “5” — building together with comrades in a fivefold-ministry team.

Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Building Relationships After God’s Own Heart
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep.

Practice 1: Take the initiative to love one person every day, rather than waiting to be loved

Don’t wait for others to treat you well first; you go and love first: a word of encouragement, a gesture of concern, some time spent alongside them.

How to practise: each day, deliberately bless one person, in word or in deed.

Information: first memorise this verse — “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) God is the one who loves first.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, so that you see how you have been “waiting” all along — waiting for the other person to speak first, to apologise first, to make the first friendly move.

Conviction: acknowledge in your heart that going “first” is the mark of God’s children, not a loss.

Implementation: do it today. Choose one person and send a sincere message — not a pleasantry, but a specific blessing.

Evaluation: in the evening, be still for three minutes and ask yourself: was I proactive today, or passive?

Correction: if you forgot today, put a time in your diary for tomorrow, just as you would schedule a meeting.

Repetition: forty days in a row, one person each day, no repeats.

Multiplication: bring this practice into your small group, and invite a brother or sister to do it with you.

Practice 2: Practise forgiveness and blessing, especially towards difficult people

When you come across someone who makes you uncomfortable: don’t avoid them, don’t judge them, choose to bless them.

How to practise: pray for three days for one person you find hard to love.

Information: remember the Lord’s command — “love your enemies … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Revelation: quieten yourself and let the Holy Spirit bring that name to the surface of your heart. Usually you won’t have to think for long; the name will come by itself.

Conviction: admit that refusing to forgive means sitting in God’s seat; admit that forgiveness is an act of the will, not the result of a feeling.

Implementation: for three days running, pray for him for three minutes each day. On the first day, ask God to bless him; on the second, ask God to change me; on the third, intercede specifically for his family, his work and his health.

Evaluation: after three days, check honestly: when you think of him, has the temperature in your heart changed?

Correction: if your heart is still hard, learn Corrie ten Boom’s prayer: “Lord Jesus, I cannot forgive him. Give me your forgiveness.”

Repetition: stretch the three days to thirty. Hatred takes a long time to grow, and it takes time to melt away.

Multiplication: when God has truly set you free, tell the story, so that someone else who is bound may go free.

Practice 3: Deliberately build relationships that pass life on

Don’t stop at friendship; take one person under your wing and help him know God better.

How to practise: begin regularly caring for one spiritual companion or new believer.

Information: remember Paul’s charge — “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Revelation: ask God to give you a name. Not the one with the most potential, but the one God lays on your heart.

Conviction: believe that you have something to give. You don’t have to become perfect first; you only need to have come to know the Lord one step ahead of him.

Implementation: arrange to meet once a week for thirty minutes. Read a passage of the Bible together, pray together, and listen to him.

Evaluation: after a month, ask him one question: “Over this past month, what has God done in you?”

Correction: if it’s just chatting with no life in it, adjust — add a passage of Scripture, add a time of prayer.

Repetition: walk with him for at least a year. Spiritual children aren’t born in a month.

Multiplication: after a year, ask him to go and take someone under his wing too. That is the four generations of 2 Timothy 2:2.

A Gentle Reminder

Relationships with people are not just a need of daily living; they are a spiritual mission.

Whom you build relationships with determines whether you are within God’s will.

Brothers and sisters, don’t just “do networking”; “make disciples”.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, we are coming to the end.

A true relationship is not just a connection; it is — letting God’s love flow, and letting life be passed on.

It flows because there is a source. It is passed on because there is a direction.

When we live out relationships like this, three things will happen: individuals will be renewed, the church will be built up, and the kingdom will be extended.

Let me go back to the two sisters at the beginning. Can a wall that has stood for seven years come down?

Yes, it can. But not by waiting another seven years — by one person walking across first.

Brothers and sisters, could the one who walks across first be you?

Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said something like this: we cannot do great things, only small things with great love.

This morning you don’t need to do anything great. You only need to do one small thing — make a phone call, say “I’m sorry”, send a blessing, pray for one name for three minutes.

Let Jesus reign as King in every one of your relationships. Let Jesus receive the glory from every one of your relationships.

May we spend our whole lives in God’s love, building genuine relationships, loving one another, building one another up, accomplishing God’s will together, and becoming overcomers.

keyVerses: “Beloved, let’s love one another, for love is of God; and everyone who loves has been born of God, and knows God.” (1 John 4:7)
“If a man says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20)
practices: Take the initiative to love one person every day, rather than waiting to be loved
Practise forgiveness and blessing, especially towards difficult people
prayer: Lord!
I want to build relationships after your own heart.
Not only to be loved, but to take the initiative to love.
Lord, I confess that I am so often waiting — waiting for others to love me first, to apologise first, to change first. Please forgive me.
I want to love my brothers and sisters, and to love the unlovable too, living out your life.
Lord, there is a name in my heart right now. I bring that person before you. I choose to forgive; I choose to bless. I cannot do it — please give me your forgiveness.
Use my life to influence lives, to bring forth life and to pass life on, so that more people may know you and build a relationship with you.
Make our church one, let the generations work in partnership, and let your kingdom be established among us.
May all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
discussion: “If a man says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who doesn’t love his brother whom he has seen, how can he love God whom he has not seen?” (1 John 4:20) Right now, is there someone whose name makes your heart tighten when you think of them? Would you be willing to tell your small group the first concrete step you intend to take?

“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2) In your life, who are your spiritual parents? Who are the spiritual children God has laid on your heart for you to lead? Please name one person, and pray for him or her.

l151.subtitle: The Priority of Relationships (Part 3): Our Relationship with Others
l151.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: Busy All Our Lives, Yet Forgetting Whom We Were Busy For
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

I’d like to start by asking you to picture a very familiar scene.

It’s ten o’clock on a Sunday night. A brother who has served for many years switches off the church lights and is the last to leave. Today he has taught two classes, carried chairs back and forth three times, and dealt with two phone calls full of complaints. He drives to the exit of the car park, then suddenly stops and sits in the driver’s seat, not wanting to pull away. He isn’t crying; he isn’t angry. He is simply tired. So tired that he says something to himself that startles even him: “I’ve done so much — but who on earth is it all for?”

Brothers and sisters, that question isn’t asked by unbelievers. It is asked by the most faithful.

Over these four lessons we have come to see that relationships have an order: first our relationship with God, second our relationship with ourselves, third our relationship with others. Today we come to the last level, and the one most easily put in the wrong place — our relationship with things.

Many people make “getting things done” the centre of gravity of their lives. We carry a ruler in our hearts, and it measures three things: how much we did, how well we did it, and whether it produced results. As children we were measured by exam scores; as adults at work we’re measured by performance; when we come into the church we measure attendance. We are so used to being measured that eventually we assume God carries the same ruler.

But, brothers and sisters, God sees things completely differently.

What God values is not things; what God values is people within relationships.

When relationships are right, things will come right of their own accord; when relationships are wrong, even the best of things will go sour. A perfect gathering can, in the course of being organised, break the hearts of the co-workers. A successful pastoral visit can, on the drive home, leave a spouse’s heart cold. The task gets done, but the people are left in pieces — and success like that is a loss on God’s books.

So today we need to understand two things. First, our relationship with things is the last in the order, not the first. Second, precisely because it is the last, it is the one most easily moved to the front.

The sociologist William Bruce Cameron, in his 1963 book Informal Sociology, wrote a much-quoted line: “Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.” That sentence isn’t Scripture, but it is like a mirror that shows up our blind spot: we very easily treat “what can be counted” as “what matters”, and so we push to the back the very thing God values most yet is hardest to quantify — relationships.

This lesson today is meant to help us put the order back the right way round. It isn’t telling us not to do things; it is telling us to do things in the right order. Because when people are right, things will be right.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Stewards, Faithfulness, and That Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias
sections.html:
To understand today’s message, we first need to step into the setting of three passages.

The first is 1 Corinthians chapter 4. The apostle Paul wrote this letter to the church in Corinth around AD 54 to 55, while he was living in Ephesus on his third missionary journey. Corinth was the capital of the Roman province of Achaia — a port city, a commercial city, and a city that prized achievement and eloquence above all. When that culture made its way into the church, it turned into factions: one said, “I follow Paul,” another, “I follow Apollos,” another, “I follow Cephas” (1 Corinthians 1:12). They were measuring God’s servants with the world’s ruler.

How does Paul respond? He doesn’t argue about who is stronger; he changes how they define their identity. “So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:1–2)

The Greek word for “steward” is οἰκονόμος (oikonomos), made up of “house” (oikos) and “to manage, to distribute” (nemō). It refers to a servant who manages the household’s affairs on his master’s behalf and hands out the food rations at the proper time. In Roman society the steward was often a capable slave, holding the keys, the account books and the granary, with a great deal of authority — but always under one unshakeable condition: the house was not his. Everything in his hands belonged to someone else.

So Paul says that what a steward is measured by is not performance but “faithfulness”. The Greek word for “faithful” is πιστός (pistos), from the same root as “faith” (pistis), meaning “trustworthy, reliable, fit to be entrusted with something”. Faithfulness isn’t an adjective about ability; it is an adjective about relationship. Whether a person is reliable is always said in relation to another person.

The second passage is the parable of the talents in Matthew 25. It is the second parable the Lord Jesus told his disciples on the Mount of Olives during Passion Week, as he spoke of the end of the age. It follows straight after the parable of the ten virgins, and is followed by the scene of the judgement of the nations. The master gave, according to each one’s ability, five talents, two talents and one. Notice the master’s praise: the one who received five gained five more, and the master said, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” The one who received two gained two more, and the master said exactly the same words (Matthew 25:23). Different results, the same praise. Because what God measures is not quantity but faithfulness.

The third passage is John chapter 21. This is the third time the risen Lord appeared to his disciples, by the Sea of Tiberias. Peter said, “I’m going fishing,” and went back to the place where he had been called three years before, back to the trade he knew best. Before the cock crowed he had denied the Lord three times, and now his heart was broken. Jesus didn’t begin by rebuking him, nor by handing out assignments. Jesus first lit a charcoal fire, grilled the fish, and invited him to breakfast. Only when breakfast was over did the Lord speak.

The Lord’s first question was not, “Are you still going to work?” but, “Do you love me more than these?” The verb in the original is ἀγαπᾷς (agapas). “These” could mean these fish, these boats, or these companions. Whatever it refers to, the Lord’s meaning is clear: before entrusting the flock, first settle the relationship of love for me.

Brothers and sisters, three passages, three scenes, all pointing to the same truth: the foundation of serving is not ability but relationship; the measure of serving is not results but faithfulness.

sections.heading: 1. Our Relationship with Things: God Values Faithfulness, Not Results
sections.html:
“It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” (1 Corinthians 4:2)

“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ ” (Matthew 25:21)

God’s standard for looking at things is not success or failure, not big or small, not much or little, but this: faithfulness.

The weight of one word: faithful

We often take “faithful” to mean “hanging on for a long time”. Hanging on for a long time is certainly not easy, but faithfulness in the Bible goes deeper than that. As we said, πιστός (pistos) means “trustworthy”. Whether a steward is faithful isn’t judged by how much is left in the storehouse, but by whether he has followed his master’s wishes and used his master’s goods where his master wanted them used.

The Lord Jesus stated the principle very plainly: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10) Faithfulness isn’t a performance in one big matter; it is consistency across countless small ones.

So whether the matter is great or small, what God looks at is whether you are faithful, whether you are acting according to his heart.

“To everyone who has will be given”

“For to everyone who has will be given, and he will have abundance, but from him who doesn’t have, even that which he has will be taken away.” (Matthew 25:29)

At first hearing this sounds very harsh, as if God favoured the strong. But we have to look at the context. The one who had everything taken away wasn’t the one who gained a little; he was the one who never put his talent to use at all. He buried his one talent in the ground, and his reason was, “Lord, I knew you that you are a hard man” (Matthew 25:24). His problem wasn’t ability; it was that he had his master wrong. His relationship with his master was fear, not trust; and since the relationship was cold, all he could do with the task was “play it safe and keep the capital”.

So what this verse means is this: to the faithful, God entrusts more; the unfaithful lose even what they had. God’s increase flows along the lines of relationship.

The key truth: God values “people being right”, not “getting lots done”

This is the first sentence today to engrave on your heart: God values people being right, not getting lots done.

Psychology offers some very sobering supporting evidence. In 1981 the psychologists Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley, and Susan Jackson set out three dimensions of “burnout”: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. Pay special attention to the second — depersonalisation. It means that a worn-out person begins to treat the people around him as “cases”, as “workload”, and no longer as people. The World Health Organization (WHO), in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) adopted in 2019, also listed burnout as a syndrome connected with occupational phenomena, defined as “resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed”.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where things end up when self-centred people do the work: first they rate the task above the person, then they turn people into tasks, and in the end they lose themselves as well.

A 321 Insight: working from the heart, or calculating with the brain

321 says it very clearly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll fret. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Work from the heart, and the result is faithfulness; calculate with the brain, and the result is comparison and pressure.

Self-centred people care about results, about comparison, about performance, because their sense of worth has to be supplied by what they achieve. Selfless people care about only one thing: am I being faithful to God? When a self-centred person finishes a job, he asks, “What do people think of me?” When a selfless person finishes a job, he asks, “Lord, are you pleased?”

A small example from daily life. A sister in one church was responsible for scrubbing the kitchen. For twenty years nobody applauded her for it. Once someone asked her whether she found it tiring. She said, “I’m not scrubbing floors. I’m getting a place ready for the Lord’s meal.” Brothers and sisters, the same cleaning cloth is drudgery in the hands of the self-centred and service in the hands of the selfless. The difference isn’t in the task; it’s in her relationship with the Lord.

Mother Teresa is generally believed to have said: “Not all of us can do great things. But we can do small things with great love.” That saying fits the Lord’s heart: God has no shortage of great things to be done; what he wants is people who love and are faithful.

sections.heading: 2. True Faithfulness: Acting According to God’s Heart
sections.html:
“I will raise up a faithful priest for myself who will do according to that which is in my heart and in my mind.” (1 Samuel 2:35)

Faithfulness isn’t only seeing a thing through and never giving up; more important still, it is doing it according to God’s heart.

What faithfulness means, seen from the house of Eli

The setting of this verse is very grave. The era of the judges was drawing to a close, and the priest Eli was old. His two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were desecrating the sacrifices in the tabernacle at Shiloh and treating Yahweh’s offerings with contempt. God sent a man of God to speak to Eli, announcing that he would raise up a faithful priest.

Notice how God defines “faithful”: “who will do according to that which is in my heart.” The Hebrew word for “faithful” is נֶאֱמָן (ne’eman), from the same root as the “Amen” (aman) with which we close our prayers. Its basic meaning is “firm, reliable, able to stand”. The faithfulness God wants is to stand firm on God’s heart like a pillar, not to spin busily inside our own plans like a windmill.

Eli’s sons were not idle. They were at work in the tabernacle every day. Their service was full, but their hearts were empty; their hands were on the altar, but their hearts were on the sacrificial meat. This reminds us that a person can do the most unfaithful things in the holiest of places.

Wrong direction: the harder you try, the further off you go

Many people work very hard, but in the wrong direction: zealous yet out of step with God’s heart, diligent yet outside God’s will.

Why does this happen? Because they have not first built a relationship with God. Without relationship you don’t know God’s heart; without knowing God’s heart you cannot truly be faithful.

Here is an example you can actually work out. If your heading is off by one degree, it looks negligible. But by trigonometry, after a hundred kilometres you’re off by about 1.7 kilometres; after a thousand kilometres you’re off by more than seventeen. One degree at the start decides which city you end up in. Brothers and sisters, our relationship with God is the first degree of our life.

The Bible spelled out this principle long ago: “to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (1 Samuel 15:22). Saul kept back the best of the cattle and sheep, saying they were to be sacrificed to Yahweh. It sounded very spiritual, but it was disobedience. God wasn’t complaining that his offerings were poor; God wanted his heart.

The Lord Jesus himself is the most perfect role model: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” (John 5:19) Jesus is my role model — his service wasn’t self-initiated; it flowed from his relationship with the Father.

The key truth: the foundation of faithfulness is our relationship with God

“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” (1 Corinthians 10:31)

Paul says this in the middle of the dispute over eating food sacrificed to idols. Those strong in faith said, “I can eat it”; those weak in faith didn’t dare; and each side judged the other. Paul moves the focus from “May this be done?” to “For whom is this being done?”

So: what you do isn’t what matters; whom you do it for is what matters.

Psychological research also catches a glimpse of this dividing line. The American psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan put forward Self-Determination Theory in 1985, distinguishing intrinsic from extrinsic motivation. And Deci’s experiments in 1971 found that when an external reward is brought into something people already enjoy, their intrinsic motivation may actually be weakened. In other words, once the reason for doing something shifts from “I love it” to “what will I get for it?”, joy begins to drain away.

Brothers and sisters, serving is just the same. When the reason we serve shifts from “I love the Lord” to “I want to be seen”, joy disappears and only weariness is left.

A 321 Insight: with your focus on Jesus, you’ll do the right things

321 reminds us: the focus is on Jesus — not on ourselves, not on others, not on our circumstances.

With your focus on Jesus, you’ll do the right things; with your focus on yourself, you’ll only do your own things.
