Here is a very practical test: when something has been done well but nobody knows you did it, does your heart go cold? If it does, your focus is still on yourself. This isn’t condemnation; it’s a health check. Once the check has shown it up, hand it to the Lord and let him bring us, little by little, out of the self-centred life and into selflessness.

sections.heading: 3. Relationship First, Then Ministry: When People Are Right, Things Are Right
sections.html:
“So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ ” (John 21:15)

Jesus’ order with Peter is crystal clear: first he asks, “Do you love me?” — that is relationship; then he says, “Feed my lambs” — that is ministry. Relationship first, then ministry.

The Lord’s three questions and three charges to Peter

The Lord asked three times, and gave his charge three times. The first: “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) The second: “Tend my sheep.” (John 21:16) The third: “Feed my sheep.” (John 21:17)

The three questions answer to Peter’s three denials; the three charges are the Lord with his own hands putting a broken man back at his post.

Notice two things the Lord did not do. First, the Lord did not say, “Go and prove yourself to me first, and then I’ll hand the sheep over to you.” Second, the Lord did not say, “Since you have fallen, the ministry had better go to someone else.” The Lord restored the relationship first, and then restored the charge. Because in God’s kingdom, relationship is the root of ministry, not its reward.

This is exactly the order 321 speaks of: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Life turned upside down: the more you do, the more tired you get

Many people do the opposite: they get things done first, and talk about relationships later. The result can be put in a few words — more work, more weariness, broken relationships and an empty heart.

This isn’t scaremongering. The story of Martha is a mirror: “Jesus answered her, ‘Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.’ ” (Luke 10:41–42)

What Martha was doing wasn’t wrong; she was serving Jesus. But the Lord said she was “anxious and troubled about many things”. The word for “anxious” in the original carries the sense of being distracted, pulled in different directions. If the things we do for the Lord do not flow out of time spent with the Lord, they will pull us away from his presence — and that is the deepest paradox of serving.

Paul puts it even more severely: “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” (1 Corinthians 13:3) Feeding the poor is a good deed; giving up one’s body is a great deed; but without love — that is, without right relationship — on God’s books it still comes to nothing.

The Lord Jesus also warned us in advance: “Many will tell me in that day, ‘Lord, Lord, didn’t we prophesy in your name, in your name cast out demons, and in your name do many mighty works?’ Then I will tell them, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.’ ” (Matthew 7:22–23) He doesn’t deny that they did things. What he denies is this: “I never knew you” — there was no relationship.

The key truth: first the right people, then the right things

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has followed the same group of people since 1938, for more than eighty years. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, has pointed out publicly many times that what best predicts whether someone will be healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships. This is the longest study of human lives ever carried out, and the direction it points in is astonishingly consistent with the order of the Bible: relationships can carry a person’s whole life better than achievements can.

The conclusions of scientific research simply confirm, from a long way off, what the Creator said long ago.

Life flowing out into ministry: the lame man stands up

“But Peter said, ‘I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk!’ ” (Acts 3:6)

“He took him by the right hand and raised him up. Immediately his feet and his ankle bones received strength. Leaping up, he stood and began to walk. He entered with them into the temple, walking, leaping, and praising God.” (Acts 3:7–8)

Why could Peter heal this man who had been lame from birth? Not because he had learnt a method, but because the Lord was in him. He wasn’t “carrying out a ministry”; he was letting the life within him flow out. He said, “I have no silver or gold” — he had no resources in his hands. He said, “what I have, that I give you” — he had Christ within.

Later the council arrested them for questioning, and the Bible says: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13) Notice this: what people perceived was not their learning, but that they “had been with Jesus”.

So when the council forbade them to preach, “Peter and John answered them, ‘Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, judge for yourselves, for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.’ ” (Acts 4:19–20)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the tone of that sentence. It isn’t “I have to do this job”, but “we can’t help telling”. They weren’t speaking for the sake of a task; their relationship with the Lord had filled them to the point where nothing could hold it back.

A 321 Insight: life flows out into ministry; ministry does not produce life

The Lord himself said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce fruit; a branch only has to stay joined to the vine. Fruit is “borne”, not “squeezed out”.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The fivefold change follows the same order: when the mindset changes, life changes; when life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships change; when relationships change, ministry naturally changes. Today many people want to skip the first four steps and change the ministry directly — and they work very hard, yet bear no fruit.

sections.heading: 4. The Faithful Steward: Doing Things Within Relationships, Building Relationships
sections.html:
“The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

God’s heart is not only that things get finished, but that life is passed on and relationships are built.

“Commit” is a relational act

When Paul wrote 2 Timothy he was a prisoner in Rome, and he knew the time of his departure had come (2 Timothy 4:6–8). These are his last words. What matters most to a man about to die? Not how many projects he leaves behind, but how many people.

The Greek word for “commit” is παρατίθημι (paratithēmi). In the commercial and legal language of the day it meant “depositing” something valuable in the hands of a trustworthy person for safekeeping. That act can only happen within a relationship; you wouldn’t hand the family fortune to a stranger.

Look at the four generations in this verse: Paul, Timothy, the faithful men who will be able to teach others, and the others they will teach. What links those four generations together is not an institution but relationships. Spiritual life has never been passed on by copying; it is passed on by walking alongside.

This is the “235 relationships” of 321: becoming the “2”, spiritual companions, with a selfless person; establishing the “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; and then becoming the “5”, a team of spiritual comrades, a fivefold-ministry team. The expansion of God’s kingdom is the expansion of relationships.

The faithful steward: not damaging relationships while working, but building them

The faithful steward has two marks: while doing the work, he doesn’t damage relationships; while doing the work, he builds relationships.

This is hard, because work always comes with pressure, deadlines and demands for quality. When the pressure comes, the first thing we’re inclined to sacrifice is people — we speak a little faster, our faces grow a little darker, and a single “I’ll just do it myself” pushes someone away. The task gets finished, and the relationship goes cold.

Here there is some powerful supporting evidence. Amy Edmondson of Harvard Business School, in a study published in Administrative Science Quarterly in 1999, put forward the concept of “psychological safety”: in a team whose members believe they can admit mistakes and raise questions without being humiliated, learning and performance are actually better. The findings of Google’s “Project Aristotle”, published in 2016, likewise named psychological safety as the most critical factor in high-performing teams.

In other words, even the world’s research on organisations has found that when you take care of people, the work actually goes better; when you sacrifice people, the work ends up worse.

God said it long ago: “he who is greatest among you will be your servant.” (Matthew 23:11)

Spiritual summary: when people are right, things are right

So we can boil today’s message down to two sentences: when people are right, things are right; when people are wrong, things go wrong.

“People being right” here means all three relationships are right: right with God, right with ourselves, right with others.

Right with God — I know whose I am and whose work I’m doing. Right with myself — I don’t rely on what I do to prove myself; in Christ I am already accepted. Right with others — I don’t treat people as tools; I treat them as brothers.

When these three relationships are right, the things we do will come right of their own accord.

An old preacher who served for many years up in the mountains once said something I have never forgotten: “We’re not getting the work done; we’re bringing people up.” Brothers and sisters, the work will pass away, but people last for ever.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: From Self-Centred Achievement to Selfless Faithfulness
sections.html:
When we set today’s message within the framework of 321, the thread becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

Jesus is my role model — he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing.” (John 5:19) The source of all he did was his relationship with the Father.

The Bible is my standard — it isn’t results that have the final say, nor other people’s opinions; it’s God’s word. It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who shows us God’s heart, so that we are not merely busy but sent.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — my diary is under his management, my priorities are his to arrange; let Jesus receive all the glory — when the work succeeds, the applause goes to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not a machine that uses people up; it is a family that brings people before God.

The self-centred life and selflessness: the deepest watershed in how we work

When self-centred people work, the task is their mirror: they want to see their own worth in the result. When selfless people work, the task is their altar: they offer everything up to the Lord.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In the way we work, pride often looks very devout: “I’ll just do it myself,” “only I can,” “it has to be me.” Humility, on the other hand, is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. Nine times out of ten, conflict between co-workers isn’t about truth; it’s about whose method gets adopted.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. When a person no longer needs his work to prove himself, Satan loses his most useful lever.

The shift of perspective: four moves “from … to …”

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: people look at results; God looks at motives.

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: earth hands out certificates; heaven hands out crowns. “Be faithful to death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (Revelation 2:10)

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: “The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:17)

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the worldly way is “get the job done first and worry about the people later”; God’s way is “bring the people right first, and the job will get done”.

The 920 practice: living out selflessness in every task

The 920 practice reminds us that every person we have a relationship with is our “2”. Today we carry that into the realm of “things”: when you and a co-worker are working on something together, that co-worker is your “2”; when you’re rushing a project at the office, that colleague is your “2”. In that task, practise living out the selfless (0) life, and let the Holy Spirit bear his fruit in all nine of its expressions: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Pay special attention to “patience” and “gentleness” — these two fruits only grow when “the job is urgent but the people are slow”. Tasks, it turns out, are the soil in which God grows fruit in us.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

321 draws the order of serving as a path: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory).

Look: “Service” comes fourth, not first. Much of the weariness in the church today comes from people starting to run at step four. Without Spirit, without Understanding, without Life, going straight to Service, we end up doing spiritual work in the strength of the flesh.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: Doing Things in the Right Order
sections.html:
Practice 1: Check every day — am I just doing things, or am I working together with God?

Don’t just be busy; make sure: am I working within God’s heart?

How to practise: each day, before you do anything, first pray one sentence: “Lord, is this what you want me to do?”

That one-sentence prayer takes only five seconds, yet it can set the direction of the whole day right. “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1) Those who work together with God are building; those who don’t are labouring in vain.

Practice 2: Practise faithfulness in small things rather than chasing big things

Don’t despise small things: be faithful in small things and God gives increase; neglect small things and your spiritual life drains away.

How to practise: each day, do one “seemingly insignificant small thing” really well.

Wash a bowl, return a phone call, set out the chairs neatly, read a message properly to the end before replying. “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” (Luke 16:10) Small things are God’s practice ground for us, and God’s examination hall too.

Practice 3: Deliberately build relationships while doing things, rather than sacrificing them

In serving and at work, don’t hurt people for the sake of efficiency; don’t damage relationships for the sake of results.

How to practise: today, in one particular task, deliberately “put people first”.

For example: before a meeting starts, greet people first; before handing out an assignment, first listen to the other person’s difficulties; when you’re desperate for results, first say, “Thank you — I know these last few days have been hard work.” “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men.” (Colossians 3:23)

Using the eight stages of changing our mindset to take the practice deeper

First, Information: copy today’s key sentence somewhere you’ll see it — God values people being right, not getting lots done.

Second, Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light, so that this sentence moves from the paper into your heart. You might pray: “Lord, let me see whether I am really loving you, or proving myself.”

Third, Conviction: admit to God, and to yourself, that in the past you put things before people and put people before God, and that this was the wrong order.

Fourth, Implementation: starting tomorrow morning, before you do anything, first ask: “Lord, is this what you want me to do?”

Fifth, Evaluation: in the evening, take three minutes to look back — today, did I hurt anyone in order to get a job done?

Sixth, Correction: if you did, go and mend it tomorrow. One apology is worth more than ten successes.

Seventh, Repetition: don’t do it for just three days. God’s work takes shape through repetition; as habits take shape, life takes shape.

Eighth, Multiplication: bring this practice to your “2”. Find a spiritual companion, and each week ask one another: “This week, did you sacrifice a relationship in order to get something done?”

A Gentle Reminder: it isn’t a lack of effort; it’s the wrong order

Many people fail not because they don’t try hard, but because they put things above relationships: to get things done, they lose God; to finish the job, they lose people.

A family falls apart in quarrels over renovating the house; a team wounds one another putting on a big conference; a father, wanting to give his children a better life, misses their entire childhood. All of these are good things, but the price is far too high.

God’s heart is this: relationships first, then things.

Paul says: “each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is.” (1 Corinthians 3:13) On that day, what the fire burns up will be the wood, hay and stubble; what remains will be everything we have faithfully offered within our relationships.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Be a Good and Faithful Servant
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, at the end of life, what counts is not how many things you did, but this: were you faithful to God, and did you build relationships?

Relationships are eternal; things are temporary.

One day we will all stand before the Lord. On that day nobody will ask you how many conferences you ran, how many contracts you signed, how many people you led. The Lord will say only one thing — the one thing we all long to hear: “Well done, good and faithful servant.” (Matthew 25:21)

So may we live our whole lives in the right order: God first, then ourselves, then others, and only last of all things.

Then our lives will not only bear fruit but have true worth, and before God we will be good and faithful servants.

When you go home today, please do one thing: open your diary and look over this week. In all those boxes, where is God? Where are you? Where are the people closest to you? If the order is wrong, put it right now. Let Jesus reign as King — beginning with your diary. Let Jesus receive all the glory — beginning with the most insignificant little task you have.

keyVerses: 1 Corinthians 4:1–2
“So let a man think of us as Christ’s servants, and stewards of God’s mysteries. Here, moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.”
Matthew 25:21
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’ ”
John 21:15

“So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I have affection for you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’ ”
declarations: Lord, I will adjust my relationship with things: no longer centred on things, but centred on you.
I will be a faithful steward, acting according to your heart in everything.
Let me first build my relationship with you, then build relationships with people, and then do my work within those relationships.
May all that I do glorify you, build relationships and live out Christ, so that I become an overcomer.
In the name of the Lord Jesus we pray. Amen!
practices: Practise faithfulness in small things rather than chasing big things
Deliberately build relationships while doing things, rather than sacrificing them
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you for speaking to us this morning.

Lord, we confess that we so often put things before you, and results before people. We are busy, but not always working together with you; we work hard, but not always within your heart. Please forgive us.

Put “faithfulness” within us, so that we are faithful even in the smallest things. Put “order” within us, so that we draw near to you first, then build relationships with people, and then do our work within those relationships.
Lord, let our serving flow out of life, not be squeezed out by pressure. May every small thing we do become a sign of our love for you.
Reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our work, reign as King in our serving. May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Corinthians 4:2: “It is required of stewards that they be found faithful.” Please share: this week, what “insignificant little thing” is God asking you to do faithfully? How do you plan to do it?

John 21:15: “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” Think about it honestly: recently, has some task become a barrier between you and the Lord, or between you and your family? How are you willing to adjust the order?
l152.title: Get People Right and Things Come Right
l152.subtitle: The Priority of Relationships (Part 4): Our Relationship with Things
l152.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: When the Order Is Wrong, All Our Effort Is Wasted
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a scene. There was a brother in a church whom everyone agreed was the best at getting things done. Give him an event, and it would run on time; give him a report, and it would be crystal clear; give him a problem, and it would be solved. One year he was put in charge of a very large conference: four months of preparation, a venue for more than a thousand people, and everything from the registration system to the car-park traffic flow was arranged beyond reproach. On the night the conference ended, the lights in the hall went out one by one, the co-workers drifted off one after another, and he sat alone among the rows of empty chairs. In that moment he suddenly realised something: in those four months, almost every word he had spoken to every one of his co-workers had been about “things” — progress, timing, budget, responsibilities. Not a single word had been about “people”.

The job got done, but the people scattered.

Brothers and sisters, stories like this don’t happen only in churches. They happen in the office, at the dinner table, between husbands and wives, and between parents and children. So many people spend their lives busy, worn out and discouraged — not because they don’t try hard enough, but because of something far more fundamental: the order is wrong.

There is a saying commonly attributed to the great German writer Goethe: if you fasten the first button of your life wrongly, you will never fasten the last one rightly. How true that is. Doing up buttons doesn’t take much strength, but it does take the right order. Get the first one wrong, and the harder you push on down the line, the more crooked the shirt becomes; the more conscientious you are, the more neatly you get it wrong.

Our lives are just the same. When the priority of relationships is wrong, life falls into disorder; when the priority of relationships is right, everything comes right.

So this morning we are coming to a crucial turning point, and its name is “rectify the priority”. And together we must answer one core question honestly:

Is our life, in the end, about “solving problems”? Or is it about “building relationships”?

Brothers and sisters, please don’t answer too quickly. This choice isn’t a slogan; it will decide the direction and outcome of your whole life. If you choose “solving problems”, you may end up with a beautiful report card, yet lose the people around you. If you choose “building relationships”, you will walk a little more slowly, but you will bring people to God.

In the 321 vision we keep repeating one phrase: life first, then relationships, then ministry. This isn’t a slogan; it is an order. It is God’s order. Today we are going to set that order right again.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: The Main Verb of the Great Commission Is “Make Disciples”
sections.html:
Before we come to the key points of the lesson, let’s first set today’s two theme passages back in their setting.

Of the four Gospels, Matthew is the one closest to Jewish readers. Its author, Matthew, had been a tax collector in Capernaum until the Lord called him and he followed him (Matthew 9:9). The book is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, to Jewish believers who knew the Old Testament well, to prove that Jesus of Nazareth is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament — the Son of David, the new Moses, God with us, Immanuel.

Matthew 28 is the conclusion of the whole book, and also its summit. The place is a mountain in Galilee; the time is after the Lord’s resurrection and before his ascension. The eleven disciples went there; some worshipped him, and some doubted. And it was before just such a group of imperfect people that the risen Lord handed over his worldwide commission.

There is a very important exegetical detail here, brothers and sisters, and you must remember it. In the Greek original this passage has only one main verb in the imperative, and that is “make disciples of all nations” (μαθητεύσατε, mathēteusate). The words for “go” (πορευθέντες), “baptising” (βαπτίζοντες) and “teaching” (διδάσκοντες) are all participles: they describe the manner and the process that surround that one main command.

In other words, the heart of the Great Commission is not “going”, not “running events”, not “setting up structures”, but this — making disciples.

The word “disciple” in Greek is μαθητής (mathētēs), meaning “a learner, a follower”. In the first-century rabbinic tradition a disciple was not a student sitting in a classroom listening to lectures, but someone who walked behind his teacher, eating, living and travelling with him. Jews of that time could even describe following a rabbi as being “covered in the dust of your rabbi’s feet”. Disciples were never formed by a curriculum, but by a relationship.

That is exactly how the Lord Jesus himself did it. Mark 3:14 says, “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” Brothers and sisters, look at the order: first “that they might be with him”, then “that he might send them out to preach”. Relationship first, ministry after. For three and a half years the Lord did not first give his disciples a method; first he gave them himself.

As for Romans, it is the letter the apostle Paul wrote around AD 57, during his third missionary journey, from Corinth to the church in Rome. Romans 3:23 is the final verdict on the whole human race before God: Jew and Gentile alike are under the power of sin, all have fallen short of the glory of God. By human logic, what should come next is judgement. And yet verse 24 opens with grace: “being justified freely by his grace.”

Brothers and sisters, this is the most stunning turn in the whole Bible. Faced with humanity’s greatest problem — sin — the first thing God did was not to get the problem dealt with, but to restore the relationship. He sent his Son not first to condemn, but first to seek; not first to settle accounts, but first to lay down his life.

The whole Bible, from Genesis to Revelation, is about one thing: God wants to restore his relationship with humanity.

sections.heading: 1. When Relationships Are Right, Things Will Come Right
sections.html:
There is a well-turned Chinese saying: “With connection, there’s no problem; without connection, there’s a problem.”

It sounds like a joke, but its spiritual meaning runs very deep. It is saying this: when the relationship is right, problems are easily solved; when the relationship is wrong, problems keep multiplying.

The very same sentence, coming from the mouth of someone you trust, sounds like care; coming from someone you don’t trust, it sounds like an attack. The very same matter, when the relationship is good, is settled with one phone call; when the relationship is bad, ten meetings won’t bring agreement. Brothers and sisters, we often think we are stuck on “things”, when really we are stuck on “relationships”.

In the 321 vision, relationships have an order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and only last with things. And this order corresponds exactly to three very real conditions of life.

First, when our relationship with God is good, we become “willing”.

Psalm 110:3 says, “Your people offer themselves willingly in the day of your power, in holy array.” Willingness flows out of our relationship with God. For someone who draws near to the Lord every day, serving is not a burden but a grace; giving is not a loss but worship. On the other hand, when someone’s relationship with God has grown distant, he will still serve, but that service slowly turns into duty, into pressure, into something forced. His hands are still moving, but his heart has already left.

Second, when our relationship with ourselves is good, we become “joyful”.

Many brothers and sisters have never thought about it, but we also need to be at peace with ourselves. Someone living in self-rejection, self-accusation and constant comparison cannot possibly be joyful. 321 often reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” When in Christ we accept the self that God has accepted, the heart relaxes, and we become joyful.

Third, when our relationships with others are good, we become “of one heart”.

Psalm 133:1 says, “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” Being of one heart is not a technique; it is a fruit.

People like this work with motivation, with joy and with unity. Conversely, when relationships are poor, people work unwillingly, joylessly and divided; however simple the task, it becomes hard. The very same job feels like grace to the willing and like punishment to the reluctant.

Brothers and sisters, here is a key truth: God’s work is not driven by pressure; it is carried by relationship.

Moses understood this all too well. In Exodus 33, after Israel had worshipped the golden calf, God said he would send an angel to lead the way and would give them the land flowing with milk and honey — only he himself would not go with them. By the logic of “solving problems”, that is a good deal: the land is still theirs, and someone still leads the way. But how did Moses reply? Exodus 33:15: “Moses said to him, ‘If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.’”

What Moses wanted was not Canaan; it was God himself. He would rather stay in the wilderness than have a promised land without God’s presence.

The Lord Jesus also made this truth as plain as it could be. John 15:5: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” Notice that the Lord did not say, “You must bear much fruit.” What the Lord said was, “Remain in me.” Fruit isn’t squeezed out; fruit grows out of connection.

Nature has prepared a beautiful picture for us. North America’s coast redwoods are the tallest trees on earth, able to grow to more than a hundred metres. The remarkable thing is that redwood roots are not deep — usually only two or three metres. But they spread out sideways in every direction, and they cross and intertwine with the roots of the redwoods beside them. So a redwood stays standing not because it is anchored deep on its own, but because it is joined to the others. When the gale comes, the whole forest bears it together.

Brothers and sisters, the church is a forest just like that.

Science is bearing witness to this truth as well. In 1938 Harvard University began a “Study of Adult Development” that has now run for more than eighty years, following several hundred men across their whole lives from youth to old age, and later including their spouses and descendants too. It is one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in human history. Its current director, Professor Robert Waldinger, has distilled decades of data into a single conclusion: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. Not wealth, not fame, not achievement — relationships. They even found that how satisfied people were with their relationships at fifty predicted their health at eighty better than their cholesterol levels did.

Brothers and sisters, the conclusion it took people eighty years of research to reach, God stated on the first pages of the Bible: “It is not good for the man to be alone.” (Genesis 2:18)

So the 321 insight is very clear: build relationships by relying on the heart, and life flows; solve problems by relying on the brain, and pressure mounts.

sections.heading: 2. Solving Problems Alone Loses People’s Hearts
sections.html:
Many people have a habit that is often held up as a virtue: “deal with the issue, not the person”. Everything is handled through systems, through rules, through efficiency.

It sounds fair, it sounds professional, and it saves a lot of trouble. But it has one big problem: it overlooks the “person”.

And the result is so often this: the problem is solved, but the person is hurt; the task is finished, but the relationship is broken.

Brothers and sisters, that cost is actually far greater. A task can be done over again; a relationship cannot easily be started over again.

Let’s look at how God does it. Romans 3:23–24: “for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;”

Notice the order here. Humanity’s problem is that “all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God”. That is a fact, and God neither denies it nor plays it down. But the way God deals with us is not “judgement first”; it is “relationship first”.

Romans 5:8 says it even more plainly: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” God didn’t wait until we had sorted our problems out before he loved us; while the problem was still there, God gave us his love first.

So when Jesus paid the price for us, he did not solve the problem first; he restored the relationship first. 2 Corinthians 5:19 says, “namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning to them their trespasses, and having committed to us the word of reconciliation.” Reconciliation is the heart of the gospel — and reconciliation is a word about relationship.

Let’s look at a few more pictures.

In Genesis 3, after Adam and Eve sinned, they hid. God’s first words when he came were not “What have you done?” but this: “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9) Of course God knew where he was. God wasn’t asking about a location; he was asking about a relationship.

In Luke 15, the prodigal son comes home. By rights the father should have settled accounts first: Where did the inheritance go? Who have you been mixing with all these years? But the Bible says, “But while he was still far off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.” (Luke 15:20) The embrace came first, the talking afterwards. Relationship first, problem after.

In John 21, Peter has denied the Lord three times. On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias the Lord lit a charcoal fire, grilled fish and invited them to breakfast. And the first thing the Lord asked Peter was not “Why did you deny me?” but this: “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?” (John 21:15) The Lord didn’t rake up the past; the Lord repaired the relationship. And once the relationship was restored, on the day of Pentecost three thousand people turned to the Lord.

Brothers and sisters, this is God’s order.

The lesson gives us a comparison that cuts to the heart: a doctor who treats only the disease and not the person may cure the illness yet wound the heart.

The medical world itself has research to back this comparison up. In 1984 two researchers, Howard Beckman and Richard Frankel, published a classic study in the Annals of Internal Medicine. They recorded conversations between doctors and patients in outpatient visits and found that, on average, doctors interrupted their patients eighteen seconds after the patients began to speak. Eighteen seconds. Before the patients had even voiced what was really worrying them, control of the conversation had already been taken away from them.

Eighteen seconds is enough to deal with a symptom, but not enough to get to know a person.

Brothers and sisters, at home, in church, at work — don’t we also often “interrupt at eighteen seconds”? Our child has said half a sentence and we’re already giving answers; our spouse has barely started and we’re already giving advice; a brother has only just mentioned his struggle and we’re already giving spiritual correction. We think we’re helping; in fact we’re shutting a door.

In Mark 2:27 the Lord Jesus said, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.” Systems are made for people, not people for systems. When we put systems above people, we have walked into the place of the Pharisees.

In Revelation 2, in the Lord’s letter to the church in Ephesus, he says, “I know your works, and your toil and perseverance, and that you can’t tolerate evil men” (Revelation 2:2). This was a church that was very good at getting things done: it had works, it had toil, it had perseverance, it had discernment. But then the Lord goes on: “But I have this against you, that you left your first love.” (Revelation 2:4)

Everything was being done right, yet the relationship had been lost. What the Lord rebuked was not that they did things badly, but that they had let go of the one thing that mattered most.

1 Corinthians 13:3 says, “If I give away all my goods to feed the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but don’t have love, it profits me nothing.” If even giving up our very bodies can “profit nothing”, brothers and sisters, do we still dare to say, “As long as the job gets done, that’s fine”?

So the 321 insight is this: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than results.

Only solving problems, we lose people; only by building relationships can we win them.

sections.heading: 3. Why Do We Turn the Order Upside Down?
sections.html:
If relationships matter so much, why do we keep turning the order upside down? Both Scripture and our own experience show us two reasons.

The First Reason: We Are Unwilling to Pay the Price

Building relationships costs something. It takes time, it takes companionship, it takes prayer, it takes patience.

Time cannot be compressed. You cannot grow three years of trust in thirty minutes. Companionship cannot be outsourced. You cannot hire someone else to be your child’s father for you. Prayer is invisible. You may keep watch in prayer over someone for half a year, and he may have no idea at all. And patience is the most expensive of all, because patience means this: I could make everything perfectly clear right now, and instead I choose to wait.

And solving problems? It’s fast, it’s efficient, and you can see the result. Hold a meeting, send an email, lay down a rule, and the matter is over. Do it today, and you have results today; do it today, and someone praises you today.

So people very easily choose the quick way rather than the right way.

But brothers and sisters, quick doesn’t mean right; only what is right will last.

Proverbs 19:2 says, “It isn’t good to have zeal without knowledge, nor being hasty with one’s feet and missing the way.” Being hasty with one’s feet and missing the way — every impatient one of us ought to copy that line onto the wall. So many of our careless words, so many misunderstandings, so many decisions we bitterly regret, come not because there is no love in our hearts, but because our feet move too fast.

The apostle Paul was a man who knew how to get things done, and yet the way he built churches was the slowest and most costly way of all. 1 Thessalonians 2:8: “Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you, not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.”

Notice that Paul says he gave two things: one was the gospel, the other was his own soul — his very life. Preaching the gospel can be done quickly; giving your life is slow. Today we are often willing to give only the first and not the second; willing to give a message, but not to give ourselves.

The management thinker Stephen R. Covey (1932–2012), in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People, put forward a very helpful idea he called the “Emotional Bank Account”. Between people, he said, there is an invisible account. Every kept promise, every time we listen, apologise or show consideration, is a deposit; every broken promise, every slight, criticism or neglect, is a withdrawal. When the account is in credit, the occasional wrong word is forgiven; when the account is overdrawn, even the right words won’t be heard. Covey has another often-quoted line: with people, fast is slow and slow is fast.

Brothers and sisters, the reason so many of our relationships break at a single word is not that the word was especially harsh, but that the account had long since run dry.

Seen from the 321 perspective, the root of “being unwilling to pay the price” is actually the self-centred life. Self-centred people are in a hurry for results, because results belong to me — they prove me, glorify me, protect me. Self-centred people are afraid of slowness, because slowness doesn’t show off me. But selfless people are not in a hurry, because what they want is not their own name but the name of Jesus.

Pride always wants to take the shortcut; humility is willing to take the long way round. And the Bible is very clear: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

The Second Reason: We Prize Time and Results

Modern people speak a language we hardly have to think about: efficiency, performance, results.

We manage time by numbers, measure success by metrics, and prove our worth with reports. None of that is bad in itself. But relationships have one fatal “flaw”: they are hard to quantify, and hard to see straight away.

You spend two hours over coffee with a young person, and it can’t be written into a report. You pray for a struggling sister for a whole year, and on the annual report it’s a blank. You hold your tongue instead of firing back that one sentence, and nobody applauds you.

So people make a choice that is very natural yet very deadly: they give up on relationships and chase results.

The management guru W. Edwards Deming (1900–1993), in Out of the Crisis, made a profound observation: the most important figures needed for management are unknown or unknowable. In other words, the things that truly decide whether an organisation lives or dies are very often exactly the things you cannot measure.

It is the same in a family — and all the more so in a church.

And what is the result? The lesson puts it precisely: we end up spending even more time repairing relationships, and paying an even greater price.

We’ve all seen it happen. To keep to a schedule, someone skipped one word of apology, and it took three years to mend the friendship afterwards. For the sake of performance, someone spent a few years less with their child, and by the time the child had grown and they wanted to be there, the child no longer needed them. To get a job finished, someone wounded a co-worker’s heart; that place now stands empty, and finding another person willing to give themselves to it is far harder than they imagined.

The best-known example is in the home of the Lord Jesus’ own friends. In Luke 10, Martha welcomed Jesus into her house. Did she love the Lord? Of course she did — otherwise she wouldn’t have opened her door. Was she diligent? Extremely. But the Bible says she “was distracted with much serving”. And so she did something very dangerous: she began to complain about her sister, and even to complain to the Lord.

How did the Lord answer? “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is needed. Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken away from her.” (Luke 10:41–42)

Brothers and sisters, the Lord didn’t say that what Martha was doing was bad. What the Lord said was this — the order was wrong. The “good part” that Mary chose was not a more important “task”; it was a more important “place”: sitting at the Lord’s feet.

The Bible has two ways of looking at time, and Greek uses two different words. One is χρόνος (chronos), the time that ticks away on the clock — time measured in quantity. The other is καιρός (kairos), the time God has appointed, the right moment — time measured in quality. Modern people manage chronos frantically, yet often miss kairos.

Ecclesiastes 3:1 says, “For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:” God is not an impatient God. For the sake of one promise, he had Abraham wait twenty-five years; to prepare Moses, he took eighty years; to send his Son into the world, he waited until “the fullness of the time came” (Galatians 4:4).

Psychology bears witness in the same direction. In the 1970s the Stanford psychologist Walter Mischel ran his famous “marshmallow test”: researchers sat young children in front of a marshmallow and told them that if they could wait until the researcher came back before eating it, they would get two. Follow-up studies found that the children who had been able to delay gratification did better on the whole, as teenagers, in schoolwork and self-control. Later researchers also pointed out that whether a child is willing to wait depends to a great extent on one thing — whether he trusts the person who made the promise.

Brothers and sisters, this point is so important. The ability to delay gratification is rooted not in willpower but in trust; not in technique but in relationship.

Isaiah 28:16 says, “Therefore the Lord Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone of a sure foundation. He who believes shall not act hastily.’”

He who believes shall not act hastily — because he knows that time is in God’s hands.

So let us engrave this key truth on our hearts: what is fast is not necessarily right; what is right is what is truly fast.

Proverbs 21:5 says, “The plans of the diligent surely lead to profit; and everyone who is hasty surely rushes to poverty.”

sections.heading: 4. Rectifying the Priority: Returning to God’s Heart
sections.html:
“Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” (Matthew 28:19)

Brothers and sisters, let’s return to the Great Commission. We saw earlier that the only main command in this verse is “make disciples of all nations”. That one phrase says everything about God’s heart.

God’s heart is not to build things, not to build structures, but to build people, to build disciples, to build relationships.

Structures aren’t bad. They exist to protect people and to serve people. But when the structure becomes the goal, people become tools; when the numbers become master, lives become costs. The Lord Jesus didn’t leave behind a constitution for an organisation; he left behind twelve men. In three and a half years he didn’t put up a building, didn’t write a book, didn’t draw up a system. What he did was give himself to twelve men — and one of them even betrayed him.

It looks wildly inefficient. Yet two thousand years on, the life those twelve men passed on has filled the whole earth.

When we turn our focus from “things” back to “people”, three things happen: lives are changed, the church is renewed, and revival comes.

This is precisely the core 321 insight: life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Get the order right, and life flows, relationships connect, and ministry bears fruit of its own accord. Get the order wrong, and ministry swells, relationships drain away, and life withers.

Brothers and sisters, let me use a tree to illustrate this. In Fishlake National Forest in Utah there is a stand of quaking aspen called “Pando” (Latin for “I spread”). Seen from above ground, it is more than forty thousand separate trees; but scientists have discovered that they are in fact one single living thing — sharing one vast root system, genetically identical. Pando is reckoned to be one of the largest known organisms on earth, and is estimated to have been alive for thousands of years.

Above ground it looks like forty thousand trees; below ground it is one life.

This is God’s system. This is the church. This is what 321 calls the “235 relationships”: with a selfless person you become a “2”, spiritual companions who hold each other up; then you move into “3”, establishing spiritual parents and spiritual children and passing life on from generation to generation; and finally you become “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades working hand in hand.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The Great Commission does not tell us to go and pull off one very big event; it tells us to build a company of very deep relationships, and to let those relationships multiply from generation to generation.

Psalm 127:1 says, “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” Labour in vain — those words describe so many busy servants of God whose work bears no fruit.

The Lord also made the mark of all this very clear. John 13:35: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

The mark by which the world recognises us as disciples is not our buildings, not our programmes, not our numbers, but our love for one another.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s put today’s truth back into the whole picture of 321.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the Lord was first with his disciples and then sent them out, and that is our pattern; the Bible is my standard — whether our order is right is judged not by our feelings but by God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who pours God’s love into our hearts, so that we can love those who are not easy to love.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — when Jesus reigns as King in me, I no longer need to prove myself by “getting things done”; let Jesus receive all the glory — so I needn’t be in a hurry for people to see my results.

The Goal: establish God’s system. A system is not an organisation; it is life joined to life — like Pando: many above ground, one below.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred person will always put tasks ahead of people, because tasks can prove me; only the selfless person can put people ahead of tasks, because he has no need to prove himself. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into and living out the fullness and victory of Jesus; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me (Galatians 2:20).

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that ministry comes last. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and when relationships are right, ministry comes right of its own accord. Today’s lesson is changing precisely our “mindset” — the first of the five changes, and the starting point of everything.

The shift in perspective: from the human perspective to God’s perspective — people look at results, God looks at the heart; from the earthly to the heavenly — earthly plans will pass away, the register of heaven endures for ever; from the temporary to the eternal — tasks will pass, relationships will remain; from the worldly to the godly — the worldly measures by efficiency, the godly measures by life.

The 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. The person God sets in front of you today — your spouse, your children, your colleague, your small-group member — is the “2” God has given you. Before that person, practise living out the selfless (0) life, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Brothers and sisters, notice: among the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit, not one is “efficiency”, and not one is “performance”. Every one of the nine can only grow within relationships.

The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — first let the Holy Spirit lead, then let Scripture open our understanding, then let our life be built up, and only then comes service, and finally everything is given back to God. The order of that path is also the order of today’s lesson.

Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When our focus is right, our order is right.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living: From Solving Problems to Building Relationships
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, truth that never touches the ground remains mere knowledge. So the lesson gives us three very concrete practices.

Practice 1: Today, deliberately put “people before tasks”

In every matter, remind yourself: care for the person first, then deal with the task.

How to practise: today, in one matter, first take time to understand how the other person feels.

One sentence is enough: “Are you all right?” “Is this going to be too much for you?” “What are you really thinking about it?” Ask about the person first, then about the task.

The Lord Jesus gave us the highest standard. Matthew 5:23–24: “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.”

Brothers and sisters, what an astonishing statement this is. Offering a sacrifice is worship, the most sacred thing there is; and yet the Lord says that if a relationship hasn’t been put right, put the gift down and go and be reconciled first. If even worship must come after reconciliation, what could possibly be more urgent than people?

Practice 2: When a problem comes, first ask “How is the relationship?” and only then “How do I solve it?”

Don’t rush to deal with the matter; first check: how is my relationship with this person?

How to practise: when conflict comes, first stop and ask yourself that question.

That pause is a spiritual battlefield. Because the moment conflict comes, the flesh’s first reaction is always “I must win”. But brothers and sisters, remember what 321 reminds us: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger;” Scripture settled long ago what should be fast and what should be slow.

Practice 3: Choose “a little slower, but a little more right”

Don’t be in a hurry to see results; be willing to spend time building relationships.

How to practise: in one matter, deliberately “slow down”, and give priority to building the relationship.

Galatians 6:9 says, “Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.” In due season — God’s harvest comes in God’s time.

A Gentle Reminder

You can be very efficient and yet bear no fruit. Because without relationship, there is no life.

Brothers and sisters, don’t let “solving problems” take the place of “building relationships”.

Taking the Practices Deeper with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset

321 teaches us that a change of mindset goes through eight stages. If today’s three practices are truly to become life in us, we need to walk through them stage by stage.

Stage one, Information: today I have heard a new message — relationships matter more than tasks, people matter more than results.

Stage two, Revelation: I ask the Holy Spirit to turn this message into my own personal seeing. I ask the Lord to give me a picture, to let me see the person whose problem I “solved” but whose heart I wounded.

Stage three, Conviction: I don’t just think it makes sense; I am convinced through and through. I admit that my order has been wrong.

Stage four, Implementation: I will do it today. Not tomorrow — today. Today I will find someone, ask first how they feel, and only then talk about the task.

Stage five, Evaluation: tonight I will quieten myself and ask — today, did I put people before tasks, or tasks before people again? At what moment did I start rushing again?

Stage six, Correction: whatever I said wrongly today, I will put right tomorrow. Where I need to apologise, I will apologise; where I need to slow down, I will slow down.

Stage seven, Repetition: once isn’t enough. For a new order to become a habit, it has to be done again and again. When I fall, I get up; when I get up, I walk on.

Stage eight, Multiplication: when this order is lived out in me, I go and bring another person along. This is “make disciples of all nations”; this is the beginning of the 235 relationships.

Brothers and sisters, the eight stages are not eight classes; they are a road of life.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, life’s greatest investment is not in tasks but in relationships.

Tasks pass away; relationships remain.

The project that keeps you busiest this year — in five years nobody will remember it. But the one sentence you said to someone when you were at your busiest — whether it was a knife or a comfort — they will remember it all their life.

1 Corinthians 13:8 says, “Love never fails. But where there are prophecies, they will be done away with. Where there are various languages, they will cease. Where there is knowledge, it will be done away with.” And verse 13 says, “But now faith, hope, and love remain—these three. The greatest of these is love.”

What remains is love; what passes away are the things we thought were so important.

So when you begin to turn from “solving problems” to “building relationships”, you begin to walk in God’s will.

Brothers and sisters, this morning the Lord is calling us: put the order right again.

Let Jesus reign as King in your heart — when he is King, you no longer need to prove yourself by results. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when he receives the glory, you no longer need to rush for people to see you.

May we, all our lives long, rectify the priority and return to God’s heart; building lives, building relationships, building disciples, and welcoming God’s revival.

From today on, let us be people who pass on life.

keyVerses: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” (Matthew 28:19–20)
“for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;” (Romans 3:23–24)
declarations: Lord! I will rectify the priority of my life, no longer chasing only after solving problems, but learning to build relationships.
Let me value people above tasks, and relationships above results.
Give me patience, love and wisdom, so that I am willing to pay the price to build real relationships.
Let my life be one that passes on life, one that makes disciples, living out Christ and becoming an overcomer.
In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen!
practices: Today, deliberately put “people before tasks”
When a problem comes, ask “How is the relationship?” before “How do I solve it?”
Choose “a little slower, but a little more right”
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you.

This morning you have shone the light of your word on the order of our lives. Lord, we confess: we so often put tasks ahead of people, efficiency ahead of relationships, results ahead of life. We have solved many problems, yet left the people around us hurt; we have finished many tasks, yet let our closest relationships grow cold. Please forgive us.

Lord Jesus, thank you. While we were still sinners, you did not first condemn us; you first laid down your life for us. You did not first solve the problem; you first restored the relationship. With your own life you have shown us what it means that “people matter more than tasks”.

Holy Spirit, please be our guide. When we are about to rush into dealing with things again, remind us to look at the people first; when we want to take a shortcut again, stop us; when our hearts are unwilling, joyless and divided, bring us back into your presence and restore our relationship with you first.
Write the order of 321 on the tablets of our hearts: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Make us people who pass on life, people who make disciples.
May our families, our small groups and our church, because the order is right, overflow with life and be joined together into God’s system, to welcome the end time revival.
Let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.
We pray in the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen!
discussion: Mark 3:14 says, “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach,” The Lord first had his disciples “be with him”, and then “sent them out”. Think of the thing keeping you busiest right now: in it, do you spend more time on “people” or on “tasks”? With which person does God want you first to fill in that step of “being with”?

Matthew 5:23–24 says, “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” Right now, is there someone whose name makes your heart sink a little when you think of them? This week, when and how do you plan to go and be reconciled to them first?
l153.title: Rectify the Priority
l153.subtitle: From Solving Problems to Building Relationships
l153.partTitle: Unit 9 · The Practice of Revival — Establishing Relationships

sections.heading: Introduction: The First Button Done Up Wrong
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to begin with a very small but very important question: have you ever done up the first button of a shirt in the wrong hole? Get the first one wrong, and every button after it goes wrong too. You look down: the collar is crooked, the hem hangs uneven, and however much you tug, it won’t sit straight. At that point the easiest fix is not to shift the lower buttons across one by one, but to go back to the first one, undo it, and fasten it again.

Spiritual life is the same. We often spend a great deal of effort adjusting the lower buttons — adjusting our emotions, our circumstances, our relationships, our plans, our schedules — yet we rarely stop to ask: is my first button done up right?

In the spiritual life there is a question that is absolutely crucial and yet so often overlooked: is our “order” right?

Very often we think the point of faith is “solving problems”. The prayer most often heard in church is “Lord, please take this thing away”; the expectation most often in our hearts is “Once this problem has passed, then I’ll have peace.” But brothers and sisters, Jesus keeps bringing us back to a deeper core — “building relationship”.

When the order is wrong, we go round and round inside our problems; when the order is right, we overcome within the relationship.

This is the second lesson on the theme “rectify the priority”. This morning God wants to show us something very concrete: the real key is not whether the problem has been solved, but whether we are connected with God.

Let me tell you about an experience many people have had. A sister once said with great honesty, “The most on-fire six months of my life were the six months my husband was ill. In those six months I prayed every day, wept every day, read the Bible every day, clung to God every day. Then his test results came back normal, and I … disappeared.” She said it very honestly, and it cuts deep. The problem pushed her into God’s presence; when the problem left, so did she. Her faith was built not on “God”, but on “need”.

Faith like this produces a very strange result: we actually need problems in order to stay devout. Once the wind drops and the sea is calm, we lose our reason for drawing near to God. So someone once half-jokingly prayed, “God, if I go too long without any trouble, please give me a little reminder.” Brothers and sisters, that is not faith; that is treating God as a tool.

There is an even more hidden version of this, and it’s found in ministry. Some people are at church all year round — leading worship, leading small groups, visiting, running the sound desk — so busy that not a single weekend is their own; yet when things go quiet, their hearts feel empty. Because they have given all their time to “God’s work”, but no time to “God”. The buttons of ministry are all neatly fastened, but the first button, the relationship, hangs loose.

In today’s lesson God wants to rectify our priority. He wants us to fasten that first button properly again — not solving the problem first, but building the relationship first; not dealing with things first, but coming back first into the Father’s presence.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, One Line
sections.html: The main passages for this lesson come from three scenes set more than a thousand years apart, yet they join into one very clear line. Once we get the background clear, the power of the text comes through.

sections.heading: 1. Matthew 6: Prayer in the Sermon on the Mount
sections.html:
The author of Matthew’s Gospel is the apostle Matthew, formerly a tax collector in Capernaum, who was sitting at the tax office when the Lord called him (Matthew 9:9). The book is generally thought to have been written between AD 50 and 70, chiefly for Jews and Jewish Christians, which is why it quotes the Old Testament so extensively — to prove that Jesus is the Messiah promised in the Old Testament.

The theme passage comes from the “Sermon on the Mount” (Matthew 5–7). Before Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray, he first corrects two wrong kinds of prayer. The first is the Pharisees’ performance prayer, standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. The second is the Gentiles’ transactional prayer: “In praying, don’t use vain repetitions, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard for their much speaking.” (Matthew 6:7) The Gentile mindset was that God is hard to please and has to be persuaded, so you must keep repeating, keep raising the stakes, keep going on longer, in order to get an answer in exchange.

Then Jesus says something that cuts the ground from under all of that: “Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) Feel the weight of this: since the Father already knows, prayer cannot be “informing God”, nor can it be “persuading God”. So what is prayer? Jesus answers with his very next words — “Our Father in heaven”. Prayer is a child coming back into the presence of the Father.

sections.heading: 2. Exodus 15: The Bitter Water of Marah
sections.html:
The author of Exodus is Moses. Scholars hold two views on the date of Israel’s exodus from Egypt, the fifteenth century BC or the thirteenth century BC; this passage is set shortly after the crossing of the Red Sea.

“Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water. When they came to Marah, they couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter. Therefore its name was called Marah.” (Exodus 15:22–23) “Marah” in Hebrew is מָרָה (marah), and it simply means “bitter”. The victory song by the Red Sea had only just been sung (Exodus 15:1–21); the tambourine in Miriam’s hand was still warm — and three days later they could no longer sing.

sections.heading: 3. Numbers 14: Unbelief at Kadesh
sections.html: Numbers 14 is that night at Kadesh Barnea when the Israelites, having heard the bad report of the ten spies, the whole congregation wept aloud and wanted to choose another leader and go back to Egypt. Barely more than a year out of Egypt, they had seen it all — the ten plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, water from the rock — not one thing missing; and yet they fell at the very gate of the promised land. God’s verdict goes straight to the heart: they had seen the miracles, yet still they did not believe.

sections.heading: 4. Romans 8: A Declaration in the Shadow of the Sword
sections.html:
Romans was written by the apostle Paul around AD 56–57, at the end of his third missionary journey, in Corinth, to the church in Rome, which he had not yet met. The believers in the city of Rome were already living in the shadow of persecution; not long afterwards, in AD 64, came the great fire of Rome, Nero laid the blame on the Christians, and persecution broke out in full force. Tradition holds that Paul himself was martyred under Nero.

Romans 8 is the summit of the whole letter. It was not in easy times that Paul wrote that nothing “will be able to separate us from God’s love”. He first lists in a single breath seven of the most savage things — oppression, anguish, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword (Romans 8:35) — and only then does he say: none of these can cut us off.

Brothers and sisters, look at this line: on one side, the bitter water of Marah; on the other, the swords of Rome. Before the bitter water, people complained; before the sword, people overcame. Where does the difference lie? Not in the size of the problem, but in the depth of the relationship. This is the order this lesson sets out to rectify.

sections.heading: 1. The Nature of Prayer: Not Solving Problems, but Building Relationship
sections.html:
“Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9)

When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, the first words were not “Lord, help me”, nor “Lord, please take this hardship away”, but “Our Father in heaven”.

This is a profound revelation: the starting point of prayer is not a problem; the starting point of prayer is a relationship.

Light from the original: not “the Most High”, but “Abba”

“Father” here in Greek is Πάτερ (pater). When Jesus prayed in the Garden of Gethsemane, he used the Aramaic Ἀββά (abba), the most natural and intimate word a child at home uses for his father. Paul twice preserves this word exactly as it is: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15)

Notice the difference between a slave and a son. A slave comes into his master’s presence always to report, to collect his wages, to ask for a reward; a son can come into his father’s presence with nothing at all on his mind — he has simply come home. The slave is concerned with “Is the job done?”; the son is concerned with “Is Dad there?” The very first words of the Lord’s Prayer settle our identity the moment we open our mouths: we are children, not employees.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: To Know God Is Eternal Life

In the same passage Jesus first says, “Therefore don’t be like them, for your Father knows what things you need, before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8) Since the Father already knows our needs, prayer clearly isn’t for passing information on to God.

Then, in the same chapter, Jesus spells out the whole order: “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) The word “first” is about order. When the order is right, things will be added to you; when the order is wrong, you can grab at things your whole life long and never gain God.

In John’s Gospel, Jesus gives a definition of eternal life: “This is eternal life, that they should know you, the only true God, and him whom you sent, Jesus Christ.” (John 17:3) Brothers and sisters, the definition of eternal life is not “all my problems solved” but “knowing”. Knowing is the language of relationship, not the language of a transaction.

The Old Testament prophets speak with the same voice: “Let’s acknowledge Yahweh. Let’s press on to know Yahweh. As surely as the sun rises, Yahweh will appear. He will come to us like the rain, like the spring rain that waters the earth.” (Hosea 6:3) “Let’s press on to know Yahweh” — not pressing on for answers, but pressing on for him.

An Illustration from Life: The Child Who Only Calls When He Needs Money

Imagine a child who has left home to study. He phones home once a month, and every call opens the same way: “Dad, this month’s money …” Of course the father sends it, because he is the father. But after he puts the phone down, how does that father feel? What he wants isn’t to send the money off; what he wants is to hear his child’s voice.

Then one day the child rings and says, “Dad, nothing’s wrong — I just wanted to talk to you.” You can imagine the look on that father’s face. Brothers and sisters, our Heavenly Father is waiting for a call like that, too.

In recent years we’ve all learned the phrase “left on read”. But there is something that hurts even more: “only replying when you need something”. With God, we so often only reply when we need something. God has never turned our requests away; he is simply waiting, all the time, for a call where “nothing’s wrong”.

Confirmation from Psychology: The Secure Base

The British psychiatrist John Bowlby (1907–1990) put forward attachment theory, and his colleague Mary Ainsworth (1913–1999) tested it in the 1970s with her “Strange Situation” experiment. The research found that infants who had formed a secure attachment to their caregiver were actually the most willing to leave their mother and explore the toys in the room — because they knew she was there and they could go back to her at any moment. Psychology calls this a “secure base”.

This is exactly a picture of the spiritual life. Someone with a secure relationship with God does not get out of facing the world; rather, he has more courage to face it, because he knows he can return to the Father at any time. By contrast, someone whose relationship is unsteady panics at the first stir of trouble, because he isn’t sure whether God is there, whether God likes him, whether God will pay him any attention this time.

In church history, Augustine opens his Confessions with words that have been repeated for well over a thousand years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The restlessness of the human heart comes not from having too many problems, but from not yet having come home to the Father who made us.

A 321 Insight

Jesus is the focal point, not our problems; Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you’ll be joyful; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

The 321 order is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Prayer is the most direct training ground of relationship. When we return to the relationship, problems no longer rule us — not because the problems have shrunk, but because God has grown bigger.

sections.heading: 2. Faith That Seeks Only Miracles Cannot Last
sections.html:
“The people murmured against Moses, saying, ‘What shall we drink?’” (Exodus 15:24)

The Israelites had only just witnessed the enormous miracle of the Red Sea parting. With their own eyes they had seen the walls of water stand up; with their own feet they had walked across the dry seabed; with their own ears they had heard the whole Egyptian army go under behind them. Miriam took up her tambourine and danced, and the whole nation sang with one voice. Yet their faith lasted only three days. The moment they met the problem of “bitter water”, they complained at once.

This exposes something very serious: if faith is built on “miracles”, it cannot last; only when faith is built on “relationship” does it stand firm.

Miracles Cannot Manufacture Faith

“because all those men who have seen my glory, and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.” (Numbers 14:22–23)

They saw the miracles, yet still did not believe — this is Scripture’s most grievous diagnosis of that generation. The problem was never whether God was at work, but whether people knew God.

In the New Testament, Jesus said the same thing: “Most certainly I tell you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves, and were filled.” (John 6:26) After the five loaves and two fish, the crowds following him were enormous; but when Jesus began to speak of the cross, people drifted away. What they wanted was bread, not the Lord who gives the bread.

John’s Gospel also records a very sobering passage: “Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the feast, many believed in his name, observing his signs which he did.
