But Jesus didn’t entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone, and because he didn’t need for anyone to testify concerning man; for he himself knew what was in man.” (John 2:23–25) They “believed”, yet Jesus did not entrust himself to them — because that kind of believing stopped at the miracles and never entered into relationship.

A Cycle: Problem-Driven Faith

When people want God only to solve their problems, they fall into a cycle: when there’s a problem, they ask God; when the problem is solved, they forget God; when the next problem comes, they ask God again.

321 has a name for this cycle: the self-centred life — putting ourselves at the centre, placing God beneath our own needs, using God to solve our difficulties. This is the very same old road of the ancient serpent in the Garden of Eden: “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Satan never urges people to do without God; he only urges them to put themselves at the centre and make God revolve around them. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place.

Confirmation from Psychology: Hedonic Adaptation

Psychology has a well-known finding called “hedonic adaptation”, also known as the “hedonic treadmill”, first put forward by Brickman and Campbell (Brickman & Campbell, 1971). In 1978 Brickman, Coates and Janoff-Bulman (Brickman, Coates & Janoff-Bulman) published a classic study comparing the happiness of lottery winners with that of ordinary people, and found that after a while the big winners were not noticeably happier than the control group.

In other words, when you get the very thing you thought would make you happy for the rest of your life, the happiness drifts back to where it started. Brothers and sisters, isn’t this the bankruptcy of the assumption “once the problem is solved I’ll have peace”? The water turned sweet, but ahead lay the wilderness of Sin; the manna came down, yet they still longed for the meat pots of Egypt. The empty place in the human heart was not made by problems, so it cannot be filled by solving problems either. Pascal says in his Pensées, in essence, that there is an infinite abyss in the human heart that can be filled only by an infinite and unchanging object — that is, by God himself.

At Marah the Point Was Not the Water, but God

Look at how the story goes on: “Then he cried to Yahweh. Yahweh showed him a tree, and he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet. There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them.” (Exodus 15:25) Of course God healed the water. But in that same place God did something more important: he laid down a statute and an ordinance, he tested them, and then he revealed his own name — “for I am Yahweh who heals you.” (Exodus 15:26)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: God did not say “I give you water”; God said “I am the one who heals you.” The water was the gift; God was the answer. The Israelites saw only the bitter water turn sweet, and missed the God who had come right up to them and revealed himself. We are often just the same — we take the gift and miss the One who gave it.

Here is a very simple comparison. A husband comes home from a business trip with a present for his wife. If she unwraps the present and then turns and walks away, how will he feel inside? He brought the present home because he wanted to see her, not because she needed that present.

A 321 Insight

Relying on the brain and ourselves, we pursue results; relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit, we pursue relationship.

Only through selflessness, letting Jesus reign as King, will our faith be steady and unshaken by circumstances. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into and living out the fullness and victory of Jesus — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The Israelites changed their route, but not their mindset; the people came out of Egypt, but Egypt did not come out of their hearts. So those forty years in the wilderness were spent going round and round — not around a road, but around a mindset.

sections.heading: 3. Those Who Build Relationship Overcome in All Things
sections.html:
“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?” (Romans 8:35)

“No, in all these things, we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” (Romans 8:37)

“For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38–39)

Paul Was Not a Man Without Problems

The Paul who wrote these words was the man who had been flogged, beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked three times, and had spent a night and a day in the open sea (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). The seven things he lists are not rhetoric; they are his CV. He wasn’t standing on a calm shore saying the storm is nothing to fear; he was standing in the middle of the storm saying: this storm cannot cut me off from my relationship with the Lord.

So he did not overcome by means of his circumstances; he overcame by means of the relationship.

Light from the Original: More Than Conquerors

“More than conquerors” in Romans 8:37 is, in Greek, ὑπερνικῶμεν (hypernikōmen). νικάω (nikaō) means “to overcome”; put ὑπέρ (hyper, “beyond”) in front of it, and together it means “to super-overcome”, “to win by far”. Not a narrow win, not a costly win, but a win with plenty to spare.

The word for “separate” is χωρίζω (chōrizō), meaning “to divide, to part”. The word Paul uses is not “attack” but “separate”. The enemy’s real aim has never been to make you miserable; it is to separate you from God. So what we really need to guard is not our comfort, but our connection.

Two Pictures: The Anchor and the Root

The first picture is the anchor. “This hope we have as an anchor of the soul, a hope both sure and steadfast and entering into that which is within the veil;” (Hebrews 6:19) A ship that has dropped anchor still rocks in the wind and waves, but it does not drift away. Overcoming doesn’t mean not rocking; overcoming means not drifting away.

The second picture is the root. California’s coast redwoods can grow to nearly a hundred metres tall, the tallest trees on earth; yet their roots are not deep, usually only a few metres. The reason they can stand for a thousand years is that root and root weave together underground into one great mat. Height in isolation is the most dangerous thing; life in connection is the most secure. Brothers and sisters, our security lies not in our own height, but in our connection.

Confirmation from Research: Relationships Shape a Whole Life

The Harvard Study of Adult Development has been following the same group of people since 1938, and is one of the longest-running studies of adult development in existence; its current director is Robert Waldinger of Harvard Medical School. More than eighty years of data point to a simple conclusion: what makes people healthier and happier across their whole lives is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Science’s conclusion stops at the relationships between people; Scripture extends that line upward, to the relationship between people and God. If human relationships can shape the health and happiness of a whole life, how much more our relationship with the ever-living God?

The Problem Remains, but the Heart Is at Rest

When people truly build a relationship with God, three very concrete things begin to show: the problem remains, but the heart is not stirred up; circumstances change, but faith is not shaken; outside there is upheaval, inside there is rest.

This isn’t numbness, nor is it escapism. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.” (Psalm 46:1) The psalmist doesn’t say God makes trouble disappear; he says God is a very present help in trouble. And the same psalm ends: “Be still, and know that I am God.” (Psalm 46:10) We become still not because everything has been sorted out, but because we know that he is God.

This is the life of an overcomer. An overcomer is not someone with no battles to fight, but someone who, in the middle of the battle, never leaves his Commander’s side.

A 321 Insight

Selflessness unites us with Christ; union means victory. “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The 321 order is life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. Today’s lesson deals with the very furthest upstream layer — our relationship with God. Only when the upstream runs clear will the downstream run clear.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: When the Order Is Right, Everything Is Right
sections.html:
The Three Foundations, the Two Core Values, the Goal

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model — the first thing Jesus did on earth was to go out into the wilderness to pray early in the morning, before it was light, drawing near to the Father first and then going out to serve people; the Bible is my standard — it is not my feelings, nor the size of my problems, that decide how closely I draw near to God, but God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide — rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King — the King is not someone I order about; the King is the one I obey; let Jesus receive all the glory — when the problem is solved, the glory goes to him; when the problem is still there, I still worship him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not piled up out of lots of people and lots of activity; it is a company of people who have a real relationship with God, being built together.

The Self-Centred Life and Selflessness

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of our problems. Treating God as a tool for solving problems is the most refined form of the self-centred life — calling on God with our lips, while “self” sits enthroned in our hearts. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

The Fivefold Change

321 says the fivefold change runs: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. What this lesson sets out to change is that very first button — our mindset. From “faith is about solving problems” to “faith is about building relationship”. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, daily living changes; when daily living changes, relationships naturally change; and when relationships change, only then will ministry bear real fruit. The order cannot be reversed.

To people whose ministry was overflowing, Jesus spoke the most terrifying words: “I never knew you. Depart from me, you who work iniquity.” (Matthew 7:23) They had preached, cast out demons and done mighty works in the Lord’s name; every box under ministry was ticked, but the box under relationship was blank. Brothers and sisters, don’t turn ministry into a substitute for relationship.

The Shift in Perspective

From the human perspective to God’s perspective: people ask, “When will this be over?”; God asks, “How much have you come to know me in this?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: on earth we see bitter water; heaven sees the tree — a foreshadowing of the cross.

From the temporary to the eternal: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

From the worldly to the godly: worldly faith seeks “things going smoothly”; godly faith seeks “being right with God”.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice is this: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2”, practise living out the selfless (0) life, and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Notice one thing: not one of the nine graces is “problems disappearing”. Fruit grows out of relationship; it isn’t handed out after a problem is solved. Someone whose relationship with God is right can grow patience, peace and joy even while the problem is still there.

The 235 relationships are these: with a selfless person become a “2”, spiritual companions; establish “3”, spiritual parents and spiritual children; become “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. When you start to have a spiritual companion with whom you don’t talk about problems but simply talk about God, your faith has moved from being problem-driven to being relationship-driven.

The Path of Serving

Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). This path begins with the Spirit, not with tasks; it ends with God being glorified, not with problems being solved. When the order is right, the path is right.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We will drive each one deep using the 321 “eight stages of changing our mindset” — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Every day, set aside a “prayer with no agenda”

Focus of the practice: for the relationship alone, not for problems.

Each day, set aside a time to pray — not to ask for anything, but simply to draw near to God. You might begin like this: “Heavenly Father, I come before you not to ask for anything, but to draw near to you.” Let your heart grow still before God, and learn to enjoy being with him.

Information: first hold on to today’s truth — the Father already knows what I need (Matthew 6:8). Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let you truly see that you are a son, not a slave. Conviction: say to God in your heart, “I believe,” and admit that in the past you have treated him as a tool. Implementation: start with five minutes; set an alarm, and for five minutes ask for nothing at all, just say, “Lord, I love you; I’ve come simply to be with you.” Evaluation: in those five minutes, where did your heart wander off to? Did you sit down and immediately start planning your schedule? Correction: write your to-do list on a piece of paper first and put it to one side, so that your heart is free. Repetition: twenty-one days in a row, at the same time and in the same place every day. Multiplication: find a brother or sister to do this twenty-one-day practice with you, and remind each other.

David’s prayer can be our model: “One thing I have asked of Yahweh, that I will seek after: that I may dwell in Yahweh’s house all the days of my life, to see Yahweh’s beauty, and to inquire in his temple.” (Psalm 27:4) What he wanted was to dwell in the house, not to grab something and leave.

Practice 2: When a problem comes, first ask, “What is God’s heart in this?”

Focus of the practice: from solving problems to seeking God.

When you meet a problem, don’t rush to get it solved; first ask: Lord, what do you want me to learn in this? Which side of you do you want me to come to know better? Let the problem become a doorway to knowing God, not a source of anxiety.

Information: remember the lesson of Marah — what God revealed beside the bitter water was “I am Yahweh who heals you” (Exodus 15:26). Revelation: ask God to let you see some aspect of himself in the midst of your hardship. Conviction: believe that if this has come to me, God surely has a good purpose in it. Implementation: get a “problem notebook”; on the left write the problem, and on the right write only one sentence — “In this, I have come to know God’s ____.” Evaluation: look back after a week — is the right-hand column still empty? Correction: if it is, it means I am still asking God for a method, not for himself. Repetition: build the reflex of “ask for his heart first, then ask for a method”. Multiplication: tell your small group the testimonies in your right-hand column.

Moses’ example is the best contrast. He did not say, “Please take the hardship away”; he said, “please show me your way, now, that I may know you” (Exodus 33:13), and again, “If your presence doesn’t go with me, don’t carry us up from here.” (Exodus 33:15) What Moses wanted was not an easy road, but God going with him.

Practice 3: Practise Holding On to the Relationship in Every Circumstance

Focus of the practice: circumstances do not decide the relationship.

In good times and bad, stay connected with God every day — prayer, Bible reading, worship. Remind yourself: I don’t draw near to God because of my circumstances; I draw near to him because I love him. A life like this will grow more and more secure.

Information: see clearly the difference between “drawing near to God because of circumstances” and “drawing near to God because I love him”. Revelation: let the Holy Spirit show you which seasons of your life you prayed in only because you were afraid. Conviction: resolve to let love be your motive — “We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19) Implementation: set an “immovable appointment” that doesn’t change in good times or bad. Evaluation: this week, was there a day you skipped it because “nothing was going on today”? Correction: shorten the time but don’t cancel it — better five minutes than zero. Repetition: three months without a break, and it becomes the skeleton of your life. Multiplication: bring one person in to keep this appointment with you.

Asaph’s testimony is worth learning by heart: “Whom do I have in heaven? There is no one on earth whom I desire besides you.” (Psalm 73:25) “But it is good for me to come close to God. I have made the Lord Yahweh my refuge, that I may tell of all your works.” (Psalm 73:28)

A Gentle Reminder: Where Peace Comes From

Many people think, “Once the problem is solved, I’ll have peace.” But the order God gives is exactly the opposite: it is not solving the problem that brings peace; it is building the relationship that brings peace.

Jesus said, “Peace I leave with you. My peace I give to you; not as the world gives, I give to you. Don’t let your heart be troubled, neither let it be fearful.” (John 14:27) The peace the world gives is to take the problem away; the peace Jesus gives is that he himself comes.

Isaiah also says it very clearly: “You will keep whoever’s mind is steadfast in perfect peace, because he trusts in you.” (Isaiah 26:3) The condition of peace is not that nothing is happening around us, but that our hearts are steadfastly trusting in him.

So don’t fix your focus on the problem; fix your focus on Jesus. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and you’ll be joyful; rely on the brain and yourself, and you’ll be troubled.

When Peter was walking on the water, the wind and waves were there the whole time; while he looked at Jesus he kept walking, and when he looked at the waves he began to sink. Brothers and sisters, it wasn’t the waves that changed; it was his focus.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: When the Relationship Is Right, Everything Is Right
sections.html:
When prayer turns from “asking for our circumstances to change” to “longing to know God”, and when faith turns from “solving problems” to “building relationship”, your life will enter a whole new level.

Problems no longer rule you, circumstances no longer bind you, because you have taken hold of what matters most — your relationship with God.

Every sailor knows this principle: set off from harbour just one degree off course, and it looks trivial; but after a hundred kilometres you will be nearly 1.8 kilometres off target. A one-degree difference in our order becomes a world of difference by the end of a life. So this morning we are not here to do one more thing; we are here to correct our heading by one degree.

Let Jesus be King — the King is not a consultant I’ve called in to solve my problems; the King is the Lord I obey all my life. Let Jesus receive all the glory — not waiting until the problem is solved to give him the glory, but now, at this very moment, while the problem is still unsolved, giving him the glory.

At the start of his book The Knowledge of the Holy, A. W. Tozer says that what comes into our minds when we think about God is the most important thing about us. Brothers and sisters, when you think of God, what comes to mind — a “God who solves problems”, or a “Father who loves you”? That answer decides the order of your whole faith.

This morning, let us rectify the priority together. Not dealing with the problem first, but coming back first into the Father’s embrace. Because when the relationship is right, everything is right.

keyVerses: “Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9)

“For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 8:38–39)
practices: Practise holding on to the relationship in every circumstance
prayer: Lord Jesus, I declare: I will no longer make solving problems my centre; I will make building my relationship with you my priority.

Lord, forgive me for treating you as a tool in the past — calling on you when I needed something, and drifting away when I didn’t. Today I return to my place as a son, back into the Father’s presence.
Whatever my circumstances, I will draw near to you, know you and trust in you. In good times I will not leave you; in hard times I will not complain against you.
I believe that nothing can separate me from your love. Not oppression, not anguish, not persecution — not even the sword.
I want to live in your presence and become a steady, joyful overcomer. Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Pray like this: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.’” (Matthew 6:9) Think back honestly: over the past month, how much of your praying has been “asking for things”, and how much has been “drawing near to God”? What does that proportion tell you? How, specifically, will you adjust it?

“Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Could oppression, or anguish, or persecution …?” (Romans 8:35) In the hardship you are facing that is still unresolved, at what moment have you felt “I’m about to be cut off”? In the light of this lesson, which side of himself does God want you to come to know in that situation? Name one practice you will begin this week.

sections.heading: Introduction: Your First Words Give Your Heart Away
sections.html:
Dear brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a very ordinary early-morning scene.

A mother walks into the kitchen and finds the floor a wreck — the milk is spilled, a glass lies shattered everywhere, and her child is standing right in the middle of it, shoes in the puddle, frozen stiff.

At that moment, what will the mother say?

For most of us, the first words out of our mouths are: “How could you be so careless!” Or: “How many times have I told you?” Or else: “Go and get a cloth, quickly!”

Brothers and sisters, notice that those three sentences have one thing in common — every one of them is aimed at the “thing.” The milk, the glass, the floor, the cloth. And the child standing in the middle, trembling inside — not one word is spoken to him.

But there is another kind of mother. She crouches down first, looks her child in the eye and says, “Did you hurt yourself?”

The same event, the same mess on the floor. A different first sentence, and a completely different outcome.

Brothers and sisters, our first words are never just words. They give away the real order inside our hearts — whether, deep down, the “task” comes first or the “person” comes first.

In this lesson we continue “rectifying the priority.” In the last two lessons God led us to rectify the priority in “prayer”; today he wants to rectify our priority in a place where it is even easier to go astray and even easier to hurt people — in “discipline.”

Because when someone does wrong, our first reaction is usually these three questions:

How do I correct the mistake? How do I solve the problem? How do I get things back to normal?

None of these questions is bad. They are even very responsible, very efficient — just what a mature adult ought to ask.

But brothers and sisters, God’s heart does not start there.

What God cares about is not only “What have you done wrong?” What he cares about even more is “Where are you, the person, right now?”

That is why, after the very first sin in human history, the first words God spoke were not an accusation but a call —

“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, did an all-knowing God need to ask where Adam was? Of course not. He asked, not to gather information, but to restore a relationship. He asked so that the man hiding behind the trees, covering himself with fig leaves, would hear a voice that was still looking for him.

In this lesson God wants to lead us into a deeper seeing:

Truly godly discipline is not for solving problems; it is for restoring relationships.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Passages, One Father’s Heart
sections.html: To truly understand this lesson, we first need to stand in the historical setting of two passages.

sections.heading: 1. The Background of Hebrews 12
sections.html:
Who wrote Hebrews? The church has held different views throughout its history. Some say Paul, some say Barnabas, some say Apollos. The third-century church father Origen made a famous remark, recorded by Eusebius of Caesarea in his Ecclesiastical History: as to who actually wrote this letter, God alone knows. That remark has always been the church’s most honest answer.

The date of writing is generally placed between AD 60 and 70. The reason is simple: when the author speaks of the temple sacrifices, he uses the present tense, as though the fire on the altar were still burning. And the temple in Jerusalem was destroyed by the Roman general Titus in AD 70.

The recipients were a group of “Hebrew” believers — Christians from a Jewish background. They had believed in Jesus, but at a very heavy price: thrown out of the synagogue, cut off by their families, their property plundered; some were imprisoned, some were martyred.

And so they began to waver. Not because they no longer believed, but because they were worn out. A very real question sat in their hearts: if God truly loves us, why has life become harder since we started following the Lord?

Hebrews 12 is the answer to that question.

Chapter 11 has just finished counting off a long roll of the heroes of faith, and chapter 12 opens: “Therefore let’s also, seeing we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, lay aside every weight and the sin which so easily entangles us, and let’s run with perseverance the race that is set before us” (Hebrews 12:1). Then it fixes our eyes on Jesus, and then — the author turns, and speaks the key to this lesson:

“It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline?” (Hebrews 12:7)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to the logic. The author does not say: you are suffering because God is angry. He says: what you endure is God disciplining you — and the evidence of discipline is not “God doesn’t want you any more.” Quite the opposite: the evidence of discipline is “you are a son.”

Verse 8 puts it even more bluntly: “But if you are without discipline, of which all have been made partakers, then you are illegitimate, and not children.” (Hebrews 12:8)

In other words, discipline is not the breaking off of a relationship; discipline is the very proof of it.

And the purpose? Verse 10 says that the Father disciplines us “for our profit, that we may be partakers of his holiness.” (Hebrews 12:10)

Not to vent his anger, not to settle the score, but “that we may be partakers of his holiness.”

sections.heading: 2. The Background of Genesis 3
sections.html:
Genesis 3 is the heaviest and also the tenderest chapter in the whole Bible.

Heavy, because in this chapter humanity left God. Tender, because in this chapter God began to search for humanity.

When Moses wrote this chapter, he was facing a people just out of Egypt, learning in the wilderness to know God. For four hundred years they had lived in Egypt’s world of myths — gods who were moody and unpredictable, where anyone who did wrong could only offer sacrifices to bribe them, to please and placate them. Moses wanted them to see an utterly different God: a God whose first move after humanity sinned was not to send down thunder and fire, but to walk into the garden and call out.

And Deuteronomy 8:5 is exactly Moses’ summing-up to this people on the plains of Moab: “You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5)

In what situation was this said? When the forty years in the wilderness were about to end and the land of Canaan lay right before their eyes. Looking back on those forty years, Moses said: “You shall remember all the way which Yahweh your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to test you, to know what was in your heart, whether you would keep his commandments or not.” (Deuteronomy 8:2)

Brothers and sisters, to human eyes forty years in the wilderness was punishment; to God’s eyes it was upbringing. It was raising a crowd of slaves into a family of sons and daughters.

The word for “discipline” in Hebrew is yasar, and the noun is musar — the word Proverbs uses from beginning to end. It does not mean “to beat”; it means “to instruct, to teach, to shape.” The Greek is clearer still: Hebrews uses paideuō, with the noun paideia, whose root is the word for “child” (pais). In Greek culture, paideia meant the whole education by which a child is raised into a complete person.

So when the Bible says “God disciplines you,” the picture is not of a judge on the bench banging his gavel; it is of a father bending down, taking his child’s hand and teaching him to walk, one step at a time.

Brothers and sisters, which kind of God is the God in your heart?

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Discipline Centred on Solving Problems Loses People’s Hearts
sections.html:
“You shall consider in your heart that as a man disciplines his son, so Yahweh your God disciplines you.” (Deuteronomy 8:5)

Notice where this verse puts its weight: “as a man disciplines his son.” Not as a jailer manages a prisoner, not as a foreman manages a labourer, not as an auditor manages a process, but as a father disciplines his son.

Yet we very easily turn discipline into something else. When we use discipline only to “solve the problem,” its nature has in fact already turned into three things:

First, controlling people with rules. Second, forcing change with pressure. Third, getting results with punishment.

In the short term this kind of discipline looks very effective. Because things really are brought under control: the child stops answering back, the co-worker stops coming in late, meetings run as normal, and the figures are back on track.

But brothers and sisters, we have to ask a deeper question: what has happened to that person’s heart?

Usually three things happen.

He feels rejected — so when I get it wrong, what you want is the result, not me.

He feels negated — so in your eyes, I am nothing more than my mistake.

He feels he no longer has the strength to get up — since nothing I do is ever good enough, I might as well not try.

And so a vicious circle sets in: the problem brings punishment, punishment brings a backlash, the backlash brings harsher punishment, harsher punishment brings a broken relationship, and once the relationship is broken, the heart is lost.

The Bible described this kind of discipline long ago

In Ezekiel 34, God rebukes the shepherds of Israel in some very sharp words:

“You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.” (Ezekiel 34:4)

Brothers and sisters, look at how this passage is built. The first five clauses are “things not done”: not strengthened, not healed, not bound up, not brought back, not sought — every one of them about “people.” The last clause is the “thing done”: ruled over them with force and with rigour — and that is about “management.”

God’s charge is clear: you did plenty of managing, but you lost the people.

Paul also warns fathers twice. Ephesians 6:4: “You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.” Colossians 3:21 is even more specific: “Fathers, don’t provoke your children, so that they won’t be discouraged.”

“Discouraged” — the original word means disheartened, deflated, losing all drive. Brothers and sisters, this is the most frightening side effect of the wrong kind of discipline: it does not remove the mistake; it removes, along with it, the person’s inner strength to want to become better.

A picture from daily life

I often think of a picture. A fruit tree has grown crooked, and the gardener has two ways of dealing with it.

The first: take an iron bar, bind the tree to it tightly and force it straight. The tree looks straight at once — very efficient. But inside, the tree has already snapped; loosen the bar and it will either fall over or never bear fruit again.

The second: the gardener sets a stake beside it, gently supports it, and then gives it time, gives it water, gives it sunshine. The process is maddeningly slow, but that tree grows straight from the inside.

Brothers and sisters, forcing straight is management; patient support — that alone is discipline.

Corroborating evidence from psychology

Between 1966 and 1971 the psychologist Diana Baumrind put forward her well-known classification of parenting styles. She divided parents into several types, two of which deserve our particular attention:

One is the “authoritarian” style — high demands, low responsiveness. Many rules, few explanations; obedience valued, relationship not.

The other is the “authoritative” style — equally high demands, but high responsiveness. Boundaries just as clear, yet a willingness to explain the reasons, to listen, to keep a warm connection.

More than half a century of follow-up research has consistently shown that children raised the first way are outwardly compliant but often carry higher anxiety and lower self-esteem inside, while children raised the second way do markedly better in self-control, social competence and mental health.

Further, Elizabeth Gershoff of the University of Texas and Andrew Grogan-Kaylor of the University of Michigan published a meta-analysis in the Journal of Family Psychology in 2016 that pooled seventy-five studies covering more than 160,000 children. They found that physical punishment had almost no positive link with “compliance,” but was significantly linked with more aggression, more antisocial behaviour and more mental health problems.

Brothers and sisters, let me say this very carefully: psychology is not our standard; the Bible is. But when science honestly observes this world, it often bears witness to what the Bible says. And its witness here is exactly this: discipline aimed only at “behaviour” can keep things under control, but it cannot keep people.

A 321 Insight

Put the task above the person, and you will lose people’s hearts. When the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong.

Brothers and sisters, the 321 order is very clear: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

When we put the “task” before the “person,” the end result is often that even the task isn’t done well. Because every task is done by people. Win the task but lose the person, and sooner or later the task will collapse anyway.

And the root of “putting the task above the person,” in the end, is the self-centred life. Because what I want is my order, my face, my schedule, my being right. When a person puts himself at the centre, without even realising it he treats others as tools for reaching his goals.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, when it comes to discipline, the hardest lesson of all is this one sentence: I am not the one who changes him; the Holy Spirit is. My originally intended position is to love him, to walk with him and to bring him before God.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: Discipline Centred on Love Says, “I’ll Walk with You as You Change”
sections.html:
“It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline?” (Hebrews 12:7)

God’s discipline has never been to toss out a “Fix it yourself!” and then turn and walk away.

God’s discipline is one sentence: I’ll walk with you as you change.

That is the heart of the Heavenly Father.

“One who spares the rod hates his son, but one who loves him is careful to discipline him.” (Proverbs 13:24)

The Chinese Union Version renders the second half “one who loves his son disciplines him at all times.” Notice those words “at all times.” At all times means continually present. Not showing up only when something goes wrong, not drawing near only when tempers flare. A father who “disciplines at all times” is a father who is always there.

True discipline has three core elements.

First, relationship

Not a reaction to sin, but something that springs from love.

“For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines” (Hebrews 12:6) — notice the order: first “whom the Lord loves,” then “he disciplines.” Love comes first; discipline follows. Discipline is one way love expresses itself, not a break in love.

Brothers and sisters, this is why David in Psalm 23 could say something very strange: “Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4)

What are the rod and the staff? They are the tools in a shepherd’s hand. The staff is a crook, used to hook back a sheep that has wandered off; the rod is a short club, used to strike wild animals and also to tap a sheep’s flank to set it in the right direction. These are tools of discipline! And yet David says: they comfort me.

Why can a rod and a staff become a comfort? Because the One holding them is the One of whom it is said, “Yahweh is my shepherd.” When the relationship is right, discipline becomes comfort; when the relationship is wrong, the very same rod and staff are nothing but fear.

Second, companionship

Not demanding change, but walking with people through change.

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

Brothers and sisters, the word “restore” here is katartizō in Greek. Where it appears elsewhere in the New Testament, it is beautiful: James and John were “in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets” (Matthew 4:21) — “mending” is the very same word. In ancient medical language it was also used for “setting a dislocated bone back in place.”

Do you see it? Restoring is not throwing away a torn net and buying a new one; it is sitting down and, stitch by stitch, mending the tear. Restoring is not cutting off a dislocated arm; it is taking hold of it, bearing the pain, and pushing it back into place.

Mending nets takes time. Setting a bone takes closeness. Neither can be done by remote control.

Paul adds one more line: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Why? Because the greatest danger for the one who goes to restore someone is pride — I am the one standing; you are the one who fell. Once that thought creeps in, restoring turns into judging.

In 2 Corinthians, dealing with the brother who had sinned and then repented, Paul says: “so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him.” (2 Corinthians 2:7–8)

“Lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow” — brothers and sisters, what Paul really feared was not that this man wasn’t suffering enough, but that he would suffer so much he would go under. That is a shepherd’s heart.

Third, restoration

Not condemnation, but bringing the person back to the right place.

Facing the woman caught in adultery, Jesus said two things, and neither can be left out: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11)

The first sentence restores the relationship; the second restores the direction. Only the first is indulgence; only the second is law. The two together — that is the gospel.

After Peter denied the Lord three times, Jesus didn’t preach him a sermon of rebuke. On the shore of the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus lit a charcoal fire, first invited him to breakfast, and then asked him three times, “Do you love me?” (John 21:15–17) Three denials, three questions, three commissions. Jesus wasn’t raking up the past; Jesus was setting a bone — pushing that dislocated arm back into place, once, twice, three times.

An example from daily life

I once heard a father say this. In high school his son did something very serious; the school was going to put a formal demerit on his record, and at home everything blew up. He said that night he could hardly speak, and in the end he said only one thing: “Son, you have to take responsibility for this. Dad won’t shield you from it. But from tomorrow, every step you take, Dad will walk it with you.”

Brothers and sisters, notice that he didn’t cancel the consequences. Love does not cancel consequences; love refuses to let a person bear the consequences alone.

Many years later that son said: the day my life really changed wasn’t the day I got the demerit; it was the day my dad said, “Dad will walk it with you.”

Corroborating evidence from psychology and a well-known saying

In 1957 the humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers set out “the necessary and sufficient conditions of therapeutic personality change,” and the most central of them was “unconditional positive regard.” He discovered something: people don’t change while they are being evaluated; people change when they are accepted.

The marriage researcher John Gottman, observing couples’ interactions over many years at the University of Washington, proposed his famous “magic ratio”: in stable relationships, positive interactions outnumber negative ones by roughly five to one. In other words, one correction needs five affirmations to carry it before the relationship can bear the weight.

Brothers and sisters, we are not using psychology to replace the Bible; we are saying that the human heart God made simply works this way. Because the One who made the human heart is himself love.

There is also a saying generally attributed to the American president Theodore Roosevelt: people don’t care how much you know until they know how much you care. Scholars still dispute where it comes from, but the point holds true: truth that has not passed through love cannot reach the heart.

A 321 Insight

Life, relationships, ministry. Win the heart first, then talk about change.

Brothers and sisters, the fivefold change of 321 goes like this: change the mindset, and the life changes; change the life, and daily living changes; change daily living, and relationships change; change relationships, and ministry changes.

Notice — “ministry” comes last. Yet we so often try to start at the very end, demanding straight away that the other person “change their behaviour.” That is swimming against the current.

This kind of discipline may not show results right away. But brothers and sisters, it brings real change of life. Quick change is often on the outside; slow change is the change on the inside.

Only when people are received in love do they have the strength to change.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: God Disciplines to Restore People, Not to Punish Them
sections.html:
“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, these are the first words God spoke after humanity sinned.

Notice what God did not say. God did not say, “What have you done?” God did not say, “I warned you.” God did not say, “You’re finished.”

What God spoke was a single Hebrew word: ayyekkah — where are you?

In that question is the Heavenly Father’s heart. Because what God cared about was not the incident, but the person’s relationship with him.

In fact, on that day it was not God who hid; it was humanity. God was still “walking in the garden”; God was still calling out. It was humanity that covered itself with fig leaves; it was humanity that hid among the trees.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you a question: this morning, is there some corner inside you where a leaf-clad version of yourself is hiding too? You think God is angry with you, but God is walking in the garden, calling your name.

Then we see God do three things.

First, God promised redemption

“I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.” (Genesis 3:15)

Church history has called this verse the “first gospel” (protoevangelium) — the first glimmer of the dawn of the gospel. Brothers and sisters, look closely at the timing: humanity had not yet repented; humanity was still shifting the blame — Adam blamed Eve, Eve blamed the serpent — and at that most undeserving moment, God spoke the promise of salvation first.

This is what “the goodness of God leads you to repentance” (Romans 2:4) means. It isn’t that you repent first and then God is kind; it is that God is kind first and leads you to repentance.

Second, God made them clothes

“Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.” (Genesis 3:21)

Humanity covered its shame with fig leaves; God made garments of skins. Leaves were humanity’s way — they wither and tear. Skins were God’s way — they required a life to shed its blood.

Brothers and sisters, this is the first time in the Bible that a life died to cover human shame. Those garments of skin point all the way to the cross on Calvary.

Picture the scene: the Lord of creation crouching down and, with his own hands, clothing two people who had just betrayed him. That is not punishment; those are a father’s hands.

Third, God drove them out of Eden

On the surface this looks like the harshest act of all, but hidden inside it is the deepest mercy.

Because if humanity, in its fallen state, had eaten from the tree of life, it would have lived forever in sin — and that would have been true hell. God drove them out so that sin would not exist forever.

Brothers and sisters, sometimes the door God closes is the door that saves your life.

So all of this reveals three things: God’s discipline carries love; God’s actions aim to restore relationship; God’s intention is to win people back.

“Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.” (Job 5:17)

This is hard to accept, yet it is true. Because if God gave up on you, that would be the most frightening thing of all. In Revelation 3:19 the Lord says to the church in Laodicea: “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent.” Standing in front of “reprove and chasten” are the words “As many as I love.”

The writer of Lamentations, among the ruins of a destroyed Jerusalem, wrote these words: “For though he causes grief, yet he will have compassion according to the multitude of his loving kindnesses. For he does not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men.” (Lamentations 3:32–33)

“He does not afflict willingly” — brothers and sisters, when God disciplines you, God’s own heart aches too.

In Hosea, God cries out to backsliding Israel in a voice that almost breaks: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel?” (Hosea 11:8)

That is the God who disciplines us.

A picture from science

I think of a very common picture: a broken bone.

When a bone breaks, the first thing the doctor often has to do is “push it back into place” — and that hurts. Then comes the cast, the immobilising, the order not to move, and every movement hurts. From the patient’s point of view, everything the doctor does seems to add to his pain.

But in fact the doctor is not punishing him; the doctor is giving him “the conditions for healing.” A bone needs three things to heal: alignment, immobilisation and time. Miss one, and it grows crooked.

Brothers and sisters, God’s discipline is just like that. He pushes us back into place (alignment), he restricts us (immobilisation), and he gives us a stretch of days that seem to go nowhere (time). At the time it doesn’t feel joyful; it feels grievous. But Hebrews 12:11 says: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”

Afterward. Brothers and sisters, remember that word “afterward.” What you are going through now is not the end of the story.

A 321 Insight

Humbly accept discipline and you receive grace; refuse discipline and you fall into pride.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5)

Brothers and sisters, discipline is hard not because it hurts, but because it forces us to admit, “I was wrong.” And admitting we were wrong is exactly what the self-centred life hates most.

So those who refuse discipline are not people who feel no pain; they are people who are too proud. And those who humbly accept discipline discover something wonderful: what they meet in discipline is not a penalty, but a Father.

From the human point of view to God’s point of view, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

Seen from the human point of view, discipline says: I am being suppressed. Seen from God’s point of view: I am being sculpted.

Seen from the earthly point of view, discipline says: I have lost. Seen from the heavenly point of view: I have been kept safe.

Seen from the temporary point of view, discipline says: this is so bitter. Seen from the eternal point of view: it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness.

God’s discipline is not meant to knock us down; it is meant to restore us and make us overcomers.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Putting Discipline Back into the Right System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if this lesson stopped at “we should be loving,” that would not be enough. 321 wants to help us put the whole matter of “discipline” back inside God’s system.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. How did Jesus discipline Peter? He lit a fire on the shore, invited him to breakfast and asked him three times, “Do you love me?” How did Jesus treat the woman who was caught? First, no condemnation; then, “Go your way.” The role model for discipline is not our parents, nor our experience, but Jesus.

The Bible is my standard. Not my emotions, not my face, not the way handed down in my family. When I need to correct someone, I must first ask: what does the Bible say? The Bible says, “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1); the Bible says, “don’t provoke your children to wrath” (Ephesians 6:4).

The Holy Spirit is my guide. When to speak, how far to go, what tone to use, in what setting — the Bible won’t list these out item by item; for these we depend on the Holy Spirit. Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled.

Brothers and sisters, a great deal of discipline fails not because the content was wrong, but because the timing was wrong, the tone was wrong, the setting was wrong. And all three of those need the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. When I face someone who has done wrong, who is on the throne? If I am on the throne, what I want is “I’m right”; if Jesus is on the throne, what I want is “he lives.”

Let Jesus receive all the glory. If discipline succeeds, who gets the glory? If what I’m thinking is, “Good thing I handled it,” then I have stolen the glory. True restoration is always the Holy Spirit’s work; we are only the pair of hands God uses.

The Goal

Establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, the closing line of this lesson puts it so well: this is the life of God’s system.

The Worldly system runs on “reward and punishment”: do well and you’re rewarded; do badly and you’re punished. God’s system runs on the “father–son relationship”: because you are my son, I discipline you; because I discipline you, it proves you are my son.

Two systems raise two kinds of people. The system of reward and punishment raises “performers” — people who spend their whole lives proving they deserve to be loved. The father–son system raises “sons and daughters” — people who know they are already loved, and so have the strength to change.

The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless

Brothers and sisters, let’s be honest. When we discipline others, our strongest impulse is often not to do them good; it is “I can’t take this any more.”

I can’t take the mess, I can’t take being answered back, I can’t take my plans being upset, I can’t take the way people will look at me.

That is the self-centred life. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Correct someone from a high horse, and he’ll answer back from a high horse, and in the end both sides lose. Draw near to someone in humility, and his heart softens — that is a win for both.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, when it is “no longer I,” I don’t need to win any more. I don’t need to prove I’m right; I only need him to live.

The 920 practice

The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in a relationship with is our “2”; with each of them we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Brothers and sisters, look at these nine graces. How many of them come into their own precisely when “someone has done wrong”?

Patience — he can’t turn around all at once, and I can still wait.

Kindness — he has fallen, and my tone is still warm.

Goodness — what I want really is his good, not my own satisfaction.

Gentleness — Galatians 6:1 says “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness”; this is the one.

Self-control — say what needs saying and then stop, without one extra hurtful word.

So the scene of discipline turns out to be the very best training ground for the fruit of the Spirit.

The 235 relationships

Become a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion: find a companion who can tell you the truth and is willing to walk with you. When you set out to restore someone, have someone praying for you first.

Build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children: true spiritual parents don’t just correct your mistakes; they walk with you through change. True spiritual children are those willing to accept discipline humbly.

Become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades: in the team, restore one another, build one another up, and together bring people back into God’s system.

The priority of relationships

Brothers and sisters, this lesson is about “rectifying the priority.” Remember the four priorities of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

When I set out to correct someone: first with God — I pray first, asking God to give me his heart; then with myself — I examine myself first: is my motive love or anger?; then with others — I draw near to him and restore the relationship first; and last with things — only then do I deal with the matter itself.

Brothers and sisters, most discipline that fails has the order upside down: deal with the matter first, then the person, forgetting to examine ourselves and forgetting to seek God first.

sections.heading: Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to work each one out in practice.

Practice 1: See mistakes with “relationship first”

When someone does wrong, don’t jump straight to “How do I deal with this?” First ask two questions:

How can I help him get back into right relationship? How can I let him feel accepted?

Learn to care for the person first, and deal with the matter second.

Information: Copy out today’s verse — “Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9) — and put it where you will see it.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you and bring to mind a time when you “dealt only with the matter and gave no thought to the person.” Has that person’s face come to mind now?

Conviction: Admit before God — put the task above the person, and you will lose people’s hearts; when the person goes wrong, the task goes wrong. This is real, not theory.

Implementation: This week, whenever someone gets something wrong, practise making your first sentence about the “person.” For example: “Are you all right?” “This can’t have been easy for you.” Ask about the person first, then about the matter.

Evaluation: Each evening, take three minutes to look back — were my first words today aimed at the matter, or at the person?

Correction: If you got it wrong, don’t wait. Go back that same day and say: “I’m sorry, I was too hasty just now. I cared about the matter first and didn’t care about you first.”

Repetition: Keep it up for forty days. A change of mindset is not a one-off decision; it is practice repeated again and again.

Multiplication: Teach this practice to your spouse, your children, your small-group members, so that “people before tasks” becomes the culture of your home and your group.

Practice 2: Cultivate the attitude of “I’ll walk with you as you change”

In the family, in the church, in every kind of relationship, don’t just demand that the other person change; express two sentences through your actions: I’m willing to walk this road with you; I won’t give up on you.

Information: Remember that the “restore” of Galatians 6:1 is mending nets and setting bones. Mending nets goes stitch by stitch; setting a bone takes getting very close.

Revelation: Let the Holy Spirit point out someone you have already “given up on” in your heart. Perhaps you have never said it aloud, but in your heart you have already filed him under “hopeless.”

Conviction: Believe one thing — only when people are received in love do they have the strength to change.

Implementation: This week, take the initiative to do one concrete thing for that person. A phone call, a meal, some time together. Don’t bring up his mistake; just let him know you’re still there.

Evaluation: Am I “walking alongside,” or “supervising”? The one who walks alongside asks, “How have you been lately?” The supervisor asks, “Have you changed yet?”

Correction: If you find you’ve turned into a supervisor again, go back before the Lord and ask him to give you a father’s heart.

Repetition: Walking alongside is not a single visit; it is a long journey together. Remember, the Chinese of Proverbs speaks of disciplining “at all times.”

Multiplication: When one day he is back on his feet, take him with you to walk alongside the next person who has fallen. That is spiritual multiplication.

Practice 3: Practise humbly accepting God’s discipline

When God shines his light on us and rebukes us, don’t run, don’t rationalise; pray instead: Lord, I am willing to be changed by you; help me turn back from my mistakes.

Let discipline become a blessing for the growth of your life.

Information: Memorise Hebrews 12:11: “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.”

Revelation: Be still before the Lord and ask one question: “Lord, what is the one thing you have kept saying to me lately that I keep dodging?”

Conviction: Admit it — refusing discipline is falling into pride. Only by humbly accepting discipline do we receive grace.

Implementation: Today, confess that very thing to God, specifically; if it involves other people, go and apologise, specifically.

Evaluation: Have I truly repented, or am I just sorry? Being sorry is an emotion; repentance is a turning.

Correction: If you find yourself rationalising again, stop at once and pray: Lord, I don’t want to explain; I want to turn back.

Repetition: Each evening set aside five minutes and let the Holy Spirit shine his light on that day’s words and attitudes.

Multiplication: Tell your testimony of being disciplined and restored to someone who is being disciplined right now. Your testimony will become his hope.

A Gentle Reminder: Love Is the Power That Truly Changes People

Brothers and sisters, many people think strictness is what brings change.

But God lets us see: love is the power that truly changes people.

Discipline without love wounds people; discipline in love saves people.

The same knife kills in a robber’s hand and saves life in a surgeon’s hand. The knife hasn’t changed; the heart holding it has.

The same words, “You were wrong,” spoken by someone who doesn’t love you, are a verdict; spoken by someone who loves you, they are a rescue.

“For judgment is without mercy to him who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.” (James 2:13)

Brothers and sisters, remember: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and all we bring is pressure.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the message of this lesson can be distilled into two turnings.

When discipline turns from “punishment” to “restoration,” when our focus turns from “the mistake” to “the relationship” — life begins to be built up, and relationships begin to be restored.

God is not looking for perfect people; God is looking for people willing to turn back.

Brothers and sisters, please take that sentence home with you this morning. You don’t have to become a perfect person before you dare to come to God. God is walking in the garden, calling your name: Where are you?

He doesn’t want to condemn you; he wants to bring you back.

And when we ourselves have been found like this, restored like this, our hands become different. We begin to treat others the way God has treated us.

We no longer rush to correct; we learn first to crouch down and ask: Are you all right?

We no longer say, “Fix it yourself”; we learn to say, “I’ll walk with you as you change.”

We no longer push people away; we learn to be like that father who, while his son was still far off, ran to him (Luke 15:20).

When we live out this order, we are not only renewed ourselves; we can also become a blessing in other people’s lives.

This is the life of God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, let Jesus be King in your family, let Jesus be King in your church, let Jesus be King in every moment when you face a mistake.

May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: “For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you endure. God deals with you as with children, for what son is there whom his father doesn’t discipline?” (Hebrews 12:6–7)
“Yahweh God called to the man, and said to him, ‘Where are you?’” (Genesis 3:9)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I declare:
I will no longer deal with mistakes the human way; I will look at people with your heart.
I choose relationships over things; I choose to bring about change through love.
I am also willing to accept your discipline humbly, and to let my life be renewed and shaped by you.
I will be someone who restores people and brings forth life!
practices: See mistakes with “relationship first”
Cultivate the attitude of “I’ll walk with you as you change”
Practise humbly accepting God’s discipline
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father,

Thank you that on the day humanity first sinned, you did not first ask, “What have you done?” You first asked, “Where are you?” Thank you that your discipline has never been meant to knock us down, but to bring us back into your embrace.
Lord, I confess that I often put the task above the person. I rush to solve the problem and forget to see the heart of the person in front of me. Please forgive me, and change the order in my heart.

Give me the Heavenly Father’s heart. When others fall, let me not stand up high passing judgment, but come down and restore them in a spirit of gentleness. Teach me to say these words: I’ll walk with you as you change; I won’t give up on you.

Lord, I am also willing to accept your discipline humbly. When you shine your light on me, give me the courage not to run and not to rationalise, but simply to say: Lord, I am willing to be changed by you.
Reign as King in my life, and may all the glory be yours.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back to a time when someone corrected you and you felt hurt, and then to a time when someone corrected you and you felt loved. What was the difference between the two? Compare Ezekiel 34:4: “You haven’t strengthened the diseased. You haven’t healed that which was sick. You haven’t bound up that which was broken. You haven’t brought back that which was driven away. You haven’t sought that which was lost, but you have ruled over them with force and with rigor.” Which kind of shepherd are you more often?

Is there someone right now whom you have already wanted to give up on in your heart? Read Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” This week, what concrete action will you take to tell him, “I’ll walk with you as you change”?
