sections.heading: Introduction: The Stone Held in Your Hand
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like you to do something first: hold out your hand and look at it — what are you holding in your hand right now?

There is an early-morning story in the Bible. John 8 opens by saying: “Now very early in the morning, he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him. He sat down and taught them.” (John 8:2) That very morning a crowd dragged a woman caught in adultery into the temple courts, pushed her into the middle and made everyone look at her shame.

At that moment two things were present in the temple courts at once: a person who had fallen, and stones all over the ground. And every single person had to make a choice — when they bent down, was it to pick up a stone, or to write?

Brothers and sisters, that scene has never disappeared in two thousand years; it has just changed location: the church corridor, the small-group chat, the family dinner table, and those trials, one after another, that we hold in our hearts and never voice.

When a co-worker fails, when a brother’s marriage runs into trouble, when a sister’s child goes astray — what is our first reaction?

The lesson puts it with great precision: when someone falls, what best reveals the true state of our lives is not what we say, but “how we respond.”

Because words can be dressed up; reactions can’t. Words are thought through before they’re spoken; reactions flow straight out from within. The Lord Jesus said: “For out of the abundance of the heart, the mouth speaks.” (Matthew 12:34) Whatever a person is carrying inside comes out in its true colours the instant someone else falls.

So today there is only one question:

Throw a stone, or throw a rope? Condemn, or restore?

Brothers and sisters, notice that this is not just a matter of attitude, still less a matter of good manners. It is a matter of “priority.”

This is the fourth lesson on “rectifying the priority.” In the earlier lessons we learned: life first, then relationships, then ministry; first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today we put that order to the test in the hardest situation of all — when someone falls.

When the order is wrong, we put the “matter” in front of the “person,” and so we deal with the sin but lose the person.

When the order is right, we put the “person” in front of the “matter,” and so we restore the person and deal with the sin as well.

Brothers and sisters, a stone and a rope weigh about the same, and both are held in the same hand. The only difference is this: do you want him to go down, or do you want to pull him up?

Today God wants to teach us one thing — how to face a person who has fallen with God’s heart.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, One Father’s Heart
sections.html:
Before we come to the three key points, let’s get clear on the background of our theme passages. Cut off from its background, a passage easily becomes a stone in our hands; put back into its background, it becomes a rope.

First, Galatians.

Galatians was written by the apostle Paul, and it is the most fiery in tone of all his letters. If its recipients were the churches of south Galatia — the places Paul founded on his first missionary journey, Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — it may have been written as early as AD 48 or 49, making it one of Paul’s earliest letters.

Why did Paul write with such urgency? Because a group of people had come into the Galatian churches teaching the Gentile believers that they had to be circumcised and keep the law to be saved. Paul says: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). The whole of Galatians fights for one thing: we are saved by grace, through faith, not by works.

Only once we understand this background are we struck by the turn in chapter 6: Paul spends five chapters firing on all cylinders against legalism, yet at the very start of chapter 6 he sets up another kind of law — “the law of Christ.”

He says: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” (Galatians 6:1–2)

In other words: a church that truly understands grace will always be a church that knows how to restore people. If you don’t know how to restore people, it proves you haven’t really understood grace yet.

More important still is the context. Just before Galatians 6:1 come 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.”

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? “Gentleness” is one of the nine graces of the fruit the Holy Spirit bears. When Paul says “restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness,” he means that restoring a fallen person does not depend on technique; it depends on fruit. Only the life the Holy Spirit grows in you has what it takes to lift up a person who has fallen.

And 5:26 is even more direct: “Let’s not become conceited, provoking one another, and envying one another.” Being “conceited” is exactly the self-centred life; it is pride. Paul is saying: if you are still chasing empty glory, what you hold in your hand will certainly be a stone, never a rope.

Now look at Romans.

Paul wrote Romans to the church in Rome from Corinth, around AD 56–57. It is his most complete and most systematic account of the gospel. Romans 5:8 stands at a crucial point: Paul has just proved in chapters 1 to 3 that “There is no one righteous; no, not one” (Romans 3:10), and in chapter 4 has shown that Abraham was justified by faith; then in 5:8 he raises God’s love to its highest point:

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”

“Commends” in Greek is συνίστημι (sunistēmi), meaning “to place side by side, to prove, to establish.” God does not just tell us in words that he loves us; he places the cross right beside our sin, sets the two side by side, to prove his love.

Brothers and sisters, remember the timing — “while we were yet sinners.” Not after we repented, not after we cleaned up our act, but when we were at our least lovable, when we most deserved to be stoned.

This is the foundation of today’s whole lesson. God’s order toward us is: love first, change after. If our order toward others is: change first, acceptance after — then we have turned the gospel upside down.

sections.heading: 1. God’s Heart: Hating Sin, Yet Loving the Sinner
sections.html:
1. God is clear about sin, and even clearer about people

Brothers and sisters, we first need to get one thing clear: God hates sin, and the Bible is never vague about that.

“You who have purer eyes than to see evil, and who cannot look on perversity, why do you tolerate those who deal treacherously” (Habakkuk 1:13). God’s holiness does not tolerate sin; that is not up for negotiation.

But God’s attitude toward “people” is even clearer.

“But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)

“He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” (Psalm 103:10)

Psalm 103 is a psalm of David. Its greatness lies in the fact that David was not a man who had never fallen. He committed adultery, he committed murder, he counted the people. It was exactly such a man who wrote these words. And in the same psalm he explains why:

“Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him. For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:13–14)

“He remembers that we are dust” — God has never overestimated us. So God is never shocked by our failures either. The people who are shocked into fury by someone else’s failure are usually the ones who have overestimated themselves.

2. The order of the gospel: love first, change after

This is the heart of the gospel, and the most crucial order in today’s lesson:

God does not first demand that you change before he loves you; God loved you already, while you were still weak.

In Romans 2:4 Paul asks a stunning question: “Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, forbearance, and patience, not knowing that the goodness of God leads you to repentance?”

Notice the cause and effect: it isn’t “repentance brings goodness,” but “goodness leads people to repentance.”

Brothers and sisters, if this verse really got inside us, it would completely overturn the way we treat people. We tend to think: first he has to know how badly he’s gone wrong, and then he’ll change. God’s way is: first he has to know how deeply he is loved, and only then can he change.

A stone can knock a person down, but it has never once changed a person.

3. “Restore” in the original: the hands that mend nets

That is exactly why Paul gives the spiritual a command:

“Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” (Galatians 6:1)

This verse has three key terms, and each deserves a close look.

The first is “caught in some fault.” The original is προλαμβάνω (prolambanō), meaning “to be seized before one can act,” “to be caught off guard.” Paul is not describing someone who sets out to do evil, but someone ambushed by sin, knocked down before he had time to react — like walking down the street and suddenly being tackled from behind. Brothers and sisters, any one of us could be the one who gets tackled.

The second is “restore.” The original is καταρτίζω (katartizō), meaning “to repair, to put in order, to make complete.” The word appears in Matthew 4:21: “Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets. He called them.” — “mending” is this very word. Commentators also point out that in the medical usage of classical Greek this word meant setting a dislocated bone back in place.

What a beautiful picture. Restoring someone who has fallen is like a fisherman mending his net — patiently, mesh by mesh, closing up the tear so the net can fish again; and it is like a doctor setting a bone — it hurts, but the aim is not punishment; it is putting things back in place.

Japan has an ancient craft called kintsugi, which repairs broken pottery with lacquer and gold powder. The craftsman doesn’t hide the cracks; instead he traces them with lines of gold, and the vessel ends up worth more than before it broke. God is that kind of craftsman: with the precious blood of his Son he traces our cracks into a testimony.

Orthopaedic medicine also tells us that when a fracture is correctly set and immobilised, then once the callus has formed and the bone has remodelled, the healed site can regain its original strength. A brother who has been well restored is often sturdier than someone who has never fallen, because he has truly come to know grace.

The third term is “gentleness.” The original is πραΰτης (prautēs) — not weakness, but “strength under control,” having power without abusing it. This is exactly one of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). When a wild horse is broken in, its strength is not reduced; that strength is simply under the rein from then on. Spiritual people are not people with no ability to point out others’ faults; their ability has been brought under the Holy Spirit’s rein.

4. That phrase, “looking to yourself”

Paul adds a phrase we most easily skip over: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”

Brothers and sisters, this phrase is a mirror. It reminds us: the person you’re lifting up today could be you tomorrow.

Psychology has a well-known phenomenon that the social psychologist Lee Ross named in 1977 the “fundamental attribution error”: when we explain “other people’s” failures, we tend to blame their character — he’s just that kind of person; when we explain “our own” failures, we tend to blame the situation — I was really exhausted that day.

The same event, two measuring sticks. This is exactly what the Lord Jesus said: “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but don’t consider the beam that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)

The obedience-to-authority experiment that the Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram published in 1963 reminds us further that, in certain situations and under the pressure of authority, many ordinary, decent people will do things they once thought they would never do. Don’t be too quick to believe, “I would never do that.”

Paul goes on in the same chapter: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” (Galatians 6:3)

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the self-centred life. The self-centred person stands on the ruins of someone else and feels like a mountain. He doesn’t realise that what’s under his feet is the very same ground.

5. A 321 Insight: only selflessness can love; the self-centred life is quick to condemn

The lesson gives us an exceedingly bright light:

Only selflessness can love people; the self-centred life is quick to condemn.

When a person is full of himself, he passes judgment; when a person is full of Christ, he shows mercy.

Why is the self-centred person especially fond of condemning? Because condemning is the quickest, least effortful way to raise yourself up. I don’t need to become better; I only need to prove that you’re worse, and I look better by comparison. The instant the stone leaves his hand, the thrower has an illusion that he is standing on high ground.

But it is an illusion. That early morning, the Lord Jesus said to the crowd holding stones: “He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone at her.” (John 8:7)

Why did those words cut so deep? Because under the law of Deuteronomy 17:7: “The hands of the witnesses shall be first on him to put him to death, and afterward the hands of all the people.” The Lord Jesus did not abolish the law; he simply handed the law’s first stone back into the accusers’ hands.

And the result? “They, when they heard it, being convicted by their conscience, went out one by one, beginning from the oldest, even to the last. Jesus was left alone with the woman where she was, in the middle.” (John 8:9)

Beginning from the oldest. The oldest left first — because the longer you’ve lived, the better you know your own hands aren’t clean.

Then the Lord Jesus said two things that are precisely the perfect order of grace and truth: “Neither do I condemn you. Go your way. From now on, sin no more.” (John 8:11)

First, “Neither do I condemn you” — this is love, this is acceptance, this is the rope.

Then, “From now on, sin no more” — this is truth, this is the demand of holiness.

The order cannot be reversed. Had he said “sin no more” first, she would never have taken it in, because she was still on the ground, crushed under humiliation. Lift her up first, and only then does she have the strength to walk out.

“The Word became flesh, and lived among us. We saw his glory, such glory as of the one and only Son of the Father, full of grace and truth.” (John 1:14) Brothers and sisters, it is “full of grace and truth,” not one or the other. Grace without truth is indulgence; truth without grace is a stone. The Lord Jesus is full of both.

So it should be with God’s people too: don’t strike people with stones; restore them with gentleness.

sections.heading: 2. Discernment: The Weak and the Wicked
sections.html:
1. God’s love is perfect; God’s principles are clear

Brothers and sisters, if we preached only the first point, we would swing to the other extreme — dealing with nothing, saying “God loves you” about everything, until the church becomes a place with no boundaries, where sin walks around freely and the wounded sheep have no one to protect them.

So the lesson goes on to give us a second key: discernment.

“Yahweh upholds the humble. He brings the wicked down to the ground.” (Psalm 147:6)

The same God, two responses. Not that God’s love is bigger or smaller, but that human hearts are soft or hard.

“Upholds” in Hebrew is עוֹדֵד (ʿôdēd), meaning “to make to stand, to lift up, to strengthen.” God stoops down and lifts up the one who has fallen. And the same God who stoops to lift people up will also bring down to the ground the one who stays hard to the end.

The Bible shows us two utterly different kinds of people.

2. The first kind: the weak

The weak have three marks: they fall; but they are willing to repent; and in their hearts they still fear God.

“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

“Confess” here is ὁμολογέω (homologeō) in Greek, made up of “same” and “speak” — literally, “to say the same thing.” Confession is not muttering to yourself “I’m no good”; it is saying “Amen” to God’s verdict — God says this is sin, and I say this is sin, and I no longer defend it.

Notice the astonishing wording of this verse: God forgives us because he is “faithful,” and also because he is “righteous.” Why is forgiveness righteous? Because sin has already been punished on the cross. God hasn’t simply written the debt off; God has paid the bill in full.

The classic example of the weak is Peter. He denied the Lord three times — an utter failure — but the Bible records one detail: “The Lord turned and looked at Peter. Then Peter remembered the Lord’s word, how he said to him, ‘Before the rooster crows you will deny me three times.’ He went out, and wept bitterly.” (Luke 22:61–62)

One look from the Lord, and he wept bitterly. That look was the rope.

David too. He committed a great sin, but when the prophet Nathan pointed it out, he said at once: “I have sinned against Yahweh.” (2 Samuel 12:13) He wrote: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (Psalm 51:17)

“For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16) Brothers and sisters, look closely: the Bible doesn’t say the righteous never fall; it says the righteous fall and “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked is not whether they fall, but whether they get up.

To people like this, God’s response is: uphold, forgive, restore.

3. The second kind: the wicked

The wicked also have three marks: no fear of God in their hearts; they keep on harming people; and they are unwilling to repent.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

James is quoting Proverbs 3:34: “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.”

“Resists” in Greek is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against.” Brothers and sisters, what a solemn picture: God himself drawing up his battle lines, standing opposite the proud.

The classic example of the wicked is Saul. Saul “confessed” too, but look at what his confession said: “I have sinned; yet please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel.” (1 Samuel 15:30) He confessed his sin, but cared about his face; what he wanted was not God’s forgiveness but people’s esteem. That is the self-centred life — even confession becomes a way to protect the self.

Judas too. He was filled with remorse, and he even said the right words: “I have sinned in that I betrayed innocent blood.” (Matthew 27:4) But the end was, “He went away and hanged himself” (Matthew 27:5).

Peter and Judas both failed, and both were filled with regret. Where was the difference?

Paul says it all in one sentence: “For godly sorrow produces repentance to salvation, which brings no regret. But the sorrow of the world produces death.” (2 Corinthians 7:10)

Godly sorrow — its focus is on God; it brings a turning back, leading to salvation.

The sorrow of the world — its focus is on the self; it brings despair, and produces death.

Psychological research happens to confirm this spiritual principle from another angle. The American psychologists June Tangney and Ronda Dearing, in their 2002 book Shame and Guilt, drew on long research distinguishing two emotions: “guilt” focuses on behaviour — “I did a bad thing” — and moves people to apologise, make amends and repair relationships; “shame” focuses on the self — “I am a bad person” — and instead makes people withdraw, hide, get defensive, and even lash out in anger at others.

Brothers and sisters, do you see now how dangerous that stone in our hand is? What a stone produces is shame, not repentance. And shame never brings anyone to the cross; it only drives them into deeper darkness.

What a rope produces is hope, and only hope has the strength to repent.

To those who stay hard to the end, God’s response is: resist, deal with, cut off.

But please be sure to remember: even when he deals with them, God’s heart does not change — “ ‘As I live,’ says the Lord Yahweh, ‘I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live.’ ” (Ezekiel 33:11)

God resists the proud not because he hates them, but because pride will kill them. God stands in their way to keep them from charging straight over the cliff.

4. A key: don’t treat everyone the same way

Here the lesson reminds us of something very important: don’t treat everyone the same way; follow the Holy Spirit and respond with wisdom.

This is not our invention; it is the plain teaching of the Bible.

“On some have compassion, making a distinction, and some save, snatching them out of the fire with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.” (Jude 22–23)

The Chinese Union Version reads these verses as three kinds of people with three approaches: on those who doubt, have mercy; those about to be burned, snatch out of the fire with all your strength; those already deep in lust, show mercy but stay on guard at the same time, lest you be stained yourself. That is spiritual discernment — love is not a formula; love is insight.

Paul says to Titus: “Avoid a factious man after a first and second warning” (Titus 3:10) — notice, it is after “a first and second warning,” not rejection the first time. God’s discipline always follows a process, and always gives a chance first.

And in 2 Thessalonians 3:15 Paul immediately adds: “Don’t count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.”

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the guardrail for all church discipline. Whatever stage things have reached, in our hearts the other person is never an enemy, but a brother.

5. A 321 Insight: humility receives grace; pride is resisted

The lesson’s second light is: humility receives grace; pride is resisted.

The core message of 321 puts it precisely: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: when we pick up a stone to strike someone, which seat are we sitting in? We’ve sat down on the judgment seat. And that seat, the Bible says, only One is qualified to occupy.

“Who are you who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls. Yes, he will be made to stand, for God has power to make him stand.” (Romans 14:4)

Judging is leaving our originally intended position; discerning is returning to it.

Judging says, “I’ll decide his fate on God’s behalf”; discerning says, “I ask God to let me see, so I know how to love him right now.”

Judging uses my standards, my emotions, my past experience; discerning uses the standard of the Bible, the guidance of the Holy Spirit and the role model of Jesus — exactly the Three Foundations of 321.

Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. Throw one stone, and the other person is sure to throw one back. And so the church becomes a quarry where everyone is wounded, everyone cries injustice, and not one person is restored.

Brothers and sisters, the discernment we’re learning this morning is not for sticking labels on people, but for knowing: this time, what should I hand out?

sections.heading: 3. Build the Relationship, but Don’t Indulge the Sin
sections.html:
1. The order the Lord Jesus himself set

Brothers and sisters, the third key point is a procedure the Lord Jesus laid down himself.

“If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” (Matthew 18:15)

Notice the Lord Jesus’ words: “you have gained back your brother.” Not “you have won the argument,” not “you have proved you were right,” but “you have gained back your brother.”

On the scoreboard of the kingdom of heaven there is only one way to score: a person is won.

The Lord Jesus goes on: “But if he doesn’t listen, take one or two more with you, that at the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. If he refuses to listen to them, tell it to the assembly. If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” (Matthew 18:16–17)

This is a clear three-step path:

Step one, restore him privately first — relationship comes first.

Step two, then take one or two others along — testimony is established.

Step three, finally bring it to the church — spiritual authority.

Brothers and sisters, I want you to pay special attention to step one. The Lord Jesus said, “between you and him alone.”

The mistake we make most often today is skipping step one and jumping straight to step three — or even to a “step four”: telling everyone who has nothing to do with it. We pass it on in the group chat, we “name it for prayer” at the prayer meeting, we’re “just sharing” over dinner. Brothers and sisters, that is not step one; that is throwing stones, only with a label on the stone that says “concern.”

The Lord Jesus’ order always keeps the number of people who know about the wound as small as possible, and the chance of restoration as large as possible.

2. The context is the real key

Matthew 18:15–17 is often used as the rulebook for church discipline, but cut off from its context it becomes a knife.

Look at what comes before it. Matthew 18:12–14 is the parable of the lost sheep: “What do you think? If a man has one hundred sheep, and one of them goes astray, doesn’t he leave the ninety-nine, go to the mountains, and seek that which has gone astray?” (Matthew 18:12) And the conclusion: “Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” (Matthew 18:14)

Now look at what comes after it. In Matthew 18:21–22 Peter asks the Lord how many times he should forgive his brother — up to seven times? “Jesus said to him, ‘I don’t tell you until seven times, but, until seventy times seven.’ ” (Matthew 18:22) And straight after that comes the parable of the unforgiving servant.

Brothers and sisters, see the order clearly: before it, God leaving the ninety-nine to look for the one; in the middle, the procedure for restoring a brother; after it, forgiving seventy times seven. The discipline of Matthew 18 is sandwiched between “seeking” and “forgiving.” Anyone unwilling to leave the ninety-nine to look for the one has no business carrying out 18:15; anyone unwilling to forgive seventy times seven has no business carrying out 18:17.

3. True love is not indulgence

But what if the other person never repents, all the way to the end?

The Lord Jesus said: “If he refuses to hear the assembly also, let him be to you as a Gentile or a tax collector.” (Matthew 18:17)

In 1 Corinthians Paul dealt with an extremely serious case. A man in the Corinthian church had taken his father’s wife, and the church not only failed to deal with it but was “arrogant” (1 Corinthians 5:2). Paul says they “are to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” (1 Corinthians 5:5)

Brothers and sisters, please read the last clause of that verse three times: “that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”

Even the severest discipline still has “salvation” as its aim.

And the story has a second half. In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8 Paul says: “This punishment which was inflicted by the many is sufficient for such a one; so that on the contrary you should rather forgive him and comfort him, lest by any means such a one should be swallowed up with his excessive sorrow. Therefore I beg you to confirm your love toward him.”

Do you see it? The end point of discipline is not throwing someone out, but welcoming them back. Paul was even worried that too much punishment would make him be “swallowed up.” That is a father’s heart.

“For whom the Lord loves, he disciplines, and chastises every son whom he receives.” (Hebrews 12:6) “All chastening seems for the present to be not joyous but grievous; yet afterward it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.” (Hebrews 12:11)

The goal of discipline is “the peaceful fruit of righteousness,” not letting off steam.

Brothers and sisters, remember the lesson’s two sentences: true love is not indulgence; true love is for rescuing.

Paul says that love “doesn’t rejoice in unrighteousness, but rejoices with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13:6). Love and truth have never been enemies; they are the two hands of the same Lord.

“The wounds of a friend are faithful, although the kisses of an enemy are profuse.” (Proverbs 27:6) A true friend dares to say what you don’t want to hear; a false friend only says what is comfortable to hear.

“But speaking truth in love, we may grow up in all things into him who is the head, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15). Love and truth-telling have to appear in the same sentence before they bring growth.

Love without truth-telling is staying down in the pit chatting with him.

Truth-telling without love is standing at the edge of the pit throwing stones at him.

Love plus truth-telling is letting the rope down, then planting your own feet firmly and pulling him up, bit by bit.

4. Examples from daily life: scaffolding and the throw rope

When the outer wall of a building is peeling, there are two ways to deal with it. One is to take photos, post them, tag them, and let everyone know how run-down the building is; the other is to put up scaffolding and repair the wall panel by panel. The first is called a commentator; the second is called a worker — the church has no shortage of commentators; the church is short of workers.

In swift-water rescue training there is a basic piece of equipment called a “throw bag.” When someone falls into the water, the most important principle is: the rescuer must not rashly jump in, but first get firm footing, and then throw out the rope.

That is the practical version of Galatians 6:1: “looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.”

Brothers and sisters, if you want to save someone, you must first stand firm. Your devotional life, your relationship with God, your own repentance — that is the rock under your feet. Jump in before your feet are firm, and the result is often that both of you get swept away.

The psychologist John Gottman, who studied couples’ interactions for many years at the University of Washington, identified four patterns that destroy relationships, and the most damaging of them, the one that most strongly predicts a relationship breaking down, is “contempt” — belittling someone from a position of superiority.

Contempt is a look down from on high. It may never be spoken, but the person being looked at always feels it. And contempt is the most typical expression on the face of the self-centred life.

Can we point out someone’s sin without a trace of contempt? We can — so long as we truly remember who pulled us out, and from where.

5. A 321 Insight: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles

The lesson’s third light is: putting relationships first does not mean having no principles; loving people does not mean approving of sin.

When the order is right, two results follow: we build people up with love, and we protect the community with truth.

Notice that these two things must happen at the same time.

Build up the individual without protecting the community — and the wounded sheep will leave, because the church isn’t safe.

Protect the community without building up the individual — and the fallen sheep will be lost, because the church has no grace.

321 says: there is one Goal, and that is to establish God’s system.

What is God’s system? God’s system is a place where a person who has fallen still dares to come back, and at the same time a place where sin cannot stay.

Does that sound contradictory? Not at all. Because in God’s system, what makes it impossible for sin to stay is not our criticism but the presence of Jesus. We don’t need stones to drive sin away; we only need to let Jesus reign as King in this community, and sin will not be able to stay.

Brothers and sisters, this is the order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Let life be restored first, then let relationships be built, and ministry will grow up naturally after. If we turn it the other way round — sacrificing relationships to protect the ministry, neglecting life to keep up relationships — we will lose both the people and the presence of God.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change from Stone to Rope
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s take what we’ve learned today and look at it once more within the framework of 321.

1. The Three Foundations: on what basis do I lift people up?

Jesus is my role model — that early morning, the Lord Jesus didn’t pick up a stone; he stooped down and wrote on the ground. He was the only one qualified to throw the first stone, and the only one who didn’t.

The Bible is my standard — the way I lift people up doesn’t follow my temperament or my mood, but the order of Matthew 18, the gentleness of Galatians 6 and the discernment of Jude.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — discerning who is weak and who is hardened is beyond my ability. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,” says Yahweh of Armies. (Zechariah 4:6)

2. The Two Core Values: who is sitting in that seat?

Let Jesus be King — when I pick up a stone, I am the king in that moment, deciding someone’s life or death. When I put down the stone and pick up a rope, I hand the throne back to Jesus. Brothers and sisters, judging is, at its core, usurping the throne.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when a fallen person is restored, who gets the glory? Not me, the one who “handled the matter so wisely,” but the Shepherd who left the ninety-nine to look for the one. If, in the course of restoring someone, I’m secretly enjoying my own nobility, what I hold in my hand is still a stone, wrapped in the outer skin of a rope.

3. The Goal: establish God’s system

Satan is building a system too, and his three steps are: make people fall, make people condemn, make people isolate one another. God’s system also has three steps: uphold, restore, build relationships.

Every time someone falls, it is the moment when the two systems meet face to face. The stone or the rope in our hand decides which side we are standing on.

4. The self-centred life and selflessness

Galatians 6:3 says: “For if a man thinks himself to be something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” This is the most precise definition of the self-centred life — treating what we don’t have as though we had it, treating what was grace as our own achievement.

When the self-centred person sees someone fall, his first reaction is comparison; when the selfless person sees someone fall, his first reaction is mercy.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. When Christ lives in me, the way I see people is no longer my way of seeing, but the way of the One who prayed for his enemies on Calvary.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan’s name in Hebrew means “adversary, accuser,” and the Greek word for “devil,” διάβολος, originally means “slanderer, one who maligns.” Revelation 12:10 calls him the one “who accuses them before our God day and night.”

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: when we condemn a brother, we are doing Satan’s work, just using church language.

5. The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry

Today’s lesson is a complete fivefold change.

Change of mindset — from “the fallen person should be dealt with” to “the fallen person should be restored.”

Change of life — once the mindset changes, the “self” inside that loves to condemn is dealt with by the cross.

Change of daily living — no more passing things on in the group chat, no more commentary over dinner, praying for that person late at night.

Change of relationships — a relationship that was about to snap is joined up again by a rope.

Change of ministry — those who have been restored are, in time, the very best at restoring others. The Lord said to Peter: “You, when once you have turned again, establish your brothers.” (Luke 22:32)

6. A change of perspective

From the human point of view to God’s point of view — people see “what he has done”; God sees “what he is going to become.”

From the earthly to the heavenly — seen from earth, this is a disgrace; seen from heaven, “there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

From the temporary to the eternal — today’s embarrassment is temporary; a soul is eternal.

From the worldly to the godly — the worldly way is to weed out the failures; the godly way is to mend the torn net.

7. The 920 practice and the 235 relationships

The 920 practice is to treat everyone we are in a relationship with as our “2,” practising living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

Look at those nine graces in Galatians 5:22–23, then look back at the “gentleness” in 6:1. Restoring a fallen person calls on almost all nine: accepting with love, sustaining with joy, defusing with peace, waiting with patience, softening with kindness, paying the price with goodness, persevering with faithfulness, speaking with gentleness, and holding our own tongues with self-control. So lifting a person up turns out to be the final inspection of all nine graces.

The 235 relationships are what the lesson’s “building relationships” concretely looks like. A person who has been restored doesn’t need a single conversation; he needs a “2” — a spiritual companion to walk with him; a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, someone ahead leading him and someone behind following him; and in the end, to enter the “5” — becoming comrades in a fivefold-ministry team.

That is why the lesson says “build relationships”: a rope can save someone once; only a team can save a whole life.

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll use the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep into our lives.

Practice 1: Throw a rope, not a stone

When you see someone fall, don’t rush to criticise, judge or condemn; instead ask yourself two questions: How can I help him stand up? How can I become his support? Become his rope through encouragement, companionship and prayer.

Information — the “restore” of Galatians 6:1 is mending nets and setting bones; Romans 5:8 says God loved us while we were still sinners.

Revelation — ask the Holy Spirit to show you a specific face. Whose name comes to mind right now? That is the person God wants you to lift up today.

Conviction — not “this is the more loving thing to do,” but “if I don’t do this, I am going against the gospel.”

Implementation — this week do three small things: don’t pass on a single word about him; pray for him specifically three times; reach out to him once, without mentioning what happened, just asking how he is.

Evaluation — at the weekend, get quiet and ask: this week, was I restoring, or collecting evidence?

Correction — if you find you’ve already thrown a stone, go and apologise. “If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.” (Matthew 5:23–24)

Repetition — this isn’t a one-off good deed; it’s a new reflex, and reflexes are only trained through repetition.

Multiplication — take someone along with you. When you walk with a brother until he learns to throw a rope, one rope becomes two.

Practice 2: Train your spiritual discernment

Faced with different people, learn to discern: is he weak, or hardened? Is he willing to repent, or does he keep resisting? Don’t treat everyone the same way; follow the Holy Spirit and respond with wisdom.

Information — Jude 22–23: three kinds of people, three approaches; 2 Corinthians 7:10: two kinds of sorrow; the contrast between Peter and Judas.

Revelation — discernment isn’t something you analyse your way to; you pray your way to it. That is exactly what Solomon asked for: “Give your servant therefore an understanding heart to judge your people, that I may discern between good and evil” (1 Kings 3:9).

Conviction — I admit that my first instinct is often wrong; I will no longer draw conclusions from impressions or hearsay.

Implementation — when you run into a problem with someone, pray before you open your mouth, wait at least one night, and ask three questions: Does he fear God? Is he willing to face it? Is he continuing to hurt others?

Evaluation and Correction — look back on a time your judgment was off: what was I judging with — my emotions, my face, or the Holy Spirit? If you once treated a weak person as wicked, go and restore the relationship; if you once indulged a hardened person as though he were merely weak, add the missing step of truth.

Repetition and Multiplication — in time this becomes spiritual eyesight; and take this discernment into your small group, so the group gets used to asking first, “Is he weak or hardened?” rather than “Does he deserve a telling-off?”

Practice 3: Centre every choice on building relationships

In your daily See, Listen, Think, Speak, Do, ask yourself: is this response building the relationship, or damaging it? Choose the actions that bring unity, restoration and connection.

See — when I look at someone, do I see his offences, or his worth?

Listen — when I hear about someone’s weakness, do I take it in and pray, or pass it on?

Think — what am I rehearsing in my mind: how to help him, or how to beat him?

Speak — is the sentence I’m about to say a rope or a stone?

Do — will what I’m about to do today bring the relationship closer, or push it further away?

Information — “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23) Seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing all flow out of the heart; guard the heart, and you have guarded all five outlets.

Revelation and Conviction — relationships matter more than right and wrong; people matter more than things. I am convinced of this order.

Implementation and Evaluation — each evening take three minutes to run through the five outlets: today, whom did I draw closer? Whom did I push further away?

Correction — deal with it the same day; don’t let it sit overnight. “Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath” (Ephesians 4:26).

Repetition and Multiplication — keep it up for thirty days without a break, until it becomes a habit; and in your small group ask one another: “This week, who did you throw a rope to?”

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Two Systems, Two Kinds of Work
sections.html:
At the end the lesson gives us a vitally important reminder.

Satan’s work is: making people fall, making people condemn, making people isolate one another.

These three steps are a production line: Satan first tempts a person to fall, then turns around and accuses him, and finally gets that person isolated. Because a sheep on its own is the easiest to devour. “Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” (1 Peter 5:8)

And God’s work is: upholding, restoring, building relationships.

“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

So don’t be someone who throws stones; be someone who throws ropes.

The lesson’s last two sentences are worth memorising:

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and life comes forth; rely on the brain and ourselves, and judgment comes.

Why? Because the “brain” only calculates: how many times he’s got it wrong, how much he owes me, whether doing this is worth it for me. But the “heart” sees: this is a created soul, bought back by the Lord with his precious blood.

Rely on the heart and you’ll be glad; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Brothers and sisters, when we judge people, there is actually no joy in it at all; when we lift someone up, an inexpressible joy wells up inside instead. That is not a psychological effect; it is the Holy Spirit’s confirmation.

sections.heading: 7. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s read the lesson’s conclusion once more.

When we face people with God’s heart, three things happen: the weak are upheld, the hardened are awakened, and the community is protected.

Relationships are built, lives are restored, and the church moves toward true revival.

Notice: revival doesn’t start with a special conference; it starts with a rope.

James 5:19–20 says: “Brothers, if any among you wanders from the truth and someone turns him back, let him know that he who turns a sinner from the error of his way will save a soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.”

“Will save a soul from death” — there is no greater ministry in this world than that.

Back to that early morning. When the crowd had all gone out one by one, beginning from the oldest, what was left on the temple floor? Stones that had never been thrown, all over the ground. And the woman was still standing.

Brothers and sisters, may the day come when the floors of our churches, our homes and our small groups are also covered with stones that were never thrown, because everyone chose to put them down.

From today, make a choice: no more stones, only ropes.

This is the life of those who belong to God.

Let Jesus reign as King in our responses, and let Jesus receive all the glory in every soul that is restored.

keyVerses: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ. (Galatians 6:1–2)
But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. (Romans 5:8)
declarations: Lord Jesus, I declare: I will look at people with your heart, no longer judging, no longer condemning.
I will be someone who throws ropes, helping others stand up when they fall.
Give me wisdom to discern, and love to restore.
Let me live out the priority of relationships, and become someone who brings restoration and unity.
practices: Throw a rope, not a stone
Train your spiritual discernment
Centre every choice on building relationships
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, thank you. Thank you that while I was still a sinner, you died for me. Thank you that you have not dealt with me according to my sins, nor repaid me for my iniquities.
Lord, forgive me. I confess that my hand is often clutching a stone, and that I even wrap it up in spiritual language. Let your precious blood wash my judging heart clean.

Open my eyes to see the person who is falling right now; give me the wisdom to discern, to know when to uphold and when to warn; give me a gentle heart, so that every word I say becomes a rope; and let me first stand firm on your rock, so that I can throw the rope out.
May my home, my small group and my church become a place where a person who has fallen dares to come back; may sin be unable to stay here, because you reign as King here.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
Yahweh bless you, and keep you. Yahweh make his face to shine on you, and be gracious to you. Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace.
discussion: Galatians 6:1: “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.” Think back to the last time someone fell in front of you. What was your first reaction? Does that reaction show that the self-centred life or selflessness is at work inside you? This week, how will you concretely throw a rope to this person?

Matthew 18:15: “If your brother sins against you, go, show him his fault between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained back your brother.” In your experience, which step is most easily skipped? Why? Share a time when “restoring privately first” led to a good outcome, or a time when getting the order wrong caused harm.
